News.title: ChatGPT down as OpenAI confirms worldwide outage
News.content:
OpenAI's ChatGPT is currently down for thousands of users (file)

OpenAI said it was 'experiencing issues' with a number of services, including ChatGPT and Codex - with users around the globe struggling to log in and send messages

A global ChatGPT outage has left thousands of users struggling to use the AI app.

ChatGPT users said they were having trouble logging in, loading their chats and sending messages, with reports of problems coming in from the UK, US, India, Japan, and Australia.

OpenAI said it was "experiencing issues" with a number of services, including ChatGPT and Codex.

The company later said it had applied a fix and that some "services are recovering".

"We have applied the mitigation and are monitoring the recovery," a message on OpenAI's status page reads.

News.title: JENNIE BOND: 'Prince William and Kate's clever move in protecting George speaks volumes'
News.content:
JENNIE BOND: 'Prince William and Kate's clever move in protecting George speaks volumes'

EXCLUSIVE: Prince George's milestone 13th birthday was marked with a traditional picture and a carefree behind-the-scenes clip - but one small detail was missing

View 5 Images A portrait released for Prince George to mark his 13th birthday

Prince George’s teenage years have officially begun with his 13th birthday marked in two very different ways.

‌



In what has become tradition for his parents, the Prince and Princess of Wales, a new official portrait was released of the future King on his big day, showing him posing for the camera in a suit following Trooping the Colour last month.

‌



While hours later, William and Kate gave a glimpse at their eldest son’s relaxed side by sharing a short behind-the-scenes clip showing a casual George on holiday grinning in sunglasses, playing cricket on the beach and petting the family dog.

‌



Prince George flashes cheeky grin in behind-scenes video released for 13th birthday READ MORE :

View 5 Images Prince George with his father, Prince William (Image: Mike Egerton/PA Wire)

Both were posted on social media with sweet messages - but notable in the fact both referred to the heir to the throne simply as ‘George’, omitting his royal title. And in birthday posts for their other children, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis, they too were referenced by their first names only.

And while it might be a small detail, royal expert Jennie Bond believes it speaks volumes - especially when it comes to his father Prince William and his vision for a modern, more relaxed and less stuffy monarchy.

‌



The former BBC royal correspondent told the Mirror: “I love the fact that they refer to him – and their other children – simply by their Christian names, without the formality or pomposity of using their titles. It sets a new tone, a tone that William has spoken about: being royal with a small ‘r’.”

This year’s photo of George to mark his milestone birthday is a marked difference from last year’s, which showed him in country casuals in Norfolk.

5 View 5 Images Prince George sports sunglasses and sports a cheeky grin in a his 13th birthday video (Image: @KensingtonRoyal/x) 5 View 5 Images The behind-the-scenes video was shot on a recent family holiday (Image: @KensingtonRoyal/x)

‌



The new snap, showing him suited and booted, is also in contrast to snaps that have been released of Charlotte and Louis, which have also shown them in more relaxed settings.

And Jennie believes this slight shift for George could be for a particular reason. She explained: “For William and Catherine, it is a way of protecting their children, and it is working well. That’s partly because the pictures are clearly quite relaxed and informal.

“And this year we got a bit of both: the fun video of George on holiday with his siblings, and the much smarter one in his suit (happily without his tie!).

‌



“These pictures will be part of the history books, so I suppose it’s important to start seeing this lovely young boy as a future King. And seeing him in his suit helps mark his transition from child to teenager.”

George made his first public appearance at just a few hours old when he was cradled in his mum Kate’s arms on the steps of the private Lindo Wing of St Mary’s Hospital in Paddington, London.

View 5 Images George with mum, Kate, and his sister Princess Charlotte at Wimbledon (Image: Andrew Matthews/Pool PA via AP)

‌



No longer the tiny baby, the youngster is now as tall as his mum, with his 13th birthday coming at a pivotal time in his life. In September, he will follow in his father William’s footsteps by starting at the £63,000-a-year Eton College, where he is expected to board full-time.

It also comes as the young prince has been making more and more public appearances alongside his parents at the likes of Trooping the Colour - while last month he carried out his first official joint engagement with his mum as they visited the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight at RAF Coningsby.

But with his parents still determined to let all of their children have as normal a childhood as possible, more public duties at this stage seem unlikely.

‌



And for Jennie, this means the birthday photo tradition for George seems likely to continue into the future.

She added: “I suspect this tradition will continue because it’s part of a bargain whereby one or two excellent images are released to keep us all informed about how George is doing – and then he is left alone.

Article continues below

“Over the years, the photos have shown a young boy smiling and laughing, happy and confident - far better pictures than a bank of press photographers could have achieved. And so it has been a highly successful tactic.”

News.title: Slain Suzy Lamplugh's brother begs for answers to solve 40-year riddle over Britain's most haunting murder
News.content:
The brother of murdered Suzy Lamplugh today issued a last-ditch plea to solve the 40-year riddle, begging: "Please help bring my sister's body home."

Suzy, 25, vanished on July 28 1986 after going to meet a client known as "Mr Kipper" in Fulham, London. Her body was never found and in 1993 she was declared dead, presumed murder. In 2002 Scotland Yard detectives named killer John Cannan as the main suspect but the Crown Prosecution Service said there was insufficient evidence to charge him. He died in 2024 while serving a life sentence for murder.

Today, just days before the 40th anniversary of Suzy's disappearance, her brother Richard, 66, said the family had given up hope of securing justice. But he said he would still love to recover her body so the family could lay her to rest.

View 7 Images Her body has never been found (Image: PA)

‌



He told the Mirror: "I wish she would walk through the door now and say, 'Hello'. I might not even recognise her. But that's not going to happen. So if someone could help us find her body that would help bring some closure and we'd be able to lay her to rest."

He added: "As far as we concerned our number one priority would be to find Suzy's body, her skeleton. We want to bury her remains or scatter her ashes where we want to and not where her killer did. If anyone has any information then please let the police know and let them deal with it.

"I'm not going to go out hunting for the body because I just don't know where to look and we've had lots of people suggesting ideas and thoughts about what happened but it's come to nothing."

View 7 Images In 2018 detectives began a dig in the garage at the home of John Cannan's mum's home in Sutton Coldfield, West Midlands (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Cold-case homicide unit detectives have been carrying out a review of Operation Phoebus, the original investigation into Suzy. She vanished in the middle of a working Monday after apparently going to show a client around a house a few minutes' walk from her office in Fulham, south west London.

A note scribbled in her appointments diary read: "12.45 Mr Kipper, 37 Shorrolds Rd o/s outside". It could not be established when the arrangement to meet the mystery man was made or whether he had come into the office or telephoned.

Suzy left her office after 12.40pm and a woman fitting her description was seen at the Shorrolds Road house. Her company car, a white Ford Fiesta, was found by cops in Stevenage Road, a mile from the flat, at 10.01pm on the day she vanished.

View 7 Images Speaking to the Mirror, Richard said the family's priority was recovering her remains so they could be laid to rest (Image: NEWSLINE MEDIA LIMITED)

‌



It was badly parked, the handbrake was off and her purse was in the door pocket. Her seat was not in its usual position but pushed further back, suggesting Suzy may have been attacked in the car or was not the last person to drive it.

It was parked outside another flat being marketed by her estate agency and one theory was she had shown her killer around that property. The spot is close to the Thames, and police frogmen searched the river in the early days of the investigation.

But it later transpired the initial probe into Suzy's disappearance had been adequate and a review of the case was launched in 1999. Cannan - who died in prison last year as he served a life sentence for abducting newlywed Shirley Banks in Bristol in 1987 and bludgeoning her to death with a rock - was identified as the prime suspect but never charged.

View 7 Images In 2002 Scotland Yard detectives publicly named convicted rapist John Cannan as Suzy's killer but he died in 2024 in prison aged 70 (Image: SWNS)

‌



He always denied Suzy's murder and before his death told the Mirror he was being fitted up by cops. Richard, who lives with his wife of 15 years, Christine, 66, and their two daughters, 24 and 18, spoke of his 40 years of hell.

He said: "Cannan died and left no confession. That's extremely sad. I would love to see my sister back but I'm not going to. We never got answers from Cannan. These guys are evil, they play with the public and they want their names out there, they crave the notoriety. They are horrible people really and they're seeking infamy. But we need to move on and I feel we've done that as a family."

In 2024 Cannan wrote to the Mirror insisting he did not kill Suzy and accusing police of prejudice against him. He claimed to have an alibi for the day she vanished and said police had pointed the finger at him to "divert attention from themselves".

View 7 Images No trace of Suzy has ever been recovered despite a series of police reviews into her disappearance in 1986 (Image: Mirrorpix)

‌



Cannan said that on July 28, 1986, the day Suzy disappeared, he had been in Birmingham “treating my mother to a spot of lunch”. In 2018 police searching for Suzy conducted a dig at the former home of Cannan's mother in Sutton Coldfield, West Midlands. However the excavation drew a blank and the search for Suzy's body continues.

Richard today said it was heartbreaking that their mother, Diana, died in 2011 eight years after being diagnosed with Alzheimer's, and their retired solicitor father, Paul, died in 2018, without ever knowing what happened to Suzy. It has left Richard and his two sisters,Tamsin, 64, and Lizzie, 56, as the last remaining custodians of Suzy's legacy.

Richard said: "The saddest part is that my parents died not knowing what happened. We might do the same but it would be amazing for some answers."

View 7 Images John Cannan was given the nickname “Kipper” by people at a bail due to his fondness for the fish and a habit of having a “kip” (Image: PA)

‌



Today Richard paid tribute to the Suzy Lamplugh Trust set up in his sister's name to tackle stalking - but warned the threat facing women is as great today as it was in 1986 when his sister was murdered. He said social media is fuelling a hatred of women with big tech companies failing to tackle the problem.

Richard said: "The trust is really something to celebrate. They've got a good team they do a great job. I've said before, I've always thought my sister was groomed, or certainly stalked, and she probably wasn't aware of it. Stalking is so important and it's becoming a real problem, particularly online as well as in person. It's really sad and it's devastating for victims."

News.title: Spain holiday hotspots on 'red alert' as deadly West Nile virus detected
News.content:
Spain holiday hotspots on 'red alert' as deadly West Nile virus detected

Mosquitoes carrying deadly West Nile virus have been detected in the Spanish regions of Fuengirola and Mijas - both of which are visited by thousands of Brits each year

View 2 Images West Nile virus has been detected in Spain (Image: Councils)

Two popular Spanish holiday hotspots are on red alert after several people were struck down by the potentially deadly West Nile virus.

‌



Mosquitoes which carry the disease have been detected in Fuengirola and Mijas, both visited by thousands of Brits every year. Health chiefs say the insects were found in traps installed in both municipalities.

‌



The Andalucían government has declared alerts in the municipalities of Bollullos de la Mitación and Fuengirola, and around Las Lagunas in Mijas.

‌



The alerts will remain in place for a minimum of four weeks or until an equivalent period in which no cases of illness are declared or no trace of the virus is found.

Checks on insects, animals and humans are being stepped up, and warnings have been issued to the public through chemists and doctors. Health officials have reported the situation to the city councils of Coria, Bollullos de la Mitación, Fuengirola, Mijas and the provincial councils of Seville and Malaga

View 2 Images The virus can be deadly (Image: Councils)

‌



Mum who spent life savings on lipo and breast augmentation dies during operation READ MORE :

The total number of people diagnosed currently stands at five. A man living in Coria del Río (Seville) presented the first symptoms on July 17. The case was confirmed yesterday following tests in the Virgen del Rocío University Hospital in Seville.

"This is a mild case identified thanks to the surveillance established by the Surveillance and Comprehensive Control Programme of West Nile Fever vectors of Andalusia for residents and visitors of the municipalities of the regions of special monitoring or who are in a situation of area on alert," a health department spokesman said. "Consequently, the Ministry has decided to extend until August 14 the period of the alert area of this Sevillian municipality."

With Bollullos de la Mitación (Seville), Fuengirola and Las Lagunas (Malaga), there are now 15 Andalusian municipalities on alert: Pulpí in Almeria; Torredonjimeno in Jaén; Salobreña in Granada; and Almensilla, Aznalcázar, Coria del Río, Constantina, Gelves, La Puebla del Río, Mairena del Aljarafe, Palomares del Río and Villamanrique de la Condesa in the province of Seville.

‌



Insects were also detected in Benacazón (Seville) and Bujalance (Córdoba), although the capture points were more than 1.5km from any urban centre, so alerts were not issued.

Since the period of high mosquito densities began, a total of 3,310 captures have been made in 213 traps that, so far, have been positive: in Pulpí (Almería), Torredonjimeno (Jaén), Salobreña (Granada); Bujalance (Córdoba); Benacazón, Constantina, Coria del Rio, La Puebla del Río, including the Dehesa de Abajo area and the town centre, Almensilla, Aznalcázar, Gelves, Mairena del Aljarafe, Palomares del Río, Bollullos de la Mitación (Seville); and Mijas (Málaga).

In addition, a progressive increase in densities is being detected, so that in the last week an abundant density of transmitting female mosquitoes has been recorded in Los Palacios and Villafranca, La Puebla del Río, Coria, Isla Mayor, Villamanrique de la Condesa and Palomares del Río, and high densities in the Seville municipalities of Mairena del Aljarafe and Almensilla. in Bailén, Baeza and Navas de San Juan (Jaén), Sanlúcar de Barrameda (Cádiz), and La Carlota (Córdoba).

‌



The Ministry of the Presidency, Health and Emergencies is telling councils and citizens to adopt protection and prevention measures - especially vulnerable people.

Doctors are stressing the need to use registered mosquito repellents for topical use, cover most of the body with light clothing and avoid intense odours (perfumes, scented soaps, etc) because they attract mosquitoes.

Authorities have also encouraged domestic measures such as installing mosquito nets, using household insecticides/environmental repellents or turning off lights if they are not necessary.

‌



Another fundamental measure is to avoid generating areas of stagnant water where mosquitoes breed their larvae, so it is recommended to properly maintain swimming pools and laundry rooms, and to empty the water that may accumulate in gardens, pots, toys or buckets.

Nile Virus is generally transmitted by mosquitoes that bite birds, which carry the virus and deposit it in both humans and horses. A significant number of infected people do not show symptoms, but the virus can lead to serious health problems and death.

According to WHO data, 20 per cent of those who become infected suffer symptoms such as fever, headache, fatigue, body pain, nausea and to a lesser extent, skin rashes or enlarged lymph nodes. The virus can also cause neuroinvasive disease such as encephalitis, meninigitis or poliomyelitis. WHO says that only occurs in one of every 150 cases. People aged over 50 or those with immune problems are at higher risk.

Article continues below

In previous years, there have been at least 10 deaths from the virus in Andalusia.

News.title: Spain and France wildfires live: Brits among 200,000 fleeing scorched tourist areas
News.content:
More than 200,000 people in France and Spain have been evacuated as wildfires continue to tear through vast areas of Europe - with temperatures expected to surge higher next week

Huge wildfires are ravaging parts of south-west France and central Spain, forcing the evacuation of an estimated 200,000 people - including British tourists.

French authorities have ordered the immediate evacuation of suburbs in Bordeaux - the largest city in the affected region - as the flames shift towards the area.

British families were among those evacuated from a Bordeaux hotel at 3.30am as staff warned smoke had been travelling over from the raging fires around 20-miles away in the Cap Ferret peninsula.

Around 141,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in France's Gironde and Landes departments, the French interior ministry said. Some residents and holidaymakers even fled by boat as flames swept through the popular tourist area of Cap Ferret on France's Atlantic coast.

In Spain, 60,000 have been forced to leave their homes in towns west of Madrid, the Spanish interior ministry said. Wildfires in the Madrid region and the nearby province of Ávila have prompted the government to declare a national emergency over wildfires for the first time.

News.title: Nigel Farage's costly stunt could have paid for thousands of kids to see dentist
News.content:
Nigel Farage's costly stunt could have paid for thousands of kids to see dentist

EXCLUSIVE: Analaysis of NHS data by the Lib Dems reveals it would cost £263,000 to ensure children in Clacton who have not had a dental check-up get one - around the same as the cost of Farage's by-election 'circus'

View 3 Images Nigel Farage is fighting a by election against Count Binface and 32 other candidates (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

The cost of Nigel Farage's by-election "circus" is enough to ensure every child in Clacton gets an NHS dental check-up, analysis shows.

‌



The Reform UK leader is locked in a humiliating battle against Count Binface and 32 other candidates after triggering the race while he was being investigated in Parliament. None of the major parties entered the race as Mr Farage's ploy backfired, sparking accusations of a money-wasting stunt.

‌



It is estimated the by-election will cost between £250,000 and £300,000. The Lib Dems pointed out this sum is equivalent to funding NHS dental check-ups for thousands of kids who have not had one.

‌



Angela Rayner rules out rent controls as she admits 1.5million home pledge getting harder to meet READ MORE :

View 3 Images Lib Dem MP Helen Maguire hit out at Mr Farage (Image: Getty Images)

Helen Maguire, the party's primary care spokeswoman, told The Mirror: "It is an absolute insult to the people of Clacton that hundreds of thousands of pounds of taxpayers' money is being spent on a self-serving by-election stunt, when local healthcare services are in complete decay. Parents are struggling to find dental appointments for their children, and thousands of local kids are missing out on basic check-ups.

"Instead of addressing the dental crisis in Clacton and across the country, we are seeing precious public funds swallowed up by political games.”

‌



NHS dental statistics reveal that in the Tendring Council area, which covers Clacton, just 53.6% of children had accessed an NHS dentist in the 12 months leading up to June 2025. As a result 7,852 children in Clacton are missing out on crucial annual check-ups.

The Lib Dems said that funding a checkup for those who have not had one would cost £263,749, based on the area's £33.59 cost of an appointment. A party spokeswoman said: "Nigel Farage has not mentioned dentistry once in Parliament in his two years as an MP."

Mr Farage announced he was stepping down as an MP to trigger a by-election earlier this month. He branded it a "people versus the establishment" contest and claimed his opponents were using "foul means" to beat him.

‌



View 3 Images Mr Farage is locked in a contest against Count Binface (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

At the time the Parliamentary Standards Commissioner was investigating him over a £5million 'gift' he received from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before becoming an MP. He did not declare the sum, insisting he did not need to, despite rules stating donations and political gifts in the 12 months before entering Parliament should be made public.

That investigation is set to resume if Mr Farage wins the Clacton contest on August 13. If he is found to have breached the rules, Mr Farage could face a suspension, potentially triggering another by-election.

‌



Labour, the Lib Dems, the Tories, the Greens and Restore UK all announced they would not be putting up a candidate, branding it a circus. If there is a second by-election after the Parliamentary Standards Commissioner's report, it is expected the parties will contest the seat.

Instead Mr Farage has to contend with a wave of parody candidates and independents. Count Binface is the bookies' favourite to be his chief challenger. Rob Pownall, who has previously fought campaigns dressed as a fox to raise awareness of animal welfare, dropped out saying the by-election had got too silly.

Reform said it offered to cover the cost of the by-election. However strict election rules to protect the integrity of contests mean candidates and parties are not allowed to fund them.

Article continues below

A Reform UK spokesman said: "Reform offered to cover the full cost of this by-election, either by reimbursing Tendring District Council directly or by making an equivalent voluntary payment to HMRC. Labour has chosen to reject that offer.

"If the Lib Dems cared as much about the people of Clacton as they claim, they would have had the courage to put up a candidate and fight the election instead of lecturing from the sidelines."

News.title: How the mystery of dead animals dumped in villages led to a hidden world of illegal hunts
News.content:
On a remote Cambridgeshire farm, where his nearest neighbour is half a mile away, Mathew Latta was making lunch when the peace was shattered by the sound of loud exhausts.

Latta ran to the window to see a convoy of more than a dozen 4x4s heading towards his farm. His iron gates were cut open with an angle grinder and concrete blocks were shifted out of the way to clear the convoy's path.

The vehicles drove right over his fields at speed, tearing up the crops and skirting the fence by the family's garden. Then more than 70 people got out of the vehicles, men dressed in military fatigues and balaclavas, cheering and playing music.

Dogs were brought out on leads and began to hunt hares.

"They were all stood up on their cars with binoculars," says Latta. "I would say this is 100% a properly organised coursing event, with competitors and competitive dogs. People watching the course - and watching and betting on that sport. It was quite terrifying."

Warning: This story contains images of dead animals

Latta and his family were trapped in their home. They kept calling the police, but nobody came. His daughter, then aged seven, was terrified and kept asking: "Are these men gonna come inside, daddy?"

More than three hours later, the bloodsport was finally over and the crowd dispersed. They left behind four cars, one of them a burnt-out wreck. It emerged that, earlier that day, the convoy had rampaged through an area 20 miles (32km) long in the county, forcing other cars off the road and even robbing a petrol station.

News.title: Police declare 'major incident' over Cairngorms wildfire
News.content:
A major incident has been declared by emergency services as they continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.

Some residents of the village of Nethy Bridge have been evacuated as a precaution.

But a local resident told the BBC the wildfire should have been declared a major incident sooner and communication from authorities had been "pretty poor".

The Scottish government said a fire break had been established around Nethy Bridge overnight and new fire breaks were being constructed.

First Minister John Swinney, who held a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience committee early on Saturday, said additional police and fire service resources were being deployed to assist with the evacuation.

He said that it was "essential people avoid the affected areas."

Swinney continued: "The wind has changed direction overnight, which means the track of the fire has altered once again and the threat to Nethy Bridge has reduced, for the moment at least.

"Ground and helicopter resources are being focused on the current path of the fire and new fire breaks constructed."

Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said people living in properties north-west of Dorback Lodge at Lain Thatchan had been also been evacuated and advised people living in Tomintoul to keep windows and doors closed due to smoke.

Police Scotland said the major incident had been declared and the decision to evacuate residents taken came after evidence on Friday night suggested the fire was spreading towards Nethy Bridge.

A spokesperson added that residents were being directed to a dedicated respite centre at the Macdonald Aviemore Hotel and access roads into the village had been closed.

News.title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous: What you had to say about wedding rule changes
News.content:
The day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.

There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.

That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.

And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham.

"For us, that day was as insignificant as possible," Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."

The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.

But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.

It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses.

"I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.

But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.

News.title: ADHD has rewired the workplace. This is what it means for bosses and workers
News.content:
Taking one of the UK's biggest grocery chains to an employment tribunal was something that Ryan Toghill says almost took over his life.

"It was all I could think about for 18 months and more," he says.

The deputy store manager at Lidl, who'd told his bosses he'd been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), was called to a disciplinary meeting after breaking company rules by using equipment he hadn't been trained to use. After that meeting, Ryan was dismissed for gross misconduct.

He successfully appealed the decision and was offered a lower-paid role. He rejected it and took his case to a tribunal. Eventually, he was awarded more than Â£45,000 when the judge found his former employer hadn't fully taken his ADHD diagnosis into account during the disciplinary process.

The judgement found reasonable adjustments during the process hadn't been offered to him, such as additional breaks.

He'd been described by a manager as showing "a lack of remorse," something the tribunal found was clearly linked with his communication differences associated with having ADHD.

"I don't show a lot of emotions," Ryan explains. "I could be incredibly happy, angry, upset, or remorseful, and my facial expressions and tone of voice would essentially remain the same."

The tribunal upheld part of his claims for unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and a failure to make reasonable adjustments. Lidl says it's "committed to ensuring that everyone receives the reasonable adjustments, clear communication and support they need to thrive."

Campaigners, lawyers and HR teams say cases like this highlight a shift that businesses should be paying attention to.

Thousands of people have been diagnosed as neurodivergent in the last few years, an umbrella term that covers autism, ADHD and other conditions such as dyslexia and Tourette's syndrome.

Since the pandemic in particular, diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism have been rising, and they're featuring more regularly in disputes in employment tribunals.

News.title: The pop band who went from playing for rescue dogs to selling out arenas
News.content:
Every band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.

At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.

But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.

At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.

Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single.

"We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin.

"It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."

The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech.

"The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time.

"We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."

News.title: OpenAI hack has turned into a whodunnit with serious questions to answer
News.content:
This week the tech world was gripped by a story that has it all - and which started like a sci-fi thriller.

Hugging Face - a kind of app store for artificial intelligence tools - announced on 16 July it had been hacked by a cyber criminal wielding enormously powerful AI.

The bombshell announcement was full of scary, highly technical terms: "a swarm of sandboxes", "agentic attacker", and "self-migrating command and control".

Hugging Face said the hack was different from anything it had handled before because it was done at superhuman speed by an AI with little or no human guidance.

The AI performed 17,000 actions in less than two days, successfully breaching the large wealthy tech company to steal secrets.

It left the tech world in shock. But who was responsible for this attack?

Hugging Face researchers guessed the mysterious attackers had used one of the big AI models but they had no idea who or where the criminals were.

The perplexed company contacted the police and investigations commenced.

News.title: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?
News.content:
When Lisa Kudrow appeared on The Claudia Winkleman Show earlier this year, she was visibly delighted to meet Linda from The Traitors.

The Friends actress, probably the most famous guest the programme had during its seven-week run, said it was "thrilling" to meet one of the reality show's breakout stars, who she revealed had even inspired one of her own recent performances.

As host of The Traitors, Winkleman was ideally placed to introduce the pair, resulting in the kind of wonderfully bizarre meeting of minds normally seen on The Graham Norton Show.

But Winkleman's own chat show did not last long enough for any more unusual guest combinations on its teal sofa. The presenter quit last week after just one series, saying she was simply "too nervous to enjoy it".

It had made sense for the BBC to commission The Claudia Winkleman Show, given the presenter's popularity on programmes such as Strictly.

There's a different level of pressure, however, hosting a show with your own name above the door.

News.title: Parents on how they get through the summer holidays on a budget
News.content:
A family's first instinct when summer is approaching may be to look at booking a trip abroad, but rising costs and travel expenses mean a holiday isn't feasible for everyone.

Mags Rivett, director at Family Holiday Charity, which supports families with UK trips, says there are many benefits to arranging time away with children that don't require expensive travel.

She says the social aspect of a holiday can help children develop their communication skills.

"Lots of kids have never really had the opportunity to meet people outside of their own community," Rivett says. "But if you go somewhere that's got social facilities, it's a really important opportunity."

She says getting recommendations from friends and family is a good place to start.

Rivett gives the example of Skegness, a coastal holiday destination in Lincolnshire, accessible by train or coach, which her charity has supported families to visit.

A family-of-four's accommodation in a holiday park there this August starts at around Â£750 for a week, while an off-peak return train from Manchester would cost around Â£280 for four.

By contrast, a last-minute trip to Majorca for a family-of-four at that time starts from around Â£2,000. Better deals can usually be found booking further in advance.

News.title: Huge explosion and fire rip through Essex industrial site
News.content:
People living near the fire - which happened close to the village of Rettendon, south of Chelmsford - were urged to keep their windows closed as smoke spread.

As of Friday evening, it was not clear whether there had been casualties, but in an update that night, Dave Bond of Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said: "While on the scene, fertiliser inside one of the units exploded and residents across the county have reported hearing and feeling it.

"This is why we declared a major incident, and I want to reassure our residents that there is no wider risk to the public at this time."

He said "everybody at the scene is safe" but that residents have been evacuated.

The fire service said the response was scaled down, with about 25 firefighters on scene as of 08:00 BST on Saturday as well as specialist officers and advisors to extinguish the rest of the blaze.

Crews are expected to remain on site for the rest of Saturday, and smoke is still coming from the scene, the fire service added.

East of England Ambulance Service said its hazardous area response team and the police were also in attendance.

Earlier on Friday evening, Bond said there was still "significant smoke" at the scene, but he believed that the fire had been "surrounded".

News.title: Teenage boy dies after stabbing in Luton as police launch murder investigation
News.content:
Police have launched a murder investigation after a teenage boy died following a stabbing in Luton.

Bedfordshire Police said officers responded to reports of violent disorder in Kingsway Recreation Ground at about 18:30 on Friday, where a number of teenagers were seen carrying large knives.

A 17-year-old, who has not been identified, was taken to hospital with multiple stab wounds but was pronounced dead shortly after, the force said.

One teenage boy has been arrested on suspicion of violent disorder and is in police custody for questioning. A second was arrested but remains in hospital with serious but non-life threatening injuries.

Police are appealing to the public for information.

In a statement, Det Ch Insp Nick Gardener condemned the "horrific violence" that has "sadly cost a teenage boy his life today".

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the loved ones of the boy who lost his life in such tragic circumstances," he said.

Such incidents have "a significant impact on our communities", he said.

He also urged the public to contact police with any information they have and not to share any images and videos circulating on social media.

An increased police presence and patrols will remain in the area.

Zanib Raja, a councillor for the Biscot Ward in Luton, asked people not to share alleged videos of the incident online.

In a statement on Facebook, she said: "A tragic incident took place today in Kingsway Park, a place many of us grew up in, played in, and built memories in.

"A place that should be safe for families, children, and every resident of our town. Instead, a man lost his life in broad daylight. A family has been shattered. Luton is hurting."

Raja urged the community to come together.

News.title: Heatwave conditions to return for many as UK temperatures to peak at 35C
News.content:
For most of England and Wales the third heatwave of the year ended last weekend when cooler air arrived, dropping maximum temperatures widely to 20-24C.

However, two locations - Usk and Exeter - have continued to just reach their heatwave criteria since then and have now reached 20 consecutive days - the longest run so far this year.

As temperatures drop further over the weekend, and parts of the UK see a little rain, even these local heatwaves are likely to come to an end.

However, it may only be a temporary break.

Next week, high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK meaning rain-bearing weather fronts will stall.

Any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland - and in southern parts of the UK temperatures look set to climb once again.

This could well mean a fourth heatwave is on the cards - although according to the Met Office isolated high temperatures might not be enough.

They say that: "If only one or two stations reach heatwave criteria, that would not be defined as a heatwave."

News.title: Horror injury overshadows gymnastics silver at Commonwealths
News.content:
A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The 19-year-old, from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club, needed lengthy treatment on the mat after a horrible fall in the final rotation of the evening at The Arena.

Langton fell head first to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar, three metres in the air, leading to a lengthy delay to the action as he was tended to by up to a dozen medical staff.

He was eventually led away on a trolley after being moved on to a stretcher with his head and neck braced and left to huge applause from the packed crowd who had spent much of the previous 10 minutes in hushed silence.

Langton was seen to be conscious and moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena floor, while team officials later said he was moving and speaking to doctors.

In a statement, Team England said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance.

"He has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."

When competition resumed, his England team-mates were unable to overhaul their deficit to Canada who claimed their first gold medal in the event in 20 years, having finished second to England at the past two games.

Langton, a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock, was unable to join his teammates on the podium as England collected their silver medals.

Team-mate Luke Whitehouse, who was first on to the apparatus after the competition restarted and posted a relatively low score of 11.700, said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time."

Whitehouse added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."

Felix Dolci, who helped Canada to gold and led qualifying for the all-around competition, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.

"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one.

"For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."

Hamish Carter from Team Scotland - who narrowly missed out on a bronze medal to Australia in the final rotation - said: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened.

"We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."

News.title: It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'
News.content:
Cleaning up after pre-drinks, AÃ©dÃ©n Rooney puts his empty BuzzBallz in the recycling.

"It's plastic and metal, so I'd just assume it's recyclable," he said.

The company behind the bright, pre-mixed cocktails that have taken Gen Z by storm said they were recyclable on its website, but experts say this is not true.

BuzzBallz cannot be recycled as the PET plastic ball cannot be separated from the aluminium lid, global environmental action body WRAP said.

"It's greenwashing. I'm shocked," AÃ©dÃ©n said.

BuzzBallz blamed a website error for claiming they were recyclable via Terracycle, a US-only scheme, but did not comment on its now-deleted FAQ that said they were recyclable where UK councils allow.

News.title: Wildfire burning one month on is 'the size of a small town'
News.content:
As darkness set in over the Peak District one Wednesday night in June, calls started to come in to Derbyshire's fire service over smoke starting to rise from the moorland overlooking the town.

More than a month on, the Tintwistle Moor fire is now a sprawling, smouldering blaze the size of a small town, which can be seen from space.

Declared a major incident on 13 July, it has come in tandem with a prolonged spell of hot, dry weather that shows little sign of easing soon, pushing the country's firefighting resources to their limits.

Now Dr Kirsten Lees, environmental sciences lecturer, specialising in zero carbon at the University of Derby, has told the BBC Tintwistle is on a par with the biggest wildfires ever seen in England - and it's still burning.

When questioned about her assertion the fire could be one of the largest in recent memory in England, she said: "It may well be, yes."

News.title: Law student is charged over intercepted bomb in car
News.content:
A 25-year-old law student has appeared in court charged over a bomb which was discovered in a car in the Republic of Ireland.

Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Abbeylands Park in Clane, County Kildare, was charged with the possession of explosives.

It was alleged she was driving the car which was intercepted by gardaÃ­ (Irish police) near Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, on Wednesday.

A defence solicitor told the court his client had been asked to take a bag to Northern Ireland and had not been aware what was in it.

Earlier on Friday, gardaÃ­ told reporters their interception was part of an operation targeting dissident republican activity.

The accused, who was arrested on Wednesday, was brought before a special sitting of Trim District Court in County Meath on Friday evening.

A member of the Garda Special Detective Unit told the court the car she was driving was stopped by officers on N2 at Aclint, south of Carrickmacross.

News.title: Sean McCann - brother of Madeleine - to swim at Commonwealths
News.content:
Sean McCann - the younger brother of Madeleine McCann - will swim for Scotland at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Saturday.

The 21-year-old - a Loughborough University student - is entered in the 400m, 800m and 1500m freestyle events as he makes his debut at a major championships.

The 400m heats begin on Saturday morning at the Tollcross Swimming Centre.

"I'm very excited. It's my first senior Games so I'm just looking forward to representing Scotland and doing my absolute best," McCann told Loughborough University earlier this week, external.

"It's the pinnacle really of representing Scotland at the Commonwealth Games, especially at a home Games.

"I've got lots of family up in Glasgow so that makes it even more special. I was there in 2014 [at the Commonwealth Games], watching as a kid, so to make it now, 12 years later, is really a full-circle moment."

McCann grew up in England but qualifies to compete for Scotland through his father, Gerry.

He and his twin sister were two years old when Madeleine, then aged three, went missing during a family holiday in Praia Da Luz, Portugal, in 2007.

It became one of the world's most high-profile missing-person cases and remains an ongoing Metropolitan Police investigation.

It is well past midnight at Jantar Mantar, and the crowd shows no sign of thinning. Music drifts across the humid air, tabla beats mixing with snatches of Bollywood songs, as new arrivals keep streaming in on foot — students, labourers, parents — even at this hour.

Somewhere near the stage, a spokesperson is trying, and failing, to keep the swelling numbers from tipping into a stampede. On walls near the protest site, fresh graffiti is still wet. "Modiji, return us our bad days," one pleads, a jab at the prime minister's campaign slogan “Achhe Din”, the promised good days that many say never came.

In the crowd is Mohan Yadav, 43, a man who doesn’t fit the profile that the government’s supporters imagine when they picture these protests. He is not, he insists, an opposition plant, or a professional agitator. He voted for Narendra Modi’s BJP party. He voted for its ally Nitish Kumar in Bihar state. Yet, he’s standing at Jantar Mantar, trying to explain why the government he once trusted has, in his eyes, turned on people like him.

"I have a son and a daughter," he says. "And I can understand that pain of a parent. Because I know how much sacrifice it takes to raise a child and then to lose them like this."

He is far from alone.

open image in gallery Protesters gather at Delhi's Jantar Mantar seeking the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan ( Namita Singh/ The Independent )

What started out as a joke by a group of students is now one of the most sustained waves of public dissent against Modi's government.

On Saturday, India's education ⁠minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned, handing a major victory to the youth protesters.

With millions of followers online and clear displays of support on the ground, the Cockroach Janta Party had said it would not stop protesting until Modi’s education minister – the powerful veteran politician Dharmendra Pradhan – resigned

The protesters said Pradhan must take responsibility for the shambolic handling of a key university entrance exam for would-be medical students, the cancellation of which affected 2.3 million young people. Activists said at least 21 students died by suicide during the debacle.

Nitesh Aryan, 26, from the northern city of Lucknow, has been at the protest site daily since 19 July. He says he is driven by the fact “that exam papers are repeatedly leaked. And when we demand our rights, the government responds by baton-charging the students, cracking our skulls, breaking legs and back.”

open image in gallery A poster at Jantar Mantar ( Namita Singh/ The Independent )

Akanksha, 31, who has lived in Delhi her whole life, frames her motivation as a slow, cumulative betrayal rather than a single scandal. "I’m a victim of the education system," she says. "I know how rigged the system is, how messed up our schools are. Teachers are demotivated. Nobody is studying in a government institution."

For Muskaan, 40, leaving the protest site with her two children close to midnight, the stakes are more immediate. She’s a labourer and her husband drives an autorickshaw. "There are poor people who with great difficulty manage to educate their children," she says. "My children will also study with as much hard work. Right now they are young. My son is in 8th standard and daughter is in 11th standard. It is about their future as well."

When papers leak, she argues, "the future of my children is being ruined. I’m here to protect their future and prevent it from being ruined."

What turned a grievance into a full-blown anti-government movement was the events of 20 July, the day police moved against the protesters at Jantar Mantar as they prepared to march towards parliament, using batons and teargas against them and leaving scores injured.

open image in gallery People gather in solidarity with Cockroach Janta Party protesters at Jantar Mantar in Delhi ( Reuters )

Birku Yadav, 26, who joined the movement after learning about it on 18 July, describes what happened to her two days later. "I was charged with baton by a male police officer who did not even have his name tag on," she says. "I feel like they were not wearing name tags because they were not police officers but supporters of the ruling regime."

Ashutosh Ranka, 30, a spokesperson for the Cockroach Janta Party, says the scale of the crackdown caught even the organisers off guard. "The kind of brutality meted out against the students, young protesters and our own volunteers who were helping them manage the crowd crossed all levels of brutality," he said. "Crossed all levels of shamelessness."

It’s this moment – the baton-charge against unarmed students demanding accountability – that Mohan Yadav can’t reconcile with the government he voted for. "I still don't know why we were assaulted by the police," he says. "It was only about the resignation of one person. The government should have just conceded to the demands of the public, 'my constituents and voters are asking for this, we should give them.' We would have been so much happier."

open image in gallery Supporters of India's Cockroach Janta Party hold placards and chant slogans during a protest in Delhi ( Reuters )

There is a striking gap between the government's public posture and what protesters describe living through. Modi has floated a proposal for fast-track courts to try paper-leak cases, a move Saurav Das, another Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson, dismisses as cosmetic.

"It's an eyewash," he says, noting that a 2024 law against organised exam-paper mafias is already meant to solve this, with little visible effect. "That law wasn’t implemented properly, that's why you have these kinds of instances again."

That disconnect between official reassurance and street anger runs through nearly every conversation.

Where the government speaks of isolated lapses and administrative fixes, the protesters describe something closer to institutional collapse, and a chain of accountability that never seems to reach anyone at the top. "Post-2014, the government takes great arrogance in not sacking its minister," Das says. "It was automatic before 2014."

For Mohan Yadav, the gap is personal, not political. He frames his disillusionment as stemming not from ideology but a broken bargain.

"If we brought Modiji to power and he is the head of the country, then he should have taken care of our well-being and happiness," he says. "But instead he went against 65 per cent of the youth of the country. In front of my eyes, so many women and children were beaten up. I felt really sad."

open image in gallery India's Cockroach Janta Party spokespersons Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka address the media in Delhi ( AFP/Getty )

Nitesh Aryan's demand is starker still: "My demand is that those responsible for it are duly punished. And all the people who were at their posts at the time this happened, resign."

Ranka insists the movement will not fold under pressure even as he acknowledges the personal risk protesters are taking on. "We expect police action but we don't fear it," he says. "This is a fight much bigger than one person and we are ready to pay the price." Asked how far organisers are prepared to go if the government refuses to budge, he allowed himself a rare smile. "The government has to concede. They don't have a choice this time."

Mohan Yadav says he still does not fully understand how he ended up here, holding a grievance against a government he helped elect. He’s careful to say he isn't asking for anything extraordinary. "I’m not asking for a plot of land in Delhi," he says. "I am not asking Modi to transfer 1.5 million rupees to my account. I am asking for accountability."

Get off the forecourt now,” shouts Dima, 65, an attendant at a petrol station on the main road into Pavlohrad, in Ukraine’s eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.

As the air raid siren wails, he points to an app on his phone tracking Russian drones — now an essential tool for those working on the country’s increasingly dangerous petrol station forecourts. An arrow is moving across the screen.

“It’s a Russian Geran-3 drone heading in our direction,” he says. “They missed us yesterday, but they are coming back for another try. You must leave immediately.”

Russia has intensified its assault on Ukraine’s retail fuel network over the past month, striking ordinary roadside stations across the east and south of the country.

open image in gallery Irada standing in front of blast protection and Sergei outside their service stations in eastern Ukraine ( Harry Stourton )

Fuel-industry estimates suggest that the rate of attacks has risen to about 20 a week, with as many as 200 stations reported to have been hit or damaged in recent months.

The campaign has turned working on a forecourt into one of the most hazardous civilian jobs in eastern Ukraine, where much of the fighting is taking place. Military authorities are urging motorists to fill their tanks and leave as quickly as possible, spending no more than 10 minutes at a station.

The previous day, a drone was shot down moments before reaching Dima’s forecourt, crashing instead into a nearby business park.

A week earlier, another station at the opposite end of Pavlohrad suffered a direct hit.

The site was destroyed, with several people reported killed or injured.

Russia previously concentrated its attacks on refineries, storage depots and other large energy installations. It is now increasingly targeting the last mile of Ukraine’s fuel network: the roadside stations used by civilians, ambulances, volunteers, farmers and military vehicles.

Russian forces have used Geran-3 attack drones — Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed — as well as smaller, long-range fixed-wing drones and, closer to the front line, short-range FPV drones.

open image in gallery A destroyed petrol station in eastern Ukraine ( Harry Stourton )

At a busy OKKO petrol station nearby, Irada, its 31-year-old manager, watches customers stream into the shop, known locally for its hot dogs.

“I’m extremely worried about my safety,” she says. “We run whenever we hear the siren, but sometimes it is difficult. Customers are paying or filling their cars, and there is no guarantee I will be able to get away in time.”

Irada is a single mother whose relatives remain trapped in Russian-occupied territory.

“If anything happens to me, who will look after my daughter?” she asks. “The rest of my family are stranded in the [Russian-occupied] territories.”

Yet she says she has little choice but to continue working.

“I need the job, but it has become so dangerous that we should be paid danger money,” she says. “So far, our bosses have offered us nothing — only this.”

She gestures towards makeshift blast protection installed around the kiosk.

“They will not say how many casualties there were when the nearby WOG [petrol] station was destroyed, but I think there were a lot,” she adds quietly.

“The Russians have changed tactics,” says Andriy, the commander of a nearby mobile air-defence unit. “They are targeting civilian infrastructure, and petrol stations are among their priorities.”

open image in gallery A flatbed truck carrying a large Browning machine gun, its barrel trained towards the sky, aiming at drones ( Harry Stourton )

He stands beside a flatbed truck carrying a large Browning machine gun, its barrel trained towards the sky.

The jet-powered Geran-3 is reported to travel at about 400km an hour and fly higher than earlier piston-engined attack drones, making it harder for Ukraine’s mobile air-defence teams to intercept.

“Our only chance of hitting them may be during their final dive,” Andriy says. “That does not give us much time.”

He gestures towards the Browning mounted on the truck.

“They are very difficult to hit with this... So now we need these,” he says, pointing to an open crate containing a long cylindrical weapon. “Heat-seeking Stinger missiles,” he adds.

The nearby Vostok Gaz station also narrowly escaped destruction after Ukrainian air defences intercepted a drone above the forecourt moments before it could strike.

open image in gallery Sergei, 59, a pump attendant, points to shrapnel marks on the kiosk: ‘I look at the sky all day’ ( Harry Stourton )

Sergei, 59, a pump attendant, points to shrapnel marks on the kiosk. He narrowly escaped injury.

“I look at the sky all day,” he says. “When I see something in the air, I run for my life and throw myself into the ditch across the road.”

He believes the stations are being attacked in retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.

“It’s revenge,” he says. “The Russians are angry that our armed forces are destroying their refineries.”

Yet Sergei remains defiant. Drivers continue to arrive, watching the sky as they stand beside their cars.

“Our customers still need petrol,” he says. “I still need to work, and I will not stop.”

Typhoon Noul is bringing winds and heavy rain to southern China and Hong Kong over the weekend, with the region on high alert and dozens of flights canceled.

Hong Kong’s Observatory said Noul, which had intensified with maximum sustained winds of 140 kph (87 mph) near its center, was moving on Saturday steadily across the northeastern part of the South China Sea and edging closer to the coast of eastern Guangdong.

The city's observatory forecasts Noul could make landfall Sunday morning around the vicinity of the southern Chinese cities of Huizhou and Shanwei, bringing strong winds and squally showers to parts of the region. China’s weather center, meanwhile, expects Noul to make landfall between late Saturday and early Sunday.

Hong Kong airport’s website showed more than 150 flights had been canceled for Saturday and Sunday.

As Noul approaches Hong Kong, parts of a large scaffolding on a high-rise building collapsed on Saturday afternoon, local police said, adding that initial reports indicated there were no injuries.

China’s National Meteorological Center expects parts of southeastern Guangdong and the southern coast of Fujian will experience heavy rain over the weekend.

More than 20,000 people had been evacuated by late Friday in the southern Guangdong province, according to local media. Train services in the province have been canceled for Sunday, according to the China News Service.

Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration said Noul was bringing rainfall to parts of southern and eastern Taiwan. It was passing over waters south of Taiwan, and was moving away from the island Saturday.

Earlier this month, Typhoon Bavi brought strong winds and rain to eastern China, leading to the evacuation of more than 2 million people. It made landfall on July 11. Another, Maysak, made landfall in southern China on July 3.

News.title: F1 Hungarian GP LIVE: FP3 updates and qualifying start time with Hamilton eyeing pole ahead of Antonelli
News.content:
Lewis Hamilton ‘firmly believes’ he can challenge for the F1 title

Formula 1 returns to the Hungaroring this weekend for the Hungarian Grand Prix and round 11 of the 2026 season.

Kimi Antonelli claimed his sixth win of the season last time out at Spa-Francorchamps, winning from pole position to extend his lead in the F1 world championship to 45 points after Mercedes teammate George Russell crashed out on the opening lap.

Lewis Hamilton is now Antonelli’s closest contender but could only finish fourth on a disappointing weekend for the Briton in Belgium, but he has won seven times in Hungary. His Ferrari teammate, Charles Leclerc, finished second with Red Bull’s Max Verstappen in third.

Reigning world champion Lando Norris won last year’s race in Budapest ahead of McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri. It is the final race before the customary summer break.

Follow live updates from the Hungarian GP with The Independent

The five new professional dancers who will join the 2026 edition of Strictly Come Dancing have been announced.

Maddie Ingoldsby, Aleksandra Isaeva, Mark Karmalita, Lethabo Monametsi, and Cristian Priori will be joining the BBC dancing competition this year, replacing outgoing pros Nadiya Bychkova, Karen Hauer, Gorka Marquez, Luba Mushtuk, and Michelle Tsiakkas.

The departures of the latter five dancers were announced earlier this year, with fans having to bid farewell to some of their long-time favourites.

There will, however, still be some familiar faces on the dancefloor with returning pros including Alexis Warr, Aljaz Skorjanec, Amy Dowden, Carlos Gu, Dianne Buswell, Jowita Przystal, Julian Caillon, Kai Widdrington, Katya Jones, Lauren Oakley, Nancy Xu, Neil Jones, Nikita Kuzmin and Vito Coppola.

This latest Strictly reveal arrives as the celebrity line-up is slowly coming together, with actor Jaime Winstone the latest to be announced. Winstone joins Paralympian cyclist Dame Sarah Storey, TV presenter Will Best, reality star Cacheral Mercer, hair stylist to the stars Chris Appleton, and more.

So, who are the five new dancers competing for the coveted Glitterball Trophy this year?

Maddie Ingoldsby

British dancer Ingoldsby, 21, is a UK National Ballroom Champion. She described joining Strictly as a “dream come true”.

My heart is so full of gratitude, excitement, and anticipation as I begin this incredible new chapter,” she said. “Dance has always been where I feel most myself, and to now share my heart, my creativity, and my love for it on a show that has inspired millions is an honour beyond words.”

Aleksandra Isaeva

Isaeva, who is from Ukraine and is ranked in the world’s top 21 Latin dancers, said joining the show is a “true honour”.

She added: “The thought of learning from and sharing this experience with such extraordinary dancers, choreographers and the whole Strictly family still gives me goosebumps.

“I can’t wait to pour my whole heart into every performance, inspire others and be inspired along the way.”

Cristian Priori

Four-time Latin dancing champion Priori, who is Isaeva’s dance partner, said it was an “easy decision” to join the show.

The Rome-born dancer said that he is “so excited” to begin the new chapter.

“I’m ready to give my all, enjoy every moment of this amazing journey, and embrace everything it has to offer,” he continued. “Strictly is where passion, hard work and entertainment come together, so being part of it is a real privilege.”

Lethabo Monametsi

Monametsi has performed with the likes of singer Diana Ross and composer Hans Zimmer, has appeared on the TV dance competition Dance Yo Dumo as a member of Urban Wave, and performed as a dancer on The Masked Singer SA.

She said: “This moment is bigger than me. I step into it with profound gratitude and deep humility, knowing it is the culmination of years of unwavering love, belief, and support from the people who dared to dream alongside me.

“Representing South Africa on the Strictly Come Dancing stage is far more than a career milestone, it is an honour beyond words, and I cannot wait to embrace every extraordinary moment of this journey.”

Mark Karmalita

Karmalita, who is a two-time National Latin Champion in his native Canada, said: “Joining Strictly feels incredibly special, and I’m honoured to be stepping into a ballroom with so much history and heart.

“I can’t wait to bring my own style, connect with the audience, and enjoy every moment along the way.”

Sarah James, executive producer at BBC Studios said: “Aleksandra, Cristian, Lethabo, Maddie and Mark are all outstanding world class dancers and we can’t wait to see them shine under the Strictly glitterball this September.”

Gu won the 2025 edition of Strictly with former England Lionesses footballer Karen Carney.

The new series will be hosted by trio Emma Willis, Johannes Radebe and Josh Widdicombe, who are taking over from Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.

Strictly returns to BBC One and iPlayer in September.

Once heralded by JB Priestley as the quintessential English village and known as the ‘Venice of the Cotswolds’, Bourton-on-the-Water is at breaking point.

Residents warn that the historic Cotswold destination is being destroyed by an influx of daytrippers and Instagrammers.

The area has always been popular with visitors, but that popularity has increased further in recent years thanks to picture-perfect shots on social media and celebrity links including to Clarkson’s Farm, with Jeremy Clarkson once rumoured to be buying a pub in Bourton.

“We are a beautiful quintessential English village, with so much heritage and people want to see it,” said Charlotte Joynes, chair of Bourton Residents Voice, which was formed to tackle the growing list of concerns among villagers.

”We want to share it but at the moment, the hordes of people that are coming means we are just being destroyed.

“It’s no longer the beautiful village that people think it is - it’s more ‘Blackpool-on-the-Water.”

Search for Bourton-on-the-Water on Instagram and you’ll quickly find a list of reasons why not to visit in the summer. The village gets so busy, it’s hard to even see the village green beneath the sea of deckchairs and picnic blankets.

According to residents, the nature of tourism has fundamentally changed since the Covid pandemic. While the village previously hosted international travellers from the US and Australia, who came for the architecture and supported the local economy with overnight stays and eating out, the current trend means increasing numbers of daytrippers from nearby towns and cities.

open image in gallery Bourton-on-the-Water's beautiful river attracts millions of tourists in the hot weather ( Charlotte Joynes )

“They are coming with their own picnics and all they’re buying is an ice cream,” said Ms Joynes. “They are using apps to find free parking and clogging up our streets. The coach park is closed and it’s become a free-for-all with coaches in residential streets.”

Residents in the village have reported tourists using hedges as toilets, leaving litter piled up beside bins and even taking chunks out of the iconic Cotswold stone wall to take home as souvenirs.

Ms Joynes, who has lived in the village for 34 years, estimates that between 5,000 and 10,000 visitors a day descend on Bourton – which only has a population of 4,000 people. The village green is often rammed with picnickers and she even reported seeing one family set up a table and chairs in the river and eat a full fish and chips.

open image in gallery Rammed - the village green at Bourton-on-the-Water ( Charlotte Joynes )

”I work in one of the pubs,” she added. “We do want visitors. It’s the picnic and paddlers, as I call them, that aren’t bringing anything to the economy.

”We now have tourists moaning about tourists in Bourton,” she said. “It’s not our own village any more.”

Read The Independent’s guide to the most beautiful places to visit in the Cotswolds

”Don’t get us wrong, Bourton-on-the-Water is one of our top locations within the Cotswolds, but for those looking for an idyllic day in the sunshine that rapidly turned into a day crammed onto a river bank with the rest of the country that had the same idea, we always wish we had a back up plan,” writes Boltholeretreats.

“Bourton-on-the-Water today: one giant communal picnic where nobody knew whose mat they were sitting on anymore,” wrote doctor_with_a_suitcase.

A recent survey of 202 residents found more than 90 per cent believed the current tourism levels in the village were not sustainable and negatively impacted their quality of life. A total of 94.6 per cent of residents said they felt visitor numbers were excessive.

Gloucestershire County Council has recently launched a consultation on transport and parking in Bourton-on-the-Water. It says: “We know people are concerned about pedestrian safety along the High Street and how vehicles, including coaches and buses, is affecting how people move around the village. We want to hear your experiences to shape the right solutions to ensure everyone can continue to enjoy this historically significant village.”

open image in gallery The quintessential Cotswold village in quieter times ( Charlotte Joynes )

Bourton Residents Voice is calling for immediate intervention and describes the current consultation process as ‘an absolute farce’ noting that consultees were not able to access a recent meeting with the county council on the issue as the link was broken.

open image in gallery Charlotte Joynes, chair of Bourton Residents Voice ( Charlotte Joynes )

“We would like enforcement,” said Ms Joynes. “The coaches coming in are doing it illegally because of traffic regulations. But we don’t have police to stop them. We want people to visit but respect where they’re coming to.

”We are a little village of 4,000 residents and we can’t cope. We need to leave something for our future generations.”
