Sports.title: Kate, Gerry and Amelie McCann look on proudly as son Sean swims in Commonwealth Games nearly two decades after his sister Madeleine disappeared
Sports.content:
The brother of Madeleine McCann is set to swim for Commonwealth gold today, some two decades after his older sister vanished.

Sean McCann, 21, will take to the pool in Glasgow for the 400m freestyle heats this morning in his major competition debut.

His parents Kate and Gerry and twin sister Amelie looked on proudly as they arrived early on Saturday morning to cheer on their son - and the rest of the Scotland team.

Sean will hope to use the home crowd behind him to progress to the final tonight, ahead of his other events later this week, the 800m and 1500m freestyle.

Almost two decades on from the infamous Portugal family holiday which saw Madeleine abducted, the McCann family's unimaginable tragedy still haunts Sean and his twin sister, Amelie, wherever they go.

But today, the family could finally see themselves talked about for a different reason as their son's remarkable story takes centre-stage.

Sean's mother Kate has previously told how he 'hated' the water when he was first taken swimming – and yet he soon found his drive, attending up to nine two-hour training sessions every week, many requiring 4am starts.

Inspired by his sporting family – Kate and father Gerry even went on a run on their first date – Sean's dedication has paid off as he sets his sights on success in his first major international meet.

He is expected to be cheered on today by both parents, as well as his sister Amelie, who herself competes regularly in triathlons.

Amelie, Kate and Gerry McCann in the stands at Tollcross International Swimming Centre in Glasgow ahead of Sean's heat on Saturday morning

The family were in the stands early on Saturday to support the rest of Britain's swimmers before their son takes to the pool

Amelie, Kate and Gerry McCann applaud as they watch the programme at Glasgow's Commonwealth Games on Saturday morning

Sean McCann, 21, of Scotland's Commonwealth Games team, has carved a successful career as an elite distance swimmer

He is the younger brother of missing Madeleine McCann and was in the room when she was abducted from her family's holiday villa in Portugal in 2007

The elite distance swimmer is eligible to represent Scotland through his father, who was born in Glasgow.

This week a former member of Sean's coaching team told the Daily Mail that the combination of a young man who was 'really driven and never one to take the easiest route', and parents who willed him on, had made him a powerhouse and his story an inspiration.

In his teenage years Sean's parents would ferry him to training sessions at Braunstone Leisure Centre, a 20-minute drive from the family home in Rothley, Leicestershire, where he would clock up eight or nine two-hour swim sessions a week, plus two or three punishing gym workouts.

Kate and Gerry 'encouraged their children, but didn't push them' said the insider, who coached Sean as a youngster.

He remembered the young man being focused on the Commonwealth Youth Games in Trinidad in 2023 and then deciding he wanted to race for Scotland and for GB in open-water events – so for swimming competitively he changed his nationality to Scottish.

'For the Commonwealth Games, I was lucky enough to be at the trials in London when he was racing. It was great to watch him and talk to him between prep, to be a part of it and see his journey unfold,' he said.

What a journey, too, for Sean, who is studying chemical engineering at Loughborough University – chosen for its unrivalled sports facilities.

Distance swimming is an unforgiving sport. Yet those who know Sean's career describe a steady, determined progression, even during the pandemic lockdown when he would train out of the pool, at home with Amelie, who is also a keen swimmer.

Sean McCann of Scotland competes in the Men's 1500m Freestyle final on day two of the 2023 Youth Commonwealth Games at National Aquatic Centre on August 06, 2023 in Couva, Trinidad And Tobago

For almost two decades Kate and Gerry McCann have been known as the parents of missing Madeleine, (bottom right) the toddler who disappeared on a family holiday to Praia da Luz, Portugal, in May 2007 - now the family will be known for something else

In the 2023 Commonwealth Youth Games, he reached the finals of the 400m and 1500m freestyle, and has since qualified for the European Open Water Championships representing Great Britain.

Sean himself said this week that he was 'very excited' about the challenges ahead. 'It's the pinnacle really – of representing Scotland in the Commonwealth Games, and especially at a home games.

'I've got lots of family up in Glasgow so that makes it even more special. I was there in 2014 watching as a kid, so to make it now, 12 years later, is really a full circle moment.

'It's my first senior games, so I'm just looking forward to be representing Scotland and doing my absolute best. I always tend to go out quite slow and build my way into a race. That's just how I like to pace it.'

It's quite the change from what Sean has been known for by many until now, solely for his close proximity to Madeleine's disappearance.

He was, after all, in the same room when she was abducted from the family's holiday apartment in Praia da Luz in 2007 when he was just two.

Although he might not remember the international fallout, both siblings have grown up in the shadow of the mystery surrounding their older sister, who would now be 23.

For Sean, and by extension his whole family, this is his opportunity to step into the light of something new.

Sports.title: The ultimate football bromance reunited as Morgan Rogers seals £117m move to Chelsea: England star and Cole Palmer share a celebration, grew up together at Man City and share a tragic bond
Sports.content:
The ultimate football bromance reunited as Morgan Rogers seals £117m move to Chelsea: England star and Cole Palmer share a celebration, grew up together at Man City and share a tragic bond

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Monday, November 2, 2020. St George’s Park, Burton-on-Trent. The FA Youth Cup final between Manchester City and Chelsea. It is 2-2 as we approach the 83rd minute. Morgan Rogers has already scored for City, a tidy finish to a low cross cut back by Liam Delap.

Then Delap breaks behind. He shoots. The ball bobbles beyond Chelsea defender Levi Colwill and trickles towards the back post, where Cole Palmer is waiting. He taps in for 3-2 and that’s that at the FA’s national football centre. City win, Chelsea lose.

Those in attendance might never have guessed what a Chelsea connection this youth match involving City would carry nearly six years later, now that Rogers is signing for £117million, the most expensive fee ever paid for a British player.

Both 18 years old at the time, neither Rogers nor Palmer performed their now customary ‘Cold’ celebrations after scoring. That trademark came later in their careers.

Instead, when Palmer grabbed the winner for Carlos Vicens’ academy class of 2020 at City, he lifted his shirt to reveal a tribute to Jeremy Wisten, his former team-mate who had died by suicide just nine days before.

Young footballers form bonds when they dream of making it big together, and we will never know what might have become of Wisten, a teenager who wrestled with his release by City. It was a poignant gesture by Palmer to reveal a ‘GBNF’ (‘Gone But Never Forgotten’) undershirt so that his late friend was involved in their first FA Youth Cup triumph since 2008.

Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers have been friends and team-mates since their days in Man City's academy

The pair share a celebration but Rogers' £117m move to Chelsea will also see them share the pitch for the first time in nearly six years

Watching back this final, it is striking how all three of City’s goals involved a player now owned by Chelsea. For their first, Delap occupied Chelsea’s centre backs as Palmer squeezed a pass by Colwill for the unmarked James McAtee to finish.

For their second, Colwill was marking Palmer as Delap crossed and Rogers scored.

For their third, Delap’s saved shot crept to Palmer to complete the 3-2 scoreline, with Colwill smashing the ball into the back of the net in frustration while City celebrated. Now they are all set to be team-mates at Stamford Bridge moving forward in a case of graduates reunited. Once City’s next generation. Suddenly Chelsea’s future.

With Rogers and Palmer in particular, this £117m move from Aston Villa rekindles a friendship, it being no secret that the two are close. They have described each other as best friends in football. They are on WhatsApp and FaceTime almost daily, as we all are with our own pals. Both believed in what the other was capable of achieving back when they were with City, and so for them personally, it is rather nice that they are teaming up again at Chelsea.

While away with England, Rogers’ team-mates liked jesting on the ownership of his celebration. Jude Bellingham was asked during one interview whose was better: his or Rogers’. Sitting next to Rogers, Bellingham pondered and said: ‘Mine or Cole’s?’ Chelsea’s content team will be buzzing with ideas for how they can play on this ‘Cold’ competition.

Rogers did it first while playing for Middlesbrough, but technically, Palmer owns it. He has it trademarked with the UK Intellectual Property Office for commercial reasons. It entered the register in November 2025, and is not due for renewal until November 2034.

Palmer debuted it in a 3-2 win away at Luton in December 2023 and has since told reporters that he did it as ‘a nod’ to Rogers. They’re mates, so Rogers does not mind too much that he pinched it from him. From Chelsea's perspective, they will hope they can score enough goals between them to take turns and share it amicably.

Palmer may have seen this move coming. Before the end of the last season, several Chelsea players held talks with the club’s owners and directors, Palmer included. It was at a time when he was being linked to Manchester United despite Chelsea sources tagging him as one of their untouchable assets. Assurances were made, and also to Reece James when the captain signed his new contract through to 2032. Palmer spoke at length with James about what he was told.

Chelsea has kept a close eye on Rogers since he was at Middlesborough (pictured in 2024)

Palmer celebrated his friend's signing with a touching Instagram post documenting their bond

Chelsea promised they were now going to recruit ‘ready-made’ signings this summer. Missing out on Champions League football – or any form of European qualification for that matter – was a complication. But they have spent big to beat Arsenal to the signing of Rogers. He meets that ‘ready-made’ criteria. James is said to have been pleading his club’s case while they were both away at this summer's World Cup.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso had his first behind-closed-doors friendly at the weekend, with Daily Mail Sport revealing the scoreline was 3-1 and the scorers were Delap, Jamie Gittens and Emmanuel Emegha. One source also told us they used a 4-2-3-1 formation. One solution would be Palmer at No 10 and Rogers on the left, or Rogers at No 10 and Palmer on the right. If Alonso uses a 3-4-2-1, both could feature behind Joao Pedro as the starting striker.

Their versatility gives Alonso options, and while Rogers has been a long-term target for Chelsea, the 44-year-old Spaniard very much sanctioned this transfer after arriving. We can sometimes suspect it is hot air when a new manager is telling us how he is on the same page as those above him, but in this particular case, it is true.

Rogers will be due some downtime after his World Cup exploits with England, three weeks being the usual break. That means he may miss their pre-season tour of Australia and Asia. Whenever he rocks up, coldness could ensue. Certainly, after spending £117m to bring the boys back together, Chelsea hope it will be positively Siberian.

Sports.title: Woking chief hits out at Jermain Defoe by revealing there were 'growing concerns' about him across the club before his shock resignation
Sports.content:
Woking director of football Jody Brown has hit out at Jermain Defoe after he resigned as manager at the National League club earlier this week.

Sources told Daily Mail Sport that Defoe did not turn up to take training on Thursday and later called the club to inform them he would be stepping down after four months in charge.

One source indicated there was internal conflict between Defoe and a member of the Woking hierarchy.

And now, Brown - who has faced heavy criticism from Woking supporters in recent days - has shifted the blame onto Defoe.

Defoe, meanwhile, has posted a picture of him driving a Range Rover captioned 'Who the cap fits, let them wear it' on Instagram - seemingly digging at his former employers.

In a statement, Brown said: 'Jermain Defoe was an outstanding player, scored a vast number of goals, and is a very likeable guy.

'The feeling I get from within the football industry and its global support is not one of great surprise, but of course our own fanbase want and deserve some kind of clarity.

'The recommendation to appoint Jermain as manager was mine, and I take full responsibility for it. After meeting with him on several occasions, I believed he was the right person to lead the club into an exciting new era. As we have seen many times before, success as a player does not always translate into management and leadership. I sincerely hope to see him succeed in whichever direction he follows.

Jermain Defoe resigned as manager of National League side Woking on Thursday

Defoe spent just four months at the non-league club, overseeing six games

'All player recruitment, staffing decisions and football matters were heavily influenced by Jermain, and he was given the necessary operational and board support. Just days before his departure, the club were delighted to finalise the signing of an excellent player identified by Jermain, again illustrating the support the club had given right up until his final day.

'Jermain's feedback was always positive, and he regularly expressed his enthusiasm and excitement for the season, both publicly and privately. I can therefore appreciate the surprise and subsequent speculation surrounding his sudden departure.

'However, in recent weeks there had been feedback from across the club, including players, staff and other departments, regarding growing concerns. To better understand the situation, I asked Jermain and Paul for a brief report outlining the squad's current depth, recruitment targets and any operational challenges, so we could provide the support required and accelerate preparations for the season. That report was requested on more than one occasion but was never received.

'A meeting was subsequently scheduled involving the directors, manager, assistant manager and head of operations to review preparations for the season. Neither Jermain nor his assistant attended that meeting or that day's training session. Throughout his tenure, Jermain had never communicated any serious concerns directly to me.

'Every football club faces challenges. Players want more game time, improved contracts or transfers. The media team might want better equipment, the medical department more interns, the strength and conditioning staff larger gym space and the car park attendants may want more coffee. But people do not just fail to turn up.

'The experience has highlighted lessons for both myself and the club, particularly around communication with Jermain and his representatives throughout the four months and six matches he was with us.'

Brown had teased revelations on X, claiming that Defoe was calling the shots at Woking in response to speculation that Brown had been overstepping in the recruitment operation.

Supporters in the replies, however, pointed to various transfer announcements in which Brown had noted that he had been tracking the players for several years.

'Of the vast number of triallists, I did not choose one,' Brown said. 'Not one. Jermain led all recruitment and all triallists. All Jermain’s contacts, all linked to him. Every single one. Empty promises? We gave everything that was asked. Everything. I’m sure it’ll all come out in due course.'

The Woking job was the first foray into management for former Spurs triker Defoe, capped 57 times by England

Former Spurs striker Defoe lost just one of his six games in charge, as the Surrey-based outfit finished 10th in the fifth tier.

In an Instagram post on Thursday night, Defoe added: 'Following recent discussions, I can confirm that I have mutually agreed to leave my position as manager of Woking FC. Unfortunately, circumstances have ultimately made it impossible for me to continue in the position.

'I am extremely proud of the work undertaken during my time at the club and genuinely felt that we were building something special.

'I would like to thank Todd Johnson for giving me the opportunity to manage the club. I am incredibly grateful to the supporters and, most importantly, the players, who I am genuinely gutted for. The group is a fantastic one, and I wish the squad every success for the season ahead.

'Really disappointed the journey has ended so soon, but I leave with great pride in what Paul Bracewell, Karl Halabi and I were building at the club.

'My time at Woking FC has been an eye-opening managerial experience and one that will undoubtedly make me stronger for the next challenge in my career. JD.'

Former Woking player Jake Hyde and goalkeeper coach/player Craig Ross have taken interim charge at the club.

Sports.title: Lando Norris hits out at F1 bosses for running world championship like a business - with half-electric engines introduced to 'make more money'
Sports.content:
Lando Norris hits out at F1 bosses for running world championship like a business - with half-electric engines introduced to 'make more money'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Lando Norris has taken a swipe at Formula One bosses for running the world championship as a 'business' rather than a sport.

The world champion was alluding to this year's controversial move to half-electric engines that have diluted the purity of racing as the batteries are depleted and recharged each lap, a process partly dictated by AI algorithms.

This has resulted in frequent and random overtaking that has potential to please uninitiated fans but has infuriated drivers and connoisseurs watching at tracks and on TV.

Norris let rip at F1's American owners Liberty Media, who employ Stefano Domenicali as the sport's chief executive, ahead of the Hungarian Grand Prix.

He said: 'Formula One is heavily led by the fact it's a business nowadays, and not about making the sport the best possible.

'It's about how you make the most money. That's not what it should be. That's not how a sport should be run.

'The fact we have hybrids, 50-50 and all that, (is the problem). It's been done because more teams wanted to come in and you make more money.'

Lando Norris is not happy with the way Formula One is currently being run

He was alluding to Audi, who were seeking a move to all-electric road cars in a mission statement that has, ironically, been watered down due to slower than expected sales, being induced on to the grid by the promise of the new technology.

The most vocal critic among the drivers has been four-time world champion Max Verstappen, who derided the new regulations as 'anti-racing' and like 'Mario Kart'.

Norris, whose McLaren team have not won a race this year, does not see a fix on the horizon despite modifications coming in next year and 2028 to reduce the electric element of the power unit.

'You can't just change your engine in the middle of the year, and you can't change it even with one or two years' notice because, as I say, it's not about doing what's best for the performance of a car – it's a business,' he argued. 'It's a shame.'

Asked if spectators can enjoy the hybrid formula, he added: 'Fans from five years ago, pre-Drive to Survive, would hate this.

Four-time world champion Max Verstappen has compared Formula One to Mario Kart

'But fans nowadays are a lot more personality-based, about the drivers, and not about Formula One as a whole sport, so are less interested in how the actual race goes. They care more about whether a driver has done well or not.

'The fans have changed, and that's completely fine. But the biggest voice should always be ours as drivers. That is not because we're selfish and chasing what we want.

'We're saying that because we have the best idea of how racing should be, how it can be, what's possible, what's not. We want the best for everything, the best for the fans, the best viewing, the best racing for us, the most fun to drive.

'At the minute, we don't have that. We have very, very little say. What they have done is because you can have Audi and other teams in F1, and that is a bigger win than the drivers being happy.'

Formula One and the governing FIA are promising to introduce V8 engines in 2031 in a tacit acknowledgement they have got it wrong.

A spokesperson for F1 responded, saying: 'The drivers are listened to more now than ever before. The sport on track is, and always will be, the priority.

‘Everyone has benefited from the commercial success of Formula 1 - the drivers included. Decisions are made for the best strategic outcome for everyone - the fans, teams and partners.’

Sports.title: Erling Haaland leads party-goers in Norway's iconic rowing celebration as he joins Man City stars at team-mate's glamorous Italian wedding
Sports.content:
Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma married his childhood sweetheart yesterday — with a host of his City team-mates in attendance at the lavish reception.

Erling Haaland was among the guests in Fasano, southern Italy, joined by his partner, Isabel Haugseng Johansen.

The Norway star, fresh from accumulating an army of new fans at the World Cup, opted for a black suit, bow-tie and sunglasses as he happily walked hand-in-hand with Johansen.

He was later filmed leading a group of guests in recreating Norway's iconic 'rowing' celebration from the tournament in North America.

City midfielder Mateo Kovacic was also pictured at the wedding. Italian football legend Paolo Maldini, former City boss Pep Guardiola and new Tottenham signing Sandro Tonali were also said to be among the attendees.

Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma married his childhood sweetheart Alessia Elefante in Italy yesterday

City stars Erling Haaland and Mateo Kovacic, joined by their partners Isabel and Izabel, and were among the guests. Haaland later led party-goers in Norway's iconic 'rowing' celebration

Donnarumma and Elefante, an interior designer, have been together for 10 years

Donnarumma, 27, tied the knot with his long-time partner Alessia Elefante, a 28-year-old interior designer.

The pair have been dating for 10 years, having met in their hometown of Castellammare di Stabia, near Naples.

They also have a son together — Leo, born in 2024. The couple announced their engagement in May with an Instagram post that read: 'Long-term contract signed.'

They wed in the Church of Saint George Martyr in the hilltop town of Locorotondo before joining the revellers in Fasano.

Haaland certainly enjoyed the night, excitedly banging a drum as chanting party-goers sat on the floor rowing — copying the post-match celebration that Haaland and his team-mates made famous in their impressive World Cup campaign.

The 26-year-old has been making the most of his break after the tournament, having holidayed in Italy with Johansen this week.

Sports.title: Reports of Aidan O'Brien's disastrous Flat campaign may have been exaggerated... and Benvenuto Cellini could bring him King George joy today
Sports.content:
Mark Twain famously wrote ‘the report of my death was an exaggeration’, after his obituary had been mistakenly published.

That was back in 1897, but a similar sentiment could well apply to Aidan O’Brien’s 2026 Flat campaign which was this week analysed using Timeform’s ‘Run to Form’ metric.

The microscopic scrutiny conducted by the racing organisation revealed that this July is the most unsuccessful month on record for the Ballydoyle handler since the metric was first introduced 14 years ago.

But not only that, Timeform also revealed their data showed that the current Flat season represents the worst for O’Brien since 2012.

Not a great omen then for his four runners in today’s King George VI And Queen Elizabeth Stakes.

O’Brien goes in search of his fifth success in the summer showpiece and should Irish Derby winner Benvenuto Cellini prevail, it will be his first victory with a three-year-old in the Group One since 2001 with Galileo.

But hang on... it seems just five minutes ago that the talk in racing was about O’Brien chasing his own record of Group One wins in a season off the back of a record-equalling seven successes at Royal Ascot.

Benvenuto Cellini goes off at around 5-1 today, behind favourite and defending champion Calandagan

That array of victories came hard on the heels of Christmas Day’s Betfred Derby win at Epsom and preceded a brilliant display by Constitution River in the Coral-Eclipse.

Surely reports of his demise are premature.

A Thursday night Group race double at Leopardstown may signal the Ballydoyle machine is about to crank back into full gear following a brief mid-summer malaise.

One thing we can all take on trust is that it will not be long before O’Brien is once again namechecking his entire roster of staff following another Group One win.

Who knows, it could be after today’s fabulous feature, but with equine stars from around the world tackling Benvenuto Cellini and Minnie Hauk, both Ballydoyle contenders will be required to post clear career bests to prevail.

The market favours last year’s conquering hero Calandagan, who is back to defend his crown. He renews rivalry with Japanese raider Masquerade Ball, who ran him to a head in an epic renewal of the Japan Cup in Tokyo last November.

Calandagan enjoyed a Saint-Cloud confidence booster three weeks ago following his Coronation Cup no-show, while Masquerade Ball lost nothing in defeat attempting to outspeed the imperious Romantic Warrior on his home patch at Sha Tin in the spring.

The old adversaries form a formidable road block for their rivals to navigate, but could last year’s runner-up Kalpana, the home team’s sole representative in a cosmopolitan affair, trouble the overseas posse and hand trainer Andrew Balding an emotional success?

Aidan O'Brien has not won the King George with a three-year-old since 2001

Andrew’s father, Ian, won this prize 55 years ago with one of Flat racing’s all-time greats in the mighty Mill Reef and, although Balding’s mare could not yet be mentioned in those circles, she has at least accumulated an impressive Ascot record.

Her handler is certainly optimistic and his confidence was increased when his star mare worked well in the lead-up to this race as she bids to turn around a length defeat by Calandagan in last year’s renewal.

‘She worked really well, and I’m very happy with her,’ reported Balding.

‘We were struggling to get weight off her last year, but this year it seems to be easier.

‘She’s very good on her day and loves Ascot, so I’m pretty sure she’ll be there or thereabouts. Calandagan is a very good horse. We couldn’t match him last year, but who knows this year?’

Sports.title: How £75m Bruno Guimaraes can take Arsenal to next level: Better numbers than Declan Rice, leading Mikel Arteta's press and how his deep passes unlock low blocks
Sports.content:
How £75m Bruno Guimaraes can take Arsenal to next level: Better numbers than Declan Rice, leading Mikel Arteta's press and how his deep passes unlock low blocks

Unlock more of the best of our journalism with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

Arsenal have been here before with Bruno Guimaraes. The Gunners wanted him four years ago when he was still at Lyon but, in the end, the Brazilian chose Tyneside.

If that were not bad enough, the announcement video he posted on his social media, captioned ‘a beautiful chapter is coming’ began with clippings of news headlines of Arsenal’s interest.

More than four years later and Arsenal are back again. This time, Guimaraes wants them too. He has told Newcastle he wants to join Arsenal and now it’s down to the clubs to thrash it out. A fee of around £75million should do it.

That’s a fair whack for a player about to turn 29, much older than the usual profile of Arsenal signings under Arteta, but in Guimaraes they would have a ready-made addition to take them to the next level, as they bid to retain their first Premier League title in 22 years and expunge the pain of the Champions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain.

As owner Josh Kroenke said at the end of the season: ’It is about trying to stay at the top knowing everyone is trying to climb the mountain after you.’

Guimaraes would help them do that. There’s good reason why Arteta wants him. He’s physical. He’s versatile. He can play box-to-box, deep-lying playmaker or destructor. Or, as we’ll come to see, all of them, all at once.

Arsenal are pushing hard to sign Bruno Guimaraes (left) from Newcastle to bolster their midfield as they bid to retain their Premier League title

Arsenal tried to sign Guimaraes from Lyon in 2022, but were beaten to the signing by Newcastle

The 28-year-old Brazilian has 48 caps for his country, representing them at the last two World Cups

BRUNO'S BRAWNS PL midfielders since Jan 2022 Tackles Joao Palhinha (Fulham/Spurs) 410 Moises Caicedo (Brighton/Chelsea) 408 Joao Gomes (Wolves) 380 Bruno Guimaraes (Newcastle) 356 Alexis Mac Allister (Brighton/Liverpool) 353

BRUNO'S BRAINS PL midfielders since Jan 2022 Open play chances created Bruno Fernandes (Man Utd) 359 Martin Odegaard (Arsenal) 276 Bruno Guimaraes (Newcastle) 197 Morgan Gibbs-White (Wolves/Nottm Forest) 197 Bernardo Silva (Man City) 197

Declan Rice needs a rest. The Arsenal and England midfielder played 69 matches for club and country last season. Arteta ran him into the ground – he has previous for this, just ask Bukayo Saka – and, by the end, you could tell.

He played through a hamstring injury from Christmas onwards and was substituted early in England’s victory over Croatia with ‘neural pain’ in his back.

'The body's been through a lot this season,’ he said after England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina. 'I think you can see I'm mentally done, physically done. I need a break now.’

Only, Arsenal’s title defence starts in less than a month. Having Guimaraes will allow Arteta to rest his linchpin.

But that’s only one reason. He’s Rice, and he’s more. In many ways, he’s the complete central player. Over his four and a half years at Newcastle, he ranked in the top five midfielders for both tackles and chances created from open play. Only Rice and Bruno Fernandes have run more miles since Guimaraes joined the Premier League.

His tenacity out of possession will be ideal for Arteta’s intense press. He wins the ball back but then he does something with it.

What has been clear in recent seasons is how over-reliant Arsenal are down the right and, conversely, how under-served they have been at playing through the middle. Saka is the main source of attacking threat while creator-in-chief Martin Odegaard also likes to drift that side.

Guimaraes is the ideal player to fix that. Nine goals for Newcastle last season was as many as Rice and Zubimendi combined, while his five assists match Rice’s figure.

Declan Rice has admitted he is suffering from neural damage in his lower back and hamstring - and did not appear to be at full fitness during the World Cup

Guimaraes' nine goals for Newcastle last season was as many as Rice and Zubimendi combined, while his five assists matches Rice’s figure

So much of his creativity for Newcastle comes through the middle. As you can see from the chances created maps below, many of Rice's come tucked into the left channel and frequently not until he gets into the final third.

Guimaraes is more focused in central areas and, quite frequently, from deep.

That could be crucial for Arteta. His ability on the ball from deeper areas will allow Arsenal to be quicker and more direct when they have possession, an aspect of their play Arteta is keen to improve if they are to push on once more.

Where Rice creates his chances from, focused largely on the left 'half-space' just outside the box

Guimaraes' map is far more varied, and he is able to create chances from deeper - which will help Arsenal against low blocks

For too long, they have struggled to break down defences with cutting passes and instead turned back to set-pieces or Saka.

Towards the back end of last season, we saw Arsenal try to implement this more, especially in their Champions League semi-final victory over Atletico Madrid where they used the pace of Viktor Gyokeres to exploit space in behind the defence.

William Saliba’s ball (below) led to the move that set up Saka’s winning goal. In the same game, however, the Arsenal crowd got on Rice’s back when he had the chance to do the same but turned it down and passed it sideways.

Guimaraes loves a pass from deep to set his team-mates away. Arsenal know that only too well, Guimaraes having sent a defence-splitting ball through to Jacob Murphy to run clear in their clash early in the season.

He attempted more through balls and line-breaking passes per game than either of them too.

William Saliba chips in behind the PSG defence to find Viktor Gyokeres

But Rice was unable to do the same, and instead passed back inside to Martin Odegaard

Guimaraes showed against Arsenal last season that he is eager to get attacks started rather than build up slowly and allow the defence time to settle

Not only that, though, he can dribble the ball with purpose himself too. Guimaraes created 13 chances for his Newcastle team-mates following ball carries last term, more than both Rice (eight) and Zubimendi (three) combined.

His delivery from set plays, the cornerstone of Arsenal’s attack, is also superb with a couple of assists coming from corners last term.

All of that shows why Arteta wants him, and why he’s so keen to splash the cash on a player that’s not far off 30. Because he can play the Rice role or he can play the Zubimendi (or Myles Lewis-Skelly) one. Rice can sit in, Guimaraes can push on. Or the other way around. He can split defences, he can run at them.

What better way to push on again than by signing a player who can do it all.

Sports.title: English gymnast taken to hospital after sickening fall onto his head at Commonwealth Games
Sports.content:
English gymnast taken to hospital after sickening fall onto his head at Commonwealth Games

Gabriel Langton fell three metres onto his head after missing a grab on the high bars and was taken to hospital in a neck brace and on a stretcher in worrying scenes

View 2 Images Gabriel Langton was brought in to replace Max Whitlock (Image: Naomi Baker/Getty Images)

An English gymnast had to be taken to hospital after landing on his head in a sickening fall at the Commonwealth Games.

‌



Gabriel Langton missed a grab on the horizontal bars and fell three metres onto his head while competing in the men's team gymnastics final in Glasgow on Friday night.

‌



Team England claimed the silver medal, but their success was overshadowed by Langton's injury. He was treated by over 10 medical staff, who put his neck in a brace before taking him away on a stretcher.

‌



The 19-year-old was conscious and could be seen moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena.

A Team England spokesperson said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance. He has been taken to hospital, and we will share more information when it is available."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Gianni Infantino accused of contempt as scale of World Cup private jet travel emerges READ MORE :

The gymnast from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club was brought into the team to replace six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock. After a lengthy delay, his team took silver after failing to overhaul Canada's total.

The injury clearly had an impact on Langton's team-mates, with Luke Whitehouse given the difficult task of following him on the high bar. He could only score 11.70, leaving him in 23rd place for the apparatus overall.

"It was really tough. We just had to reset, try to put it to one side mentally and focus on the job we had to do," Whitehouse said. "I think everyone should be proud of the way we carried on after Gabe's fall. We all agreed we'd take another warm-up and bring our energy back into it. There was a delay after the first warm-up, but we regrouped.

‌



View 2 Images Gabriel Langton was injured while competing for Team England in the gymnastics final (Image: Matthias Hangst/Getty Images)

"The coaches were fantastic, and the boys who had to go up on high bar were incredible. The togetherness of the team really showed, and I couldn't be prouder of everyone."

He added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."

‌



Felix Dolci, who helped Canada win the gold medal, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.

"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one.

"For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."

Article continues below

Hamish Carter from Team Scotland added: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened. We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."

Sports.title: Olympic champions spearheading Emirates GBR's bid for glory on home waters in Portsmouth
Sports.content:
Olympic champions spearheading Emirates GBR's bid for glory on home waters in Portsmouth

Hannah Mills and Dylan Fletcher are backing Team Emirates GBR to bounce back from a freak crash in their last race

View 2 Images Emirates GBR athletes Dylan Fletcher and Hannah Mills and team principal and CEO Sir Ben Ainslie. (Image: Jason Ludlow for SailGP)

Olympic champions Hannah Mills and Dylan Fletcher are hoping to get Team Emirates GBR back to winning ways in their home SailGP race this weekend.

‌



The British team suffered a freak crash at the last race in Halifax, Canada, but have regrouped and are now on a mission in Portsmouth this weekend, in front of 20,000 home supporters. A stellar start to the season has been followed by a slight slump, leaving them level on points with second-placed Los Gallos, from Spain, but a grand final appearance at the end of season is still on the cards.

‌



Mills said: “It was obviously a tough day in Halifax with some damage during the race. A lot of frustration from everyone. But ultimately, it's important for individuals and teams to let that out, have those moments of just being frustrated or whatever the feelings are, and then it's all about how quickly we can come back together.

‌



“Not that long after we got off the water, we came together as a team, we talked about it, we evaluated it and got everyone back on the same page. Since then, we've been building on the learnings and focusing on this event.”

In SailGP, boats exceed 100km/h in close to shore, stadium racing. EGBR are reigning world champions - and will be looking to get a home win in front of a sold-out crowd. The team finished second in Portsmouth’s debut on the SailGP circuit last year and are targeting the top step this time around to move closer to the Grand Final later this year.

Mills, a double Olympics champion in the women’s 470 event in 2016 and 2020, has enjoyed a glittering career, but a win in Portsmouth would be among her finest achievements.

‌



View 2 Images Presenter David Garrido speaks with Hannah Mills, strategist of Emirates Great Britain SailGP Team, and Dylan Fletcher, driver of Emirates Great Britain SailGP Team, during the pre-event press conference in the Adrenaline Lounge ahead of the Emirates Great Britain Sail Grand Prix in Portsmouth (Image: Jason Ludlow for SailGP)

The 38-year-old said: “I think it would be up there. Nothing can compare with racing in front of a home crowd, let alone winning in front of a home crowd, so yeah, it'll be interesting. Hopefully we'll get to find out on Sunday.

“This is one of the longer races we have in SailGP which is nice. Particularly for me as a strategist, it gives me a little bit more time to get your head out and to do a bit more boat on boat strategical decisions.”

‌



Fletcher, the team’s driver, was an Olympic gold medallist at the Tokyo 2020 Games in the men’s 49er event, as well as the helm for INEOS Britannia’s America’s Cup tilt in 2024. And despite his experience, Emirates GBR’s catamaran pitched forward into the water in relatively mild conditions in Halifax.

He said: “It was a very unusual mistake for us, but it's sport and mistakes happen. You always must pick yourself up and move on. We felt as though we haven't delivered our best yet this season, so we're just really looking to build up from here to that grand final when we need to be at our very peak.”

It’s Australia’s Bonds Flying Roos who are leading the way following three wins on the bounce before Canada, but at the halfway point of the season, there are plenty of teams who will fancy their chances of reaching the Grand Final. That includes debutants Artemis, from Sweden, as well as the United States team, lurking just behind the Brits in fourth.

Article continues below

Fletcher said: “We're racing against the world's best from several different classes, with gold medallists from different backgrounds. And what I love about the F50s, and SailGP is all the boats are identical. We have loads of data, but ultimately it comes down to sailor skill.

“As with any event we want to win, but this is one we want to win most outside the Grand Final. But in reality, this is about the big picture building up through the season. There's lots of jeopardy. If we can just come away from the weekend feeling as though we've sailed well, then we'll be happy. But we also know if we sail well, we'll be at the top.”

The Emirates Great Britain Sail Grand Prix returns to Portsmouth on 25-26 July. Limited tickets are still available via //SailGP.com/Portsmouth .

Sports.title: Caoimhin Agyarko used stabbing to fuel attempt at creating history
Sports.content:
Caoimhin Agyarko used stabbing to fuel attempt at creating history

Caoimhin Agyarko will challenge super-welterweight world champion Josh Kelly tonight as he attempts to fulfil his dream

View Image Caoimhin Agyarko challenges for a world title tonight

Caoimhin Agyarko will always carry the scars.

‌



Not just the seven-inch reminder staring back at him in the mirror every morning. But also the mental trauma which lingers nine years after he was stabbed in an unprovoked attack. Agyarko came within inches of death when he was assaulted by a gang in Belfast at the age of 20.

‌



The Irishman found himself having to choose between revenge and motivation. He opted for the latter and tonight has the chance to become Ireland's first black world champion when he takes on Josh Kelly. "I don't think I'll ever mentally recover fully from it," Agyarko admitted.

‌



Anthony Joshua's injuries from car crash revealed before comeback fight READ MORE :

"I've come a hell of a long way since then in terms of what it took from me, but it has also given me a lot. I think it changed my mindset and made me realise that if I wanted to achieve something in boxing that I have to give it my all and live with no regrets. As much as it sounds crazy, I think I'm a better person for getting stabbed.

"I have to look at my scar every single day knowing nobody was ever found guilty and nobody was ever arrested. The guy who stabbed me is still running the streets and living his life The main thing for me is the fact I had to make a very tough decision over whether to seek revenge or continue to chase greatness.

Article continues below

"I had to put my ego and pride to the side which was a very hard thing to do, but I knew the greater cause was to become the first black Irish world champion, and I couldn't mess up those plans because one person did something to me." Agyarko was born in London before moving to Belfast aged seven and the super-welterweight admits he stood out in his white neighbourhood.

"It was difficult in the early years because mine was one of the first mixed-race families in west Belfast," Agyarko added. "It was very unusual for the local people to see someone who was mixed-race. "When I moved to Belfast, I had an English accent and I think it was confusing for them.

"At the start they didn't really think I belonged there, but because my family's Irish, I’ve always considered myself Irish. I always felt like I was one of them and not long after, the British accent faded and I was treated like one of their own. I want to leave a legacy behind that says no matter where you're from, what culture or religion you are, you can achieve great things. I'm just a regular kid from Belfast trying to achieve something great."

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua fight undercard, running order and exact fight times
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua fight undercard, running order and exact fight times

Former two-time heavyweight world champion Anthony Joshua will look to secure a fight with long-time rival Tyson Fury with a win over Kristian Prenga tonight

View Image Anthony Joshua takes on Kristian Prenga tonight

Anthony Joshua will look to make his highly-anticipated fight with Tyson Fury official by beating Kristian Prenga later this evening.

‌



The former two-time heavyweight world champion saw his long-time rival Fury get the job done on Friday night after he forced Mariusz Wach to quit on his stool in their behind closed doors encounter in Thailand. Now, all eyes are on Joshua to see how he fares on his return to the ring.

‌



Providing 'AJ' comes away unscathed, he will trade leather with Fury later this year. While an official date or venue is yet to be announced, the pair are expected to fight in November. But unknown heavyweight Prenga will look to spoil the party over in Saudi Arabia. The 35-year-old Albanian has not fought at the top level, but truly believes he has the power to stop Joshua. And so, here are the official UK start times for tomorrow's fights...

‌

Anthony Joshua vs Kristian Prenga - 11pm

Anthony Joshua is back for the first time since his destructive six-round knockout victory over YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul. The former two-time heavyweight champion was due to return back in March but was involved in a tragic car crash just days after his win over Paul. While many assumed he would retire, the Brit is back for one last run. The 36-year-old will take on unknown heavyweight Kristian Prenga - with the Albanian vowing to score a monumental upset.

Hamzah Sheeraz vs Simon Zachenhuber - 9:40pm

Playing chief support tonight, British star Hamzah Sheeraz will defend his WBO super middleweight title for the first time against Simon Zachenhuber. Sheeraz, 27, picked up the title in dominant fashion after knocking out Alem Begic in the second round at the Pyramids of Giza back in May. Many were left stunned after Zachenhuber was awarded a crack at the title soon after his shock defeat to Pawel August, but the German will be itching to show why he is one of the best in the division with a huge upset in Jeddah.

‌



Josh Kelly vs Caoimhin Agyarko - 8:37pm

Josh Kelly knows he is in for a tough test this evening when he defends his IBF light-middleweight title for the first time against Caoimhin Agyarko. Sunderland native Kelly showed real heart en route to defeating Bakhram Murtazaliev for the coveted gold strap earlier this year. But undefeated Irishman Agyarko will not go down without a fight as he has aspirations of snatching Kelly's coveted prize away from him.

Reito Tsutsumi vs Alvino Herrera Meza - 7:43pm

23-year-old super-featherweight contender Reito Tsutsumi is a real star in the making. After a glittering amateur career, the undefeated Japanese sensation turned pro last year and has taken to the professional ranks like a duck to water - winning three of his first four fights by way of knockout. But he faces a tough step up in competition against the hard-hitting Alvino Herrera Meza.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua ready to defy Tyson Fury in build-up to mega-fight
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua ready to defy Tyson Fury in build-up to mega-fight

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury are on a collision course for later this year and Joshua has vowed not to let his trash-talking rival get under his skin

View Image Anthony Joshua gestures towards Tyson Fury

Anthony Joshua has vowed to haunt Tyson Fury long after they belatedly settle their bitter rivalry.

‌



The two British heavyweights each ruled the world in their prime without ever crossing paths in the ring. But providing Joshua, 36, swats aside Kristian Prenga tonight, he and Fury, 37, will finally collide later this year. Their long-awaited showdown will be a clash of personalities as much as a contrast of fighting styles.

‌



Joshua has held his tongue for a decade in the face of a tirade of abuse from his fellow countryman. The Olympic champion has been a poster boy for his bluechip sponsors while Fury thinks nothing of crossing the line between class and crass. The Gypsy King believes he can shatter his rival's corporate veneer and expose his raw working-class roots. But Joshua is confident he won't let his mask slip.

‌



Watch Anthony Joshua vs Kristian Prenga live on DAZN This article contains affiliate links, we will receive a commission on any sales we generate from it. Learn more £19.99 or £0 DAZN Order the fight here Product Description Anthony Joshua returns to the ring to face Kristian Prenga on Saturday, July 25, in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Fans can order the fight on DAZN PPV for £19.99 or watch it at no extra cost with DAZN Ultimate.

"Tyson Fury won't get under my skin," he said. "It's about boxing and it's about skill; I'm not trying to win a press conference, I'm not trying to win a weigh-in. I'm trying to win a fight. I don't think the Anthony Joshua from Watford needs to come out in that aspect, it needs to come out in the ring. I will let him talk and let him have his fun.

‌



"I've seen Fury's community, and they're unbelievable talkers; that's the culture they're from. They have no problem calling each other out and saying, 'I'll drive 60 miles next week and meet you down there'. I can't go up against someone who has been doing it since he was 10 years old and think I'm going to win.

"I've got to let him do what he's good at, and my job is to beat him in the ring. There will be nothing better than getting my hand raised." Fury has taken every opportunity to run his mouth throughout his colourful career. He has even allowed Netflix into every crevice of his life through his hit series At Home With The Furys.

But while Joshua is happy to remain in the shadows for now, he is relishing the day that changes. "I'm too tired half the time, to be honest," he added. "My main focus is the sport and it's draining. Just trying to achieve a little bit in boxing is draining. It's not just turning up and training, it's trying to make the right decisions, trying to sleep better... it's a lot of pressure

Article continues below

"I don't know how Fury has the energy for it, to be honest; he boxes, he does Netflix, and he talks! I don't really get too involved in the he-said-she-said, but once this part of my life is done, you'll hear a lot more from me. When Fury wants to relax, when he's finished, I'll just be revving it up and he will see me coming.

"I'll let him win the first 100m, the first 200m, but after that I will still be going. It will be that last 100m, when the race is ending, that I will be coming for him."

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
