World.title: Why public servants have less than a month to update pension records
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Public servants given until August 14 to update pension records [File]

Government has directed all public servants to update their records with the Public Service Superannuation Fund (PSSF) by August 14, 2026, in the latest step towards modernising pension administration.

In a circular signed by Principal Secretary for Public Service and Human Capital Development Dr Jane Imbunya, all PSSF members are expected to update their personal information and beneficiary details through the PSSF Member Self-Service Portal or the PSSF Mobile Application.

The circular was addressed to Ministries, State Departments, Constitutional Commissions, Independent Offices, County Public Service Boards and County Governments.

The exercise is expected to streamline pension administration and accelerate the processing of retirement benefits supported by a new Pension Administration System (PAS), a digital platform developed by PSSF to deliver faster, more transparent and more efficient pension services.

The registration exercise targets 529,635 members drawn from across the public service, including 332,950 teachers under the Teachers Service Commission (TSC), 120,084 officers in the disciplined services, 60,322 employees in Ministries, Departments, Constitutional Commissions and Agencies (MDCAs), and 16,279 county government employees.

PSSF Chief Executive Jonah Aiyabei said updating member records is critical to the success of the pension reforms and the delivery of efficient retirement services.

“By updating their records, public servants will enable quicker processing of retirement benefits, reduce administrative delays, improve data integrity, allow members to access pension services seamlessly through digital channels and ensure that the right benefits reach the right beneficiaries at the right time,” he said.

Under the new system, members can access their pension statements in real time, monitor contributions, view projected retirement benefits, update beneficiary nominations and personal details and initiate and track pension claims remotely.

The platform also features a Sponsor Portal that enables employer institutions to submit payroll information, contribution schedules and member data electronically, significantly improving efficiency and accountability in pension administration.

Dr Aiyabei said the Pension Administration System marks a significant milestone in the government’s efforts to digitise pension administration and restore dignity to retirees through faster, more accessible and transparent services.

“It will provide our members with real-time access to their pension information, enable seamless engagement with the Fund and support a fully digital, paperless pension administration process. Ultimately, our goal is to restore dignity in old age by ensuring every public servant receives timely and efficient pension services,” he said.

World.title: Inside Kenya's Ebola defences as seven Americans enter quarantine
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A doctor provides care to a patient with Ebola virus disease at the Rwampara Ebola Treatment Centre (ETC) in Bunia, Ituri, July 13, 2026. [AFP]

Seven American humanitarian workers are spending 21 days under medical observation in Kenya not because they are ill, but because they could become ill.

A Reuters report published today confirms they are seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART) staff from the Christian humanitarian organisation Samaritan's Purse . Franklin Graham, the organisation's President and CEO, confirmed this, saying:

“Samaritan's Purse has seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team staff members there. None of them have any symptoms, but they are being quarantined by the Kenyan government for 21 days."

The aid workers, all returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where they were involved in responding to the world's largest recorded outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, have no symptoms and have not tested positive for the virus.

Yet under new US public health rules, they cannot travel home immediately. Instead, they are completing a precautionary quarantine on Kenyan soil.

Their arrival has reignited debate over Kenya's role in regional outbreak preparedness and raised a question that extends far beyond the fate of the seven Americans:

If Ebola crossed Kenya's borders tomorrow, is the country ready?

The answer, infectious disease experts say, lies not in panic but in years of quiet preparation that most Kenyans have never seen.

That preparedness became evident during a recent visit by The Standard to Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH), where access to one of the hospital's high-security isolation areas was restricted.

Hospital officials informed the reporting team that patients with Mpox were being managed in the unit and, for safety reasons, journalists were not allowed to enter or film inside.

The brief encounter offered a glimpse into the strict infection prevention measures that underpin Kenya's readiness for dangerous infectious diseases.

According to an infectious disease physician at the Kenyatta National Hospital and head of the isolation ward, preparedness is far more than having an isolation room.

"One thing we should never do as Kenyans is panic," he says. "Panic only makes the situation worse. Instead, we should ask ourselves one question: Are we prepared?"

His answer is unequivocal. "As a government and as health institutions, we are in preparedness mode."

Dr Nyukuri explains that preparedness begins long before the first patient arrives at a hospital.

It means evaluating whether enough trained personnel are available, whether laboratories have the necessary testing reagents, whether protective equipment is adequate, and whether health workers understand every step required to safely manage a suspected Ebola patient.

"Here at Kenyatta National Hospital, we have conducted extensive training for healthcare workers," he says. "We have carried out readiness assessments, simulated patient scenarios and practised every stage of care from the moment a suspected patient arrives, through admission, isolation and treatment."

The simulations, he explains, are designed to ensure that no decision is being made for the first time during a real emergency. "When we eventually encounter a suspected case, it should not be something new to us." Dr Duncan Nyukuri, an Infectious Diseases specialist, during an interview with The Standard on July 16, 2026 at Kenyatta National Hospital. [Benard Orwongo, Standard]

Preparedness also extends beyond hospitals. Health surveillance teams remain stationed at airports and land border crossings, screening travellers arriving from affected regions while rapid response teams stand ready to investigate suspected infections.

"So far, Kenya has done a good job," Dr Nyukuri says. "We have not recorded a confirmed case despite the increasing numbers in the DRC. We pray that remains the case. But if we receive one patient, we are prepared."

How Ebola jumps from animals to people

Although Ebola is often associated with outbreaks, the virus begins its journey quietly in nature.

Dr Nyukuri explains that fruit bats are believed to be the natural reservoir of the virus. "They carry the virus without becoming sick themselves," he says.

Problems arise when increasing human activity brings people into closer contact with wildlife.

Mining, logging, hunting, charcoal burning, expanding settlements and encroachment into forests all increase the likelihood of viruses crossing from animals into humans.

"We call these zoonotic diseases," Dr Nyukuri explains. "Once the virus infects a human being, it can then spread from person to person through contact with infected body fluids, leading to outbreaks within families and communities."

You see, Ebola is a family; many people speak about Ebola as though it were a single virus.

In reality, scientists recognise five different species.

The best known is the Zaire strain, responsible for the devastating West African epidemic between 2014 and 2016.

"It is highly infectious and highly deadly," says Dr Nyukuri. "But because we have studied it extensively, we now have licensed vaccines and effective treatment options."

The Sudan strain, which has repeatedly caused outbreaks in Uganda, is the second most significant.

The current emergency, however, involves the Bundibugyo strain, first identified in Uganda's Bundibugyo District.

"This is the third recorded outbreak caused by Bundibugyo," Dr Nyukuri explains. "We have not studied it nearly as much as the Zaire strain."

There is currently no licensed vaccine specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola.

Instead, researchers are evaluating experimental vaccines while clinical trials in eastern DRC are testing promising treatments, including the monoclonal antibody MBP134 and the antiviral drug remdesivir.

"That is why this outbreak concerns many of us," he says. "We still have limited tools compared to what exists for the Zaire strain."

While Kenya has not recorded a confirmed case linked to the current outbreak, neighbouring countries remain on high alert.

Uganda on Thursday declared its last Ebola patient and has begun the mandatory 42-day countdown required before the country can officially be declared Ebola-free.

In contrast, eastern DRC continues battling sustained transmission, placing enormous pressure on treatment centres and frontline health workers.

It is against that backdrop that Kenya has found itself playing an increasingly important role in regional preparedness.

Their presence has nevertheless fuelled public debate over Kenya's preparedness infrastructure and the country's place in global health security.

Earlier this week, two American humanitarian workers who contracted Ebola while working in eastern DRC were medically evacuated to Germany for specialised treatment after receiving initial care in Bunia. Their evacuation underscores an important distinction: Kenya is currently serving as a precautionary observation site for exposed but healthy personnel, while confirmed Ebola patients requiring advanced clinical care have been transferred to Germany.

For Dr Nyukuri, the conversation should remain grounded in science rather than fear.

Preparedness, he says, is not measured only by isolation wards or specialised equipment, but by the ability of an entire health system to detect threats early, respond quickly and protect both patients and healthcare workers.

"My prayer is that Kenya never records a case," he says. "But preparedness means planning for the day you hope never comes."

As seven healthy humanitarian workers quietly complete their quarantine in Kenya, that preparation is no longer an abstract exercise.

It is being tested in real time. The development has also drawn attention to the contrasting roles played by East African countries during the current outbreak.

Uganda, widely regarded as one of Africa's most experienced countries in responding to Ebola, recently brought its own outbreak under control and has now entered the 42-day countdown required to be declared Ebola-free. Over the years, the country has built a reputation for rapidly detecting cases, tracing contacts and isolating patients, earning praise from the World Health Organization for repeatedly containing outbreaks before they spread widely.

Yet despite that experience, Uganda did not become a destination for foreign humanitarian workers requiring precautionary quarantine or post-exposure observation.

Instead, that role has fallen to Kenya, where seven American aid workers are now completing a mandatory 21-day quarantine after working in Ebola-affected areas of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

The contrast raises broader questions about how countries are selected to support international outbreak responses. While Uganda has demonstrated its capacity to treat Ebola patients within its own borders, Kenya's involvement appears to reflect a different function—serving as a precautionary observation site for exposed personnel rather than a treatment centre for confirmed cases.

Health experts caution against interpreting the distinction as a measure of either country's clinical capability. Instead, they say such decisions are often influenced by a combination of bilateral agreements, operational logistics, evacuation arrangements and the specific objectives of international public health partners.

World.title: MPs push for urgent resolution of higher education funding crisis
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

HELB Chief Executive Officer Geoffrey Monari before the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Education on July 16, 2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

The National Assembly Departmental Committee on Education has called for urgent and coordinated action to address persistent funding challenges affecting Kenya's higher education sector.

The MPs proposed a joint engagement involving Parliament, the National Treasury and the Ministry of Education to streamline implementation of the Higher Education Funding Model.

The committee, chaired by Vice Chairperson Eve Obara, made the recommendation after holding separate meetings with officials from the State Department for Higher Education, the Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) and the Universities Fund during a review of the 2025/2026 Budget Implementation Status.

Appearing before the committee, Higher Education Principal Secretary Dr. Beatrice Inyangala said the Higher Education Funding Model is operational but continues to face implementation challenges due to inadequate alignment between the funding framework and budget allocations.

"The funding model is functional. However, the main challenge lies in budget alignment," Dr. Inyangala told Members.

The funding model was introduced to allocate financial support to university students based on their level of need, while ensuring sustainable financing for public universities.

However, implementation has generated debate over affordability, funding adequacy and delays in disbursement of resources to institutions.

MPs observed that the mismatch between policy and budgetary allocations has undermined effective financing of universities and agreed that a joint meeting involving the National Treasury, the Ministry of Education and Parliament would help harmonise the funding framework.

The committee also sought explanations over the growing stock of pending bills owed by public universities.

Dr. Inyangala informed Members that most of the outstanding obligations were inherited over several years, with universities continuing efforts to clear the debts despite increasing interest charges.

According to the State Department for Higher Education, public universities had accumulated pending bills amounting to Sh100.3 billion as of January 2026.

The ministry said institutions are prioritising settlement of pending obligations, suspending stalled development projects and exploring alternative revenue streams to prevent further accumulation of debt.

During a separate session, Members questioned HELB officials on how the board allocates student loans when available funding cannot meet demand from all eligible applicants.

Led by Chief Executive Officer Geoffrey Monari, HELB officials were asked to explain the criteria used in determining beneficiaries during periods of constrained resources.

Legislators emphasised that the allocation process should be fair, transparent and predictable to protect deserving students from being unfairly excluded.

World.title: Egyptian, Dutch FMs discuss strengthening bilateral relations, regional developments
World.content:
Foreign Minister, International Cooperation, and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty welcomed the progress witnessed in Egyptian-Dutch relations in recent years during a meeting on Friday, July 24, 2026, with Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen.

The meeting was held on the sidelines of Abdelatty’s participation in the ASEAN Ministerial Meeting in Manila, where the two sides discussed ways to strengthen bilateral relations and exchanged views on regional developments.

Abdelatty expressed Egypt’s keenness to continue enhancing bilateral ties across various fields, stressing the importance of capitalizing on promising opportunities to boost economic relations and increase Dutch investments in Egypt, particularly in new economic zones, major national projects, port and infrastructure development, digitalization, artificial intelligence, and green hydrogen.

He also voiced Egypt’s aspiration to strengthen cooperation on issues of mutual interest, especially migration and water management, while praising the Netherlands’ support for Egypt within various European Union institutions.

The two ministers discussed a number of regional issues, foremost among them the Palestinian cause.

Abdelatty stressed the importance of completing the implementation of the commitments of the first phase of the US president’s plan, ensuring the full and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip, expediting the work of the committee tasked with administering the Strip, and the swift deployment of the international stabilization force.

He also called for an end to Israeli violations in the West Bank to help contain escalation and create conditions for restoring security and stability in the region.

Regarding the rapidly unfolding developments in the region, Abdelatty stressed the need to de-escalate tensions, prioritize diplomacy and dialogue, and adhere to the memorandum of understanding signed between the United States and Iran, with the aim of resuming negotiations and reaching a final agreement between the two sides.

The Egyptian foreign minister briefed his Dutch counterpart on Egypt’s intensive efforts to reduce tensions in the region, emphasizing the importance of concerted international efforts in this regard in light of the severe economic, security and geopolitical repercussions of the war on the region and the world as a whole.

World.title: FM highlights Egypt’s investment potential at Philippine business roundtable
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty participated on Friday, July 24, 2026, in a roundtable discussion with leading Philippine business executives and representatives of the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PCCI), in the presence of a delegation of Egyptian business leaders.

The meeting was held on the sidelines of his participation in the 59th ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting (AMM) in Manila.

In his remarks, Abdelatty said Egyptian-Philippine relations are gaining momentum, reflecting the shared political will to strengthen bilateral cooperation.

He described the Philippines as an important partner for Egypt in Southeast Asia and expressed Egypt’s keenness to expand economic and investment ties between the two countries.

The minister reviewed recent developments in the Egyptian economy and outlined the structural reforms undertaken to improve the investment climate and enhance competitiveness.

He also highlighted major national projects that have upgraded infrastructure and created a more attractive business environment, pointing to promising investment opportunities in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, new and renewable energy, food industries, logistics, tourism and the digital economy.

Abdelatty underlined Egypt’s strategic position as a gateway to African and Arab markets, emphasizing the country’s competitive advantages for investors.

He also reaffirmed the Egyptian government’s commitment to strengthening the role of the private sector as a key driver of economic growth.

He called for expanding partnerships between the business communities of the two countries, boosting trade and investment, and stepping up contacts between Egyptian and Philippine companies to explore new opportunities and launch joint ventures.

The foreign minister further stressed Egypt’s commitment to deepening ties with Asian countries and strengthening its partnership with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), citing the bloc’s growing economic influence and the opportunities it offers for expanding trade and investment cooperation to the mutual benefit of both sides.

Abdelatty also witnessed the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the Federation of Egyptian Chambers of Commerce and the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry to strengthen cooperation between the business communities of the two countries.

The roundtable included discussions with representatives of leading Philippine companies, during which Abdelatty highlighted investment opportunities in Egypt and answered questions on the investment climate, economic reforms and incentives available to investors.

He affirmed the readiness of the relevant Egyptian authorities to provide all necessary support and address any challenges facing investors seeking to enter the Egyptian market.

Representatives of the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry and leading Philippine business executives praised Egypt’s economic progress and comprehensive reform program, expressing interest in exploring investment opportunities and strengthening cooperation with their Egyptian counterparts to further expand bilateral economic ties.

World.title: FM affirms Egypt’s commitment to developing relations with Timor-Leste
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty affirmed Egypt’s keenness to further strengthen relations with Timor-Leste during a meeting on Friday, July 24, 2026, with Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation of the Democratic Republic of Timor-Leste Bendito dos Santos Freitas on the sidelines of the ASEAN Ministerial Meeting in Manila, the Philippines.

Abdelatty highlighted the importance Egypt attaches to developing bilateral ties, noting that this year marks the 20th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries.

He said the relationship is built on a distinguished historical foundation, particularly Egypt’s participation in UN peacekeeping missions in Timor-Leste before and after independence, which provides a solid basis for advancing cooperation in the coming period.

The Egyptian foreign minister congratulated Timor-Leste on joining ASEAN, expressing hope that its membership would enhance its integration into the regional cooperation framework and open broader prospects for development, capacity building, and economic and technical cooperation.

Abdelatty stressed Egypt’s growing interest in strengthening ties with ASEAN countries as part of its foreign policy approach to expanding partnerships with influential regional blocs and benefiting from opportunities in Southeast Asia to serve common interests and support development and stability.

The minister reviewed prospects for expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in training and capacity building, including agricultural cooperation through grants offered by the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA), support for capacity building in the petroleum sector, joint training programs for military and police personnel participating in UN peacekeeping missions, cooperation in disaster response, and the revival of diplomatic training programs for Timorese officials through the Egyptian Diplomatic Institute.

In the cultural and educational fields, Abdelatty praised existing cooperation between the two countries, highlighting scholarships provided by Al-Azhar Al-Sharif to Timorese students, which contribute to preparing qualified cadres to support development efforts in Timor-Leste.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the two ministers stressed the importance of maintaining coordination and consultations in international forums and strengthening cooperation on issues of mutual interest, including support for each other’s candidacies in international organizations, reflecting the friendly relations and shared interests between Egypt and Timor-Leste.

World.title: FM: Egypt views preventive diplomacy as cornerstone for preserving security, stability
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty affirmed on Friday, July 24, 2026, that Egypt believes preventive diplomacy is one of the most important tools for maintaining security and stability.

He stressed that its success requires adopting a comprehensive approach based on supporting national state institutions, promoting economic and social development, building peace, and addressing the root causes of conflicts in order to prevent their outbreak or recurrence.

Abdelatty made the remarks in a speech delivered on Friday during his participation in the High-Level Conference of High Contracting Parties to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC), held in Manila, the capital of the Philippines.

The minister said Egypt’s participation in the conference reflects the country’s foreign policy approach of strengthening engagement with influential regional groupings, particularly ASEAN, and enhancing relations with Southeast Asian countries.

He noted that such engagement contributes to expanding areas of political, economic and developmental cooperation, while enhancing coordination and consultations on regional and international issues of common interest, in light of ASEAN’s growing role in supporting security, stability and development.

During his address, Abdelatty outlined Egypt’s vision on ways to advance preventive diplomacy and prevent conflicts, noting that the world is facing growing challenges amid escalating crises and conflicts and their increasingly interconnected dimensions.

He stressed the need to strengthen joint international efforts to address the root causes of conflicts and mitigate their repercussions, which are no longer confined to the countries where they occur but increasingly affect international peace and security, economic stability and development efforts, particularly in developing countries.

The foreign minister highlighted the importance of bolstering multilateral action and supporting the role of the United Nations and regional organizations, including the African Union, the League of Arab States and ASEAN, in enhancing the international community’s ability to respond to shared challenges while taking into account the priorities and needs of countries of the Global South.

He also underscored the need to continue efforts to reform the international financial system and increase investments in development, infrastructure and basic services, describing them as key elements in promoting stability and addressing the drivers of conflict.

Abdelatty pointed to the importance of strengthening international cooperation in confronting cross-border challenges, particularly terrorism and organized crime, through respect for state sovereignty, enhanced information exchange and cutting off terrorist financing sources.

He added that supporting peacebuilding and national reconciliation efforts, while promoting a culture of dialogue and tolerance, would contribute to strengthening societal stability and protecting communities from the risks of extremism and violence.

The minister concluded his remarks by affirming that investing in preventive diplomacy, enhancing multilateral cooperation and promoting values of moderation and tolerance through religious institutions and responsible media represent essential pillars for building a more stable international order capable of addressing current challenges, achieving international peace and security, and supporting sustainable development.

World.title: Trump bombed at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner — and proved its point
World.content:
President Donald Trump bombed at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner Friday night. He knew he was bombing, too, and he even tried to meta-joke his way out of it.

But no. Even the president’s jokes about his bad jokes fell flat, and he was widely ridiculed for the comedy routine afterward.

Members of the media mocking the leader’s dismal performance on live TV and all across the internet? In some other countries, that’s a criminal offense. But in the US, it’s the norm, so maybe Trump’s speech unwittingly underscored the theme of the dinner: America’s robust First Amendment protections.

In a rambling hour-long speech, Trump insulted journalists by name, repurposed old nicknames for political opponents, made a strange number of fat jokes that weren’t funny at all, and sounded mad at his unnamed writers for giving him weak material to work with. “Does anyone understand this stuff?” he said at one point, and the answer was generally no.

Some of Trump’s remarks were “vicious,” as press secretary Karoline Leavitt promised. But more than anything, the speech was just… boring.

And boring is one thing Trump never, ever wants to be. He claimed to be singlehandedly keeping the news business afloat, commenting, “When I’m gone, you’re all going to be broke.”

“Nobody gives a damn about anybody else,” he said, and proceeded to count how many stories on The New York Times front page are about him.

Trump’s low energy led more than one TV executive to muse that the president had stumbled upon a new technique against the media: Tank the ratings with a snoozefest.

Some attendees said they were surprised that Trump didn’t bring more original material, given how highly anticipated the dinner was, in part because his attendance ended his years-long boycott of the White House Correspondents’ Association’s annual fundraiser.

Friday’s dinner was a smaller-scale redo of the April 26 black-tie affair that was postponed after a gunman tried to rush into the ballroom of the Washington Hilton hotel.

The do-over dinner was held across town at the Waldorf Astoria, a building Trump once operated as his namesake DC hotel — and an unofficial clubhouse for his first administration.

“See those beautiful chandeliers? I can tell you everything about them,” he threatened.

Trump did strike some notes of unity, praising the Secret Service and denouncing political violence. “In this country, we believe in freedom of speech,” he said. “We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate. And no deranged loser with a gun will ever change that.”

Then he joked about dinnergoers wearing bulletproof vests under their fancy outfits, “which many people didn’t want to wear because they’d rather die than look 20 pounds heavier.”

Trump covets control of media

Trump’s remarks showed how he understands the power of the press — and that he gets angry when he can’t control it. He singled out several CNN journalists by name.

In response, CNN CEO Mark Thompson said in a statement, “We stand by our journalists and the integrity and fairmindedness with which the CNN team reports the news. Honest, accurate journalism may sometimes irritate politicians, but our right to report and present that reporting to the public without government interference is fully protected by the US Constitution. CNN will continue to exercise this right.”

Trump also gave shoutouts to media executives whom he views as allies, namely Larry and David Ellison, who took control of Paramount last year and are now trying to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN’s parent company. Paramount suffered a major setback earlier on Friday when it agreed to accept a months-long delay to the merger while legal challenges are resolved.

Invoking the fact that Paramount owns CBS News, Trump said David Ellison is “going to make, I think, fantastic changes and keep some of the great stuff going.”

Trump also made a convoluted joke about the controversial changes implemented by Ellison’s handpicked editor-in-chief of CBS News, Bari Weiss: “Under my administration, a once-feared and powerful regime that relentlessly attacked America has finally been toppled. Their former leaders have been removed, and they’re now being run by a gay dictator facing internal divisions. But I, for one, wish Bari Weiss all the best at CBS News. She’s a wonderful woman.”

Toward the end of the speech, the president donned a red “Trump 2028” hat. His choice of attire seemed like a deliberate troll, given the outrage that erupts every time he talks about a constitutionally barred third term.

He also said that he was only kidding about running again. Earlier in the evening, during a lengthy digression about his White House ballroom addition, he remarked that “I’m only going to be using it for about six months” before leaving office, a rare acknowledgment that his term has an expiration date.

Losing the room

The more resentful and recycled Trump’s speech got, the more attendees seemed to tune it out.

CNN’s Betsy Klein, who was in the room, said many people were on their phones or talking amongst themselves. Others were eating macarons from the dessert trays, using the bathroom or mingling in the lobby.

“The person at the table next to me has just poured himself a comically large glass of wine,” she observed nearly an hour in.

CNN’s Kristen Holmes said a Republican source of hers in the room said to her, “Whoever wrote this speech should be fired.”

But a few of the jabs will surely travel well on right-wing social media platforms, and Daniel Dale predicted that “the silence in the room will be portrayed by the president’s allies as evidence he roasted the ‘fake news’ so bad they were stunned into submission.”

One of the most intriguing parts of the evening involved the correspondents’ association’s annual journalism awards presentation. Trump sat through multiple prizes, including one for “courage and accountability” in reporting that went to a team of Wall Street Journal reporters for their investigative work on a lewd birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein bearing Trump’s name.

“Trump quickly filed a $20 billion lawsuit against the Journal, revealing reporter Khadeeja Safdar’s home address,” CNN’s Wolf Blitzer said while presenting the award.

Trump laughed and threw up his hands in an aw shucks-like gesture.

“Her family had to be relocated,” Blitzer continued. “The Journal was kicked off of Air Force One, but the reporters continued to file revelatory stories.”

Trump then stood up and shook hands with each reporter. He is currently suing the Journal’s parent company over the investigation, and legal experts say he will most likely lose the case.

The outgoing president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, Weijia Jiang, introduced Trump after discussing the importance of press freedom. Jiang drafted her remarks knowing that the president would be sitting next to her and listening.

Jiang said there is “an existential difference between criticizing the press and trying to undermine it. One is healthy, and it makes all of us better. The other is exactly what the founders hoped to prevent.”

The CBS correspondent also addressed Trump directly: “When we ask questions, you push back. You give us answers, and we push back. You have always been a deal guy. Well, that’s the deal. And the First Amendment is a done deal. And that’s what we toast tonight.”

World.title: Firefighters battle one of Spain’s biggest-ever wildfires during heat wave across the Mediterranean
World.content:
The fire in rural Guadalajara comes less than two weeks after a deadly blaze devastated a small expat community in southern Spain. That small but extremely virulent fire killed 13 people, including several foreigners, in one of the southern European country’s deadliest wildfires.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Wednesday visited the fire-ravaged area in Guadalajara, and called for a pact between political parties to fight climate change.

Firefighters battling the La Mierla fire on Tuesday. Ana Beltran/Reuters

“Year after year we clearly see how climate change kills and destroys wealth in our communities,” Sánchez said in the village of Tamajón, located less than two hours by car northeast of Madrid. “This isn’t politics. It is science, it’s about facts.”

Some 34 villages have been evacuated in the area but there are no reported serious injuries or deaths. More than 200 firefighters were supported by land vehicles and aircraft on Wednesday.

Spain this year has already suffered 22 major forest fires, defined as a fire that burns more than 500 hectares (1,235 acres.)

A helicopter helps the operation on July 22. Lorena Sopena/Europa Press/Getty Images

The Socialist leader said more than 100,000 hectares (247,000 acres) had already been scorched through the first half of the year, matching the total yearly average for Spain over the last decade.

Spain’s Minister for Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, described the Guadalajara fire as “one of the largest in the recent history of our country” and the largest ever for the region of Castilla La Mancha.

The Guadalajara blaze is the second-largest on record in Spain’s history after some 37,000 hectares (91,000 acres) were burned last year in the northwest of the country, according to data from the ecological transition ministry, as cited by EFE news agency.

The blaze is the second-largest on record in Spain. Ana Beltran/Reuters

Regional authorities said firefighters supported by water-dumping aircraft had so far protected homes in all 40 villages in the burned area, 90% of which belongs to a national park. Firefighters hope to have the nearly week-old fire under control by Friday, said Emiliano García-Page, regional president of Castilla La Mancha.

Miguel Ángel Moreno, mayor of the village of Zarzuela de Jadraque, said its 100 residents were evacuated Friday, with 14 taking refuge at a Red Cross shelter.

Moreno said that the firefighters should receive as much admiration as the soccer players who won the World Cup on Sunday.

The firefighters “had to run from one side of the village to the other putting out fires,” Moreno told Spanish national television TVE. “Besides the heroes who won the World Cup, we have other heroes who remain nameless.”

Smoke from the La Mierla fire. Ana Beltran/Reuters

New heat wave could complicate firefighting efforts

Spain’s weather agency said a heat wave that began Tuesday was expected to reach its peak between Wednesday and Thursday, with temperatures pushing 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) in several inland areas and crossing 42 Celsius (108 Fahrenheit) in parts of Andalusia, in southern Spain.

Guadalajara and large areas of Spain were under alert for high temperatures.

Like many other European countries, Spain is experiencing extreme heat, which is combining with wind and limited rainfall to create ideal conditions for small wildfires to grow unchecked.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, with temperatures increasing twice as quickly as the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Globally, 2025 was the third-hottest year on record, bringing severe heat waves across Europe. Scientists warn that climate change is exacerbating the frequency and intensity of heat and dryness especially in southeastern Europe, making the region more vulnerable to health impacts and wildfires.

A wildfire burns in a forest area in the Gironde department on Wednesday amid worsening drought conditions following a heatwave and water shortages across much of France. Stephane Mahe/Reuters

Europe facing hot, dry weather

In Sicily, firefighters said they had carried out more than 1,000 operations since Saturday and have put all the Italian island’s fire departments on double shifts to cope with the blazes.

The latest was a wildland-urban blaze in Agrigento, in central western Sicily that required the evacuation of 100 people from homes and a clinic, with 22 patients transferred to other facilities, the national service said. Firefighters were particularly concerned about an oxygen storage plant nearby.

For days, Italy’s Civil Protection agency has declared all of Sicily at the highest risk for wildfires. Winds and temperatures near or above 40C (100F) have fueled blazes from near Palermo on the northern coast to Catania in the east and now Agrigento in the west.

Greece was sweltering under what was forecast to be the last of a four-day heat wave. Temperatures were predicted to top 42 C (107 F), while several regions in southern and central Greece, including the wider Athens area, were on the highest alert level for wildfire danger.

Cyprus, meanwhile, issued a warning for high temperatures expected to reach 43 C (109 F).

In Britain, it hasn’t rained in more than a month in some areas, and much of the southern half of England is in a state of “prolonged dry weather,” one step before a drought. Thames Water, the country’s biggest water company, has banned its 10 million customers from using hoses to water lawns or wash cars starting Thursday.

France’s public health agency on Wednesday said the country recorded at least 5,700 more deaths than usual during a historic heatwave last month, sharply increasing its estimates of the feared toll from record-shattering temperatures.

Public Health France said regions hit by the heat between June 17 and July 2 recorded 21,674 deaths from all causes. But without a heatwave, those same regions would have been expected to have seen far fewer deaths, or 15,910, based on statistical modeling using data from previous years, it said.

World.title: Israel prepares major military operation in West Bank after four Palestinians and two Israelis killed
World.content:
The Israeli military began preparations for a large-scale operation in the occupied West Bank on Friday after four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers were killed in clashes there.

The military said a group of settlers entered an area of the West Bank restricted to Israeli civilians Friday for an “unauthorized and uncoordinated hike.” As the group approached the Palestinian village of Tell, clashes broke out between the settlers and residents of the village.

In the ensuing gunfire, four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers – one of whom was also a settler – were killed, part of a surge of violence across the West Bank.

Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the demolition of Palestinian villages in the area in response to the killings.

“The population must be evacuated for its own protection, and these villages must be cleared of terrorist infrastructure and terrorists in order to restore deterrence and security to the area,” he said Friday.

Video of the incident shows soldiers and armed Israeli settlers appearing to force Palestinians from the area, with calls for “revenge” in Hebrew heard in the background. An armed settler approaches two Palestinian men, apparently trying to use his rifle to push them away. One of the Palestinians can be seen grabbing the strap of the weapon.

Several seconds later, after the video refocuses on the incident, one of the Palestinian men is seen holding the weapon. The sound of at least a dozen shots rings out from what appear to be several different locations.

The military said the Palestinian man took the weapon from a security officer from the nearby Havat Gilad settlement. The officer was killed in the incident, it said. The military said a second soldier was also killed during the incident. It is not clear if the incident captured in the video shows the precise moment the officers were killed.

The Palestinian Ministry of Health said the four Palestinians who were killed were shot by Israeli soldiers.

Walid Zeiden, leader of the Tell village committee, said they were all members of the same family, including two brothers and two cousins. At least three others were wounded by Israeli gunfire, the health ministry added.

The UN called for “urgent action” to end the escalating violence in the West Bank amid “unabated” Israeli settler attacks against Palestinian communities.

“Israel must take immediate steps to prevent settler violence, protect Palestinian communities, and ensure that those responsible for attacks are held accountable,” said Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, in a statement. “Palestinians must unequivocally reject violence and incitement and take immediate steps to prevent attacks against Israelis.”

The Palestinian Authority condemned the settler attacks and criticized Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz for “accelerating the establishment and legalization of colonial outposts” and reinforcing the IDF’s presence in the West Bank. It also called on the US to intervene and “compel Israel to halt its escalation and the crimes committed by Israeli colonists,” according to Palestinian news agency WAFA.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) announced that it had imposed a curfew on the Palestinian villages of Tell and Bureij, as well as the nearby Jewish settlement of Shiloh.

Despite video of the incident showing an altercation that escalated and the Israeli military acknowledging that the killing of the Israelis was not planned in advance, the IDF is treating the event as a terror attack and announced a “large-scale” operation in the area to go after “dozens of Palestinians” involved in the incident.

The IDF said it had cancelled leave for soldiers operating in the area and was preparing to send in reinforcements. Amid reports of settler attacks and raids on Palestinian villages in the area, the IDF said it was concerned by the possibility of settler violence.

Settlers set fire to buildings in the West Bank village of Faraata. Abeer Salman/CNN

Settler attacks continued in nearby areas in the West Bank, including in the towns of Faraata, Imatin, Jit, Iraq Burin, and the Masafer Yatta area in Hebron.

Video and photos obtained by CNN from Faraata residents show settlers setting fire to homes, cars and businesses in their village. In one area of the town, settlers sprayed the word “revenge” on the walls and uprooted an olive field with two bulldozers.

The Palestinian Red Crescent said on Friday afternoon that 8 people had been injured the Faraata attack, with six of them in hospital with gunshot wounds.

Photos obtained by CNN from residents in the West Bank village of Faraata show settlers setting fire to homes, cars and businesses in their village. Obtained by CNN

In a statement after the Tell incident, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the military to accelerate the establishment of more settlement outposts or farms in the area and the legalization of existing ones.

West Bank settlements are considered illegal under international law and by most of the international community and the United Nations, but settlers have successfully established dozens of unauthorized outposts in recent years and eventually secured Israeli government approvals.

Friday’s incident comes amid a marked escalation in settler violence across the occupied territory. Two Palestinians were fatally shot by Israeli forces in Beit Furik on Thursday after settlers reportedly set fire to Palestinian-owned fields and vehicles, according to local accounts.

Two more Palestinians were killed days earlier in the village of Deir Jarir, near Ramallah, during a settler raid, according to Palestinian health officials.

CNN’s Oren Liebermann contributed reporting.

World.title: Recap: The latest developments on the Iran war and tensions in the region
World.content:
After pummeling Iran daily for almost two weeks, there was no announcement from US Central Command that it was launching strikes on the country on Friday. It is not clear if that was because the US did not take military action against Iran that day.

In the region, tensions remain as US President Donald Trump said while Washington is actively negotiating with Tehran, it’s possible the military continues its bombing campaign or escalates it.

Here’s the latest:

No update from CENTCOM: For the past 13 nights, CENTCOM had posted on X it was striking military targets in Iran. There was no such announcement on Friday Eastern Time.

Trump weighs in: The president said the war was “going extremely well” and that the US has “hit Iran very hard.” He added that he thinks Iran would “love to make a deal” but that he doesn’t “think they’re ready to.”

Alerts issued: Saudi Arabia issued multiple warnings of “potential danger” at major port Yanbu and Jazan province early Saturday local time. The alerts were lifted shortly after and the authorities did not specify the nature or source of the potential danger. Yanbu is located on the Red Sea and Jazan province has a coastline on the same sea.

Maritime tensions: US forces disabled a tanker in the Gulf of Oman on Friday after the crew attempted to get through the US naval blockade of Iran at least four times prior, a US military official told CNN. And in the Red Sea, Saudi Arabia carried out strikes against what it said were Houthi targets in Yemen’s port city of Hodeidah after the militant group attacked another Saudi vessel.

Netanyahu’s visit: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will visit the US next week, Trump confirmed on Friday. The Israeli leader’s office earlier said in a statement Netanyahu will meet Trump at the White House on Tuesday.

Tori B. Powell, Tal Shalev, Laura Sharman, Kareem El Damanhoury, Zachary Cohen, Eyad Kourdi, Mitchell McCluskey and Aditi Sangal contributed reporting.

World.title: They Just want to Steal Again – HH
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has told voters across Southern Province that opposition leaders are “salivating” to return to power so they can once again steal and mismanage the country’s resources.

Addressing a community engagement in Choma District, Hichilema said Zambians must not allow those he accused of plundering national resources and leaving the country burdened with unsustainable debt to return to office.

The address formed part of a marathon campaign swing through Itezhi-Tezhi, Namwala, Monze and Choma, during which the President moved away from the traditional rally speech in favour of direct, interactive dialogue with supporters in their own language.

With no interpreter present, Hichilema posed questions that crowds answered in unison, often followed by laughter, cheers and applause. The format turned the campaign rallies into extended exchanges between the President and supporters rather than conventional set-piece speeches.

The President credited his administration with restoring the country’s image locally and internationally through debt restructuring, the reintroduction of free education, and what he described as sustained peace and stability.

“We shall not go back to the days of borrowing and plundering national resources. Those who over-borrowed must never be allowed to come back to power,” Hichilema said.

He urged voters to back all UPND candidates, saying Zambia should not “go back to Egypt” but continue its journey to “Canaan, the land of plenty” by renewing the party’s mandate next month.

In Choma, Hichilema announced plans for a new General Hospital and an international airport intended to reduce reliance on connecting flights for travellers from Southern Province. He also promised upgraded township roads and a dual carriageway, warning that contractors who failed to meet required standards risked being replaced.

In Itezhi-Tezhi, the President turned his attention to a stalled road project, accusing contractor Build Trust of receiving an advance payment without completing the works. He linked the company to NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile.

“The money meant for the construction of this road was stolen by this one who is contesting the presidential election,” Hichilema said.

He said a re-elected UPND government would complete the road and deliver a district hospital, classroom blocks, clinics, maternity wings, boreholes and a skills training centre. He also pledged work on the Itezhi-Tezhi-Namwala-Lubwe-Basanga-Dundumwezi-Kalomo Road.

The Southern Province campaign swing also produced a political development in Namwala, where former Fisheries and Livestock minister Greyford Monde formally rejoined the UPND and endorsed Hichilema’s re-election bid.

Monde said he was pleased that those he blamed for previously pushing him out of the party were no longer part of its leadership. He urged voters to support leaders he said were capable of growing the economy.

Further pledges followed in Monze and Namwala, including the construction of a roundabout near Monze Secondary School, upgrading township roads to bituminous standard, building a dual carriageway and constructing additional dams to support agriculture and improve water security.

Hichilema described his first term as a period of restructuring that had laid the foundation for economic transformation, urging citizens not to return to what he described as the challenges of the past.

“There is every reason to continue with the UPND government,” Hichilema said.

World.title: Shamenda insists regime change is coming next month
World.content:
Former Minister of Labour and Social Security Fackson Shamenda says he expects a change of government in Zambia next month, urging citizens to disregard what he describes as propaganda being circulated by individuals and platforms aligned with the United Party for National Development.

Speaking in an interview, Shamenda dismissed reports suggesting that National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity presidential candidate Brian Mundubile would lose the August 13 general election, describing them as false and deliberately calculated to mislead Zambians.

He said claims attributed to UPND media personalities, bloggers and affiliated platforms had misrepresented his position and created the false impression that he had changed his view on the likely outcome of the election.

“My position remains exactly as stated in The Mast of 21 July 2026, where I made it clear that I foresee the opposition forming the next government,” Shamenda said.

“That position has not changed, and I stand by it.”

Shamenda said it was regrettable that some individuals and media platforms had chosen to distort his statements for political purposes, maintaining that his position on the August election remained unchanged.

He said he was considering taking appropriate action against those responsible for publishing and circulating what he described as defamatory statements and false attributions concerning his political views.

“I am currently considering taking appropriate action against those responsible for publishing and circulating these defamatory statements and false attributions regarding my political views,” he said.

Shamenda urged members of the public to disregard reports that did not accurately reflect his position and instead rely on statements issued by him directly or published through sources carrying his actual remarks.

He also rejected reports attributed to him suggesting that Mundubile should withdraw from the presidential race ahead of the August 13 general election, describing the claim as unfounded and a complete fabrication.

Shamenda did not identify the specific individuals or platforms he believes were responsible for misrepresenting his remarks, nor did he indicate what form the action he is considering might take.

The former labour minister has previously criticised the ruling party and maintains that the opposition is positioned to form the next government after the August polls.

Neither the UPND nor NRPUP had issued an official response to Shamenda’s remarks by the time of publication.

August date fast approaching with Shamenda maintaining that his prediction of a change of government remains unchanged and rejecting claims that he has called on Mundubile to withdraw from the presidential race.

World.title: Police deny blocking NRPUP campaign in Ndola
World.content:
Copperbelt Province Police Commanding Officer Mwala Yuyi has dismissed claims that police blocked the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) from campaigning in Ndola, insisting officers only intervened to stop an unauthorised procession while the party’s rally proceeded as planned.

Responding to allegations made by NRPUP president Brian Mundubile, Yuyi said police facilitated the party’s campaign meeting in Twapia and deployed officers solely to maintain law and order. He said the rally itself was allowed to proceed without interference.

Yuyi explained that police only intervened after some NRPUP supporters embarked on a roadshow and procession that was not part of the agreed campaign programme.

“We never stopped their campaigns. We allowed them to campaign freely and the rally went ahead. The only thing police stopped was the illegal procession because it was not part of the agreed programme,” Yuyi said.

He disclosed that 14 NRPUP supporters were arrested for unlawful assembly after allegedly participating in the unauthorised procession. Yuyi said it was therefore misleading to suggest that police had frustrated the opposition party’s campaign when its scheduled rally was held without interruption.

Mundubile had earlier alleged that police attempted to block the Twapia rally because they did not want the NRPUP addressing supporters on what he described as stolen Food Reserve Agency funds. He claimed police had been instructed to stop the meeting and that it eventually proceeded because of the large number of supporters who turned up.

Yuyi rejected the allegations, maintaining that police neither interfered with the rally nor sought to prevent the party from campaigning. He said officers deployed to political activities were mandated to ensure public safety, peace and order, rather than intimidate political parties or disrupt their campaign programmes.

In a separate matter, Yuyi dismissed reports linking opposition members to a recent break-in at the United Party for National Development (UPND) Dag Hammarskjöld Constituency secretariat in Twapia. He said preliminary investigations indicated that unknown burglars were responsible and that investigations were continuing.

Meanwhile, Mundubile alleged in a Facebook post that some NRPUP members were attacked by unknown people in Kitwe on Thursday, with several campaign vehicles reportedly stoned around 12:30 hours. Police had not confirmed the alleged attack by press time.

Separately, UPND youths in Kitwe distanced themselves from a reported altercation involving members of the Tonse Alliance. Kitwe District UPND Youth Information and Publicity Secretary Chambala Mazimba said the ruling party had no connection to the incident.

Mazimba maintained that the fracas was an internal matter involving Tonse Alliance members led by Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, and should not be politicised or linked to the UPND. He urged the public to reject misinformation and called on UPND members to remain calm and disciplined as the country prepares for the general election.

World.title: Suspected UPND cadres smash seven NRPUP vehicles in Kitwe
World.content:
Suspected United Party for National Development (UPND) cadres smashed seven vehicles belonging to the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) campaign team in Kitwe yesterday, allegedly in full view of armed police officers.

The vehicles were parked at Sherbourne Hotel and nearby premises where NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu were lodging ahead of a scheduled campaign stop on the Copperbelt.

Tonse Alliance presidential affairs chairperson Binwell Mpundu confronted officers at the scene, accusing them of failing to protect property and lives. He said the Kitwe Officer Commanding, identified only as Mkandawire, instead suggested that NRPUP may have damaged its own vehicles, a claim Mpundu described as dismissive.

“Zambians and NRPUP officials are on their own and need to protect themselves,” Mpundu said, before adding that they needed protection “from UPND thugs.”

Mundubile questioned whether the alleged attack reflected the peace President Hakainde Hichilema has repeatedly promised the nation during the campaign period.

“My dear brother, Hakainde Hichilema, is this the peace you have been preaching about?” Mundubile asked.

President Hichilema has made peaceful campaigning a recurring theme at his rallies in recent weeks. Mundubile, however, said his members on the Copperbelt had endured repeated harassment, including assaults and now the destruction of campaign property, warning that the country risked drifting towards a culture of political violence.

The Kitwe incident followed a separate standoff on Thursday in Ndola’s Twapia Township, where masked and heavily armed police officers attempted to block Mundubile’s convoy from reaching a rally venue. Local residents intervened, chanting for change until officers withdrew and allowed the convoy to proceed.

Copperbelt Province Police Commanding Officer Mwala Yuyi later addressed a related complaint from NRPUP over police conduct in Ndola, saying officers had only stopped an unauthorised procession while the party’s sanctioned rally proceeded without interruption. Fourteen supporters were arrested for unlawful assembly in connection with the procession.

Police had not confirmed the Kitwe vehicle-smashing incident or indicated whether any arrests had been made by the time of publication. The ruling UPND had also not responded to allegations that its supporters were responsible for the damage.

Zambians go to the polls on 13 August, with the conduct of political campaigns increasingly becoming a point of contention between the governing party and the opposition alliance as the election race enters its final stretch.

World.title: OPINION: Nyon’go, Nyon’go Nyon’go: Has the ‘Mufasa Effect’ of the Two Boys Gotten Under HH’s Skin?
World.content:
Nyon’go, Nyon’go: Has the ‘Mufasa Effect’ of the Two Boys Gotten Under HH’s Skin?

By Mabvuto Banda

There are moments in an election campaign when a politician says far more through his temperament than through the actual words coming out of his mouth. President Hakainde Hichilema’s repeated “Nyon’go, Nyon’go, Nyon’go” utterances, directed at Gary Nkombo, may have been intended as political theatre, but they revealed something else: a President appearing increasingly willing to abandon presidential restraint and descend into the language of irritation and ridicule. The “Nyon’go” remarks were not directed at Brian Mundubile or Makebi Zulu, and that distinction matters. But so does the temperament behind them. At this stage of an increasingly competitive campaign, such an outburst inevitably raises questions about whether the pressure is beginning to show.

For a man who is not only Head of State but also an elder in the church, the tone was particularly striking. A President is entitled to campaign aggressively, defend his record and challenge his opponents, but there is a difference between campaigning hard and appearing to lose the dignity that comes with the office. The presidency does not disappear simply because there is a microphone, a rally and an opponent to attack. And perhaps that is where the real story lies. Something appears to be getting under the President’s skin.

The “Nyon’go” episode may have involved Nkombo, but elsewhere on the campaign trail, the two men Hichilema repeatedly dismisses as “boys” have brought something to this election that also seems to be testing his patience. The confidence remains, but increasingly, so does the irritation.

THE MUFASA EFFECT

It is becoming something of a Mufasa effect. In The Lion King, Mufasa’s name alone carried weight. Mention it in the wrong company and the reaction was immediate: fear, discomfort and a sudden change of mood. Mufasa did not even have to enter the room. Sometimes the name alone was enough.

That is increasingly what Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu appear to be doing to President Hichilema politically. These are the same two men he has repeatedly reduced to “boys”, yet listen to how much political attention they now command. The more dismissive the language becomes, the harder it is to believe that the people being dismissed are politically irrelevant. If the “boys” do not matter, why do they appear to provoke such a reaction?

That is the Mufasa effect. It is not necessarily about who is stronger or who will ultimately win on August 13. That decision belongs to the Zambian people. It is about the psychological effect an opponent begins to have on another. Right now, Mundubile and Zulu appear to have found a way of occupying political space that their supposed insignificance should never have allowed.

THEN CAME THE COPPERBELT

Then came the Copperbelt, where NRPUP campaign vehicles were reportedly attacked and their windows shattered by people the opposition identified as UPND cadres. A driver was allegedly assaulted, while cash and a mobile phone were reportedly stolen from the convoy. Later came the extraordinary scenes in Luanshya, where Mundubile’s convoy encountered a police blockade as it attempted to reach supporters waiting in Mpatamatu.

And that begs an even bigger question: what peace is President Hakainde Hichilema actually talking about? On the ground in Mpatamatu on Friday, peace looked like this: an opposition convoy pelted with stones, a road into Luanshya sealed off by the very police force that is supposed to protect every candidate equally, and a presidential hopeful forced to talk his way past a blockade simply to reach voters who had been waiting for him.

If this is what the President’s “peace” produces, it is worth asking who it is actually peaceful for, because it was certainly not peaceful for Mundubile’s campaign. Vehicles were stoned. Police blocked the road. And this was not an isolated incident. On the same day, NRPUP campaign vehicles elsewhere on the Copperbelt reportedly had their windows smashed, a driver assaulted, and cash and a phone stolen.

Mundubile said his people had been attacked, assaulted and their vehicles vandalised while the government continued to speak of a peaceful campaign season. That description of peace is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with what Zambians are seeing.

KALINGALINGA CANNOT BE ERASED

And Luanshya did not happen in a vacuum. Only a week earlier came Kalingalinga, where police used teargas during a confrontation surrounding an opposition campaign event and reports emerged that a young girl had been shot. Government officials subsequently disputed aspects of the account, maintaining that police had used teargas and that no lives were lost. Whatever version one accepts, Kalingalinga raised uncomfortable questions about the policing of opposition political activities during an already heated election campaign.

Then, on the same afternoon as the Luanshya blockade, police walked onto Mundubile’s campaign stage in Ndola. By the time his convoy encountered trouble in Luanshya, interaction with law enforcement was becoming part of the opposition’s campaign story rather than something happening at its margins. Kalingalinga, Ndola and Luanshya have different circumstances and must each be judged on their own facts, but taken together with the reported attacks on campaign vehicles, they leave an uncomfortable question about the environment in which the opposition is being expected to campaign.

THE DISCIPLINE OF THE ‘TWO BOYS’

What is remarkable is not simply that stones reportedly flew or that police blocked a road being used by a presidential candidate. What is remarkable is that Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu refused to give the provocation the reaction it appeared capable of producing. They did not turn the convoy around. They did not allow shattered windows, stones or a police blockade to become bigger than the political message they had travelled to deliver.

They proceeded to Mpatamatu and addressed the people who had been waiting for them. Zulu stood before miners, youths and farmers and told them in Bemba that their cries had been heard. Mundubile, rather than spending his speech attacking those accused of trying to prevent him from reaching the rally, pledged to establish a National Miners’ Day to honour the men and women whose labour has helped build Zambia’s economy.

That is discipline, but it is also political calculation. The opposition appears to understand that one angry reaction could change the entire story. A scuffle, a retaliatory stone, a broken window or an exchange with police could quickly provide the excuse to stop a procession, disrupt a rally or portray the opposition itself as the source of disorder.

The opposition therefore finds itself carrying an extraordinary burden. It must campaign, absorb provocation and simultaneously police its own reaction. It must remain calm enough not only to protect its supporters, but also to deny those confronting it the very excuse that could be used to restrict its campaign further.

WHAT PEACE ARE WE TALKING ABOUT?

That is why the President’s own temperament matters. “Nyon’go, Nyon’go, Nyon’go” was directed at Gary Nkombo, not Mundubile or Zulu. But the episode remains relevant because it offered a glimpse of a President appearing increasingly impatient at precisely the moment when Zambia needs presidential restraint most.

When the same Head of State is also reducing political opponents to “boys”, while opposition vehicles are reportedly being damaged and opposition convoys are encountering police blockades, the contrast becomes difficult to ignore. The President may regard some of this language as campaign banter, but presidential words carry a weight that ordinary campaign rhetoric does not. The office requires more.

President Hichilema cannot demand peaceful conduct from everyone beneath him while creating the impression that political pressure is eroding his own patience. He cannot preach restraint while allowing his language to drift towards ridicule. And those entrusted with maintaining law and order cannot allow circumstances to develop in which opposition candidates appear to require extraordinary patience simply to exercise their right to campaign.

The burden of maintaining peace cannot rest on the opposition simply refusing to retaliate. Real peace is not achieved when one side throws a stone and the other side decides not to throw it back. Real peace exists when nobody is allowed to throw the stone in the first place, and when the police stand between competing political forces without fear, favour or partisan appearance.

WHEN THE REACTION SAYS IT ALL

This is where the Mufasa effect becomes politically interesting. Nobody needs to pretend that Mundubile and Zulu have already won anything. Zambians will make that decision themselves on August 13. President Hichilema remains the incumbent and continues to campaign on his government’s record. Elections are decided by voters, not metaphors.

But you do not need to win an election before you begin affecting the behaviour of your opponent. Sometimes you simply need to get into his head. Perhaps the “boys” have brought more to the table than was anticipated. Perhaps Mundubile and Zulu have discovered that refusing to be provoked can itself become a political weapon.

Perhaps the scenes from Kalingalinga to the Copperbelt matter precisely because they allow voters to compare the temperament of those wielding power with the restraint of those seeking it. Government officials have denied wrongdoing in relation to previous incidents, while responsibility for the reported Copperbelt attacks must ultimately be established through proper investigation rather than political accusation. Police had offered no comment on Friday’s reported convoy attack at the time of writing.

But politically, the images already carry their own weight. Zambians vote on August 13. The closer that date gets, the less useful speeches about peace become if the experience on the ground tells another story. Kalingalinga happened. Then came Ndola, the reported attacks on campaign vehicles and the confrontation in Luanshya. Against that background stands a President whose language appears increasingly impatient as the “two boys” he has repeatedly dismissed refuse to disappear.

“Nyon’go, Nyon’go, Nyon’go” was directed at Gary Nkombo, but perhaps its wider significance was the glimpse it offered of a President under pressure. And that is what makes the Mufasa effect interesting.

Mundubile and Zulu do not have to say they are getting under the President’s skin. Sometimes, the reaction says it for them.

World.title: Nkombo Urges President Hichilema to Stay Out of Presidential Contest
World.content:
Independent Mazabuka Central parliamentary candidate Gary Nkombo has advised President Hakainde Hichilema not to be drawn into the contest between the UPND and the Tonse Alliance presidential candidate.

Mr. Nkombo said his focus remains on serving the people of Mazabuka Central and securing his position as Member of Parliament, rather than taking sides in the presidential race.

He said his priority is to address issues affecting residents of Mazabuka Central and continue working for their interests.

Mr. Nkombo’s remarks come amid heightened political activity as various candidates and political parties intensify their campaigns ahead of the elections.

World.title: Brian Mundubela Raises Concern Over Alleged Political Violence in Kitwe
World.content:
Opposition figure Brian Mundubela has questioned whether the reported acts of violence during the campaign period reflect the peace that President Hakainde Hichilema has consistently advocated for.

In a statement, Mr. Mundubela said Zambians should begin to look beyond political rhetoric and assess political parties based on their actions, emphasizing that violence has no place in a democratic society.

The statement follows an alleged incident in Kitwe on the Copperbelt, where Mr. Mundubela and other opposition members were reportedly attacked while conducting campaign activities. He alleged that their members were assaulted, while campaign vehicles were vandalized and stones were thrown during the incident.

Mr. Mundubela called on all political parties to be allowed to campaign freely and peacefully, urging stakeholders to promote tolerance and respect for democratic freedoms ahead of the elections.

He further appealed for political players to uphold peace and ensure that citizens can participate in the electoral process without fear or intimidation.

World.title: President Hichilema assures completion of Monze – Niko Road
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has assured the people of Namwala District of Southern Province that the government will ensure that the construction of Monze – Niko Road is completed on time in order to spur economic development in the district.

And President Hichilema has directed the Road Development Agency RDA to ensure that a roundabout is also constructed on the road to reduce road accidents in the area.

The Head of State has further directed RDA to also work on Namusonde – Mala Road as well as to open up a road that will lead to Itezhi-Tezi District.

President Hichilema said this today when he addressed Namwala residents at Mangwele Primary and Secondary School grounds.

President Hichilema also noted that the government will ensure that Chitingo Livestock Centre is opened in order to vaccinate cattle and protect them from different diseases.

“This road that you are seeing today did not just come from nowhere, we saw the challenges you were facing, and we planned as a government and ensured that the road was constructed and it is here.

“It is now my job to ensure that the road is completed with a roundabout to ensure that no accidents should be recorded as well as construct other roads,” he noted.

On employment, President Hichilema stated that the government has employed teachers and health workers among others to ensure that the living standards of people are uplifted.

President Hichilema also outlined different social protection programmes as well as implementation of the free education policy as some of the interventions that the government will continue to implement once voted back into power on August 13.

“Am urging you to vote for the United Party for National Development (UPND) so that more of such development should continue,” he stated.

The Head of State also noted that farmers supplying their produce to the Food Reserve Agency FRA will be paid upon delivering.

“From today onwards, you will be getting paid immediately you supply your produce to FRA,” he stated.

Meanwhile, UPND Aspiring Candidate for Namwala East, Clara Chibola, and UPND Aspiring candidate for Namwala West, Herbert Mapani, urged Namwala residents to vote for UPND in the forthcoming General Elections for continued development.

The two aspiring candidates noted that the district has registered unprecedented development which needs to be continued, hence the need to vote the UPND back into power.
