World.title: Africa: Nigeria Emerging As Africa's Renewable Energy Knowledge Hub, By Abba Aliyu
World.content:
opinion

Today, our nation is being recognised across the African continent and beyond as a premier pioneer and leader in renewable energy innovation.

For the first time in our modern history, Nigeria is no longer on the global energy map simply as a case study for grid fragility and power deficits. Today, our nation is being recognised across the African continent and beyond as a premier pioneer and leader in renewable energy innovation.

While successive administrations laid important groundwork over the years, what we are witnessing right now is a catalytic, unprecedented period of execution and growth.

This momentum has been made possible by the political willpower of the Federal Government led by our visionary leader, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, alongside my boss, the Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, who remain determined to make Nigeria's electricity sector sustainable, and highly attractive to investors.



This environment of trust and structural reform has transformed Nigeria into a magnet for global clean energy capital.

The recently published Sub-Saharan Africa Clean Energy Market Outlook 2026 by BloombergNEF highlights Nigeria as the continent's largest and fastest-growing market for distributed solar and small-scale renewable energy, having attracted a $80m debt facility dedicated to expanding off-grid solar home systems and business power solutions across Nigeria.

Similarly, UK-backed clean energy company MOPO signed a $75m deal aimed at deploying a new smart battery programme under a strategic partnership with the Rural Electrification Agency (REA).

WeLight, the operator of nearly 190 mini-grids across Madagascar and Mali, serving more than 800,000 people has also announced plans to invest in Nigeria's off-grid market.

These massive capital injections demonstrate that international financial institutions and global developers no longer view Nigeria as a risky bet, but as the most viable and scalable off-grid energy market on the continent.

Beyond international investments, we are actively deepening our alignment with state governments and government Ministries, Departments, and Agencies to ensure that mini-grid deployment, electrification planning, and regulatory frameworks function as a cohesive national system.

This internal momentum is driving a powerful shift, as Nigeria has evolved into a vital hub for Pan-African peer learning and South-South knowledge exchange.

When we welcomed our first delegation from Mozambique to the Rural Electrification Agency last year, I remember reflecting on how transformative it is when African nations choose to grow together by learning directly from one another.

Today, that vision has become our operational reality. Hosting a delegation from the Zanzibar Utilities Regulatory Authority (ZURA) reaffirmed just how far we have come, proving that beyond executing landmark projects within our borders, REA is maturing into a continental nexus where the future of African energy is actively being shaped.

Our sessions with ZURA were rooted in total transparency, exploring not only our successes, but the complex operational hurdles, policy adjustments, and sustainability lessons we have gathered while scaling off-grid renewables.

From capital mobilization and grid stability to system operations and local implementation, one truth stood out, Africa will achieve universal energy access far faster through radical collaboration than by working in silos.

Close 

What fills me with immense pride is that REA's institutional experience has become a continental resource. Every Nigerian should take pride in this milestone because we are no longer just building power infrastructure across Nigeria, we are establishing the blueprint for how rural electrification can be scaled across Africa.

This is only the beginning. With an incoming delegation from Sierra Leone next week and several more exchange missions queued behind them, we are witnessing a defining moment where African nations choose shared progress over isolated effort. Because when one of us succeeds, the entire continent moves forward.

The work continues.

*Abba Aliyu is the Managing Director of Nigeria's Rural Electrification Agency (REA)

World.title: Michigan father alleges bomb threat to home after daughter spoke up about facing trans athlete without knowing
World.content:
A Michigan father says his family received alleged death threats, racist insults and threats that someone would blow up their home after he and his teenage daughter spoke publicly about her unknowingly competing against a transgender athlete in girls' volleyball.

"We've been threatened with violence, called Nazis, subjected to racist insults, and even received threats to blow up our home," Sean Lechner told Fox News Digital. "The situation became so serious that the FBI contacted us."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the FBI for comment.

VOLLEYBALL STAR SKEWERS DEMOCRAT STATE LAWMAKER FROM VIRAL SPAT AFTER 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' BILL PASSES

Lechner said his family received an "overwhelming amount of support" but also the hostile responses after he and his 16-year-old daughter, Briley, spoke out in support of protecting girls' sports. They originally spoke out last fall before resuming interviews about the situation this past week on "Fox & Friends" and with Moms for Liberty.

"All of this because I'm a father standing beside my daughter, her teammates, and every female athlete who deserves safety, privacy, fairness, and equal opportunity," the father said.

Briley, a student-athlete at Monroe High School in Michigan, said her father absorbed most of the abuse after the family went public. She has also received alleged messages accusing her of attacking transgender people and spreading hate.

"We've received death threats and threats of people coming to our house or going to my father's work," she told Fox News Digital.

"Of course, I never want to spread negativity. I don't want to spread hate or anything, and it does hurt to see that that's how people are viewing me. But I also stick to my ground, and I know what I'm standing up for, and I know what I'm battling for."

The backlash left Briley feeling as if she and her family had been abandoned by some of the adults in positions of political and educational power in her state.

"It makes me feel like I'm almost on my own, in a way," she said. "Those are the people that we expect to protect us and give us female athletes a fair game, and that's the last thing that it seems like they're prioritizing.

"For me, a 16-year-old girl, to have to be the one that speaks out about it and fights for the change, it’s just not right, in my opinion."

CALIFORNIA GIRLS' TRACK AND FIELD STARS SPEAK OUT AS GAVIN NEWSOM'S TITLE IX CRISIS GROWS

The controversy began when Briley competed against a biological male trans athlete from another school. She competed against the athlete in Fall 2024 as a freshman, and early in the 2025 season before finding out later in 2025. Fox News Digital is not disclosing any identifying information about the athlete.

Sean Lechner filed a Title IX complaint last December claiming that his daughter and her teammates had to share a locker room with the trans athlete ahead of that early-season matchup.

"I wasn't aware that it was a male," she said.

"It was about a day or two where rumors were spread around afterwards, and my dad and I were talking about it and he said that a fellow parent and friend talked to him about it, and then my teammate started saying things."

After she found out, she said she was "devastated."

"I was devastated and, of course, concerned," Briley said. "I was very much caught off guard."

"We were asking why we weren't informed ahead of time," Briley said. "We were told that there was nothing they could do about it and that they had to protect this trans athlete."

She said she received no apology or acknowledgment from school officials.

The discovery also forced her to reflect on what she had seen across the net.

"They could jump much higher. They could swing much harder, get the ball down a lot harder, move quicker. It just seemed like they were stronger all the way around."

When Monroe played the trans athlete's team in a rematch, Briley and her teammates went into it knowing that they were facing a biological male.

"It was very weird," she said. "It was something that I knew shouldn't have been happening, and it kind of made me put my focus on that rather than just thinking about playing a regular game."

"I 100% think that knowing that there was a male on the other side mentally got in my teammates’ and my head."

Monroe lost the second matchup as well.

Briley first spoke publicly about the controversy after the season ended on Dec. 8, standing before a bank of cameras outside the Monroe County Courthouse as her father announced his Title IX complaint, with a swarm of local media in attendance to cover the controversy as it had garnered national attention throughout the season.

"I knew that it was for the best," she said, "and I knew that fighting for female athletes is definitely what I want to continue to do."

She says the harassment began shortly after that first speaking appearance at the courthouse.

The U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights opened investigations into Monroe and Ann Arbor Public Schools in June. The department said it would examine allegations that Monroe required female athletes to compete and share facilities with a biological male and then failed to respond appropriately to parents’ concerns.

The Michigan High School Athletic Association's policy allows the association’s executive director to determine a transgender girl’s eligibility for postseason competition on a case-by-case basis. Schools make their own regular-season participation decisions.

The national legal landscape shifted on June 30, when the Supreme Court ruled that Title IX allows schools to maintain separate boys’ and girls’ teams based on biological sex. All nine justices agreed on the Title IX question, while the court divided 6-3 on the athletes’ constitutional claims.

The decision allows states to protect sex-separated teams but does not require every state to do so. The MHSAA has said Michigan’s Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act still requires its current transgender participation policy unless state lawmakers change the law.

Briley said she recognizes that the opposing athlete may also feel targeted.

"I do feel that they might feel like we're attacking them, and it does suck that they have to be the one person that this is blowing up on," she said. "But it only takes one person."

But she also said the experience has made her more hesitant to attend college in Michigan. She hopes to play soccer at the collegiate level and now plans to examine schools’ policies before deciding where she would feel comfortable.

Sean said the threats have only strengthened the family’s resolve.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I never imagined that simply trying to be a good father and protect my daughter would result in this level of hatred," he said. "But instead of letting that hate and anger consume us, we turned it into purpose. We leaned on our faith, stood together as a family, and dedicated ourselves to advocating for what we believe is right."

"We won't be intimidated, and we won't be silenced," he added. "We will continue to fight until my daughter—and every female athlete—has the safety, privacy, fairness, and opportunities they deserve."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Monroe Public Schools, the Michigan High School Athletic Association and Ann Arbor Public Schools for comment.

World.title: MIKE DAVIS: Why criminal referral of Jack Smith was 100% justified
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former Biden administration special counsel Jack Smith is finally facing legal accountability for his abuse of power in his failed effort to defeat President Donald Trump's candidacy through two sham federal indictments. As part of that process, Smith provided testimony to Congress via deposition, and omitted crucial information necessary for the proper exercise of congressional oversight. House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan referred Smith to the Department of Justice for potential prosecution, and Smith should be gravely concerned.

18 U.S.C. § 1001 prohibits making knowingly and willfully false statements during government proceedings. Telling a half-truth is equivalent to making a false statement—a witness cannot omit material information and then claim his testimony was technically accurate. The congressional investigators who deposed Smith warned him of his obligation, consistent with the standard oath all witnesses take: to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help me God.

After President Trump left office, the Biden Justice Department obtained the contents of text messages of 44 Members of Congress, including 20 senators and 24 representatives. Those members included then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, the most powerful Republican in government. The government seized those contents while scouring phone records between President Trump, his associates, and members of Congress concerning the profoundly troubling 2020 election.

BIDEN SPECIAL COUNSEL’S 'RUNAWAY TRAIN’ SCOOPED UP SENSITIVE LAWMAKER INFO: 'ABUSE OF POWER'

During his deposition, Smith asserted that he had sought toll records through search warrants. But toll records only reveal who called whom and when. They do not reveal the contents of conversations. When asked whether he had obtained the contents of communications through a search warrant, Smith explicitly denied that he had done it. What he conveniently neglected to mention was that he had obtained the contents of those texts through the National Archives. One of Smith’s henchmen, Thomas Windom, obtained the contents of the communications without properly subjecting them to review by a "taint team" to ensure that Smith did not receive communications privileged under the Speech and Debate Clause of the Constitution.

Smith and his defenders audaciously argue that he should not be expected to read the minds of his questioners. He answered that he did not receive the texts through a search warrant, and that is all he was required to say, the Smith sycophants claim. This argument makes a mockery of the "whole truth" portion of the oath. Smith obtained the texts through a separate improper channel that Congress–through the dedicated work of Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley–uncovered just last month. That information incontrovertibly would have been essential to congressional oversight. Congress must know that the National Archives provided Smith with the contents of congressional texts, and that Smith improperly reviewed them.

Smith and his supporters also claim this referral is part of a retaliatory prosecution scheme against him, citing President Trump’s repeated calls for Smith to be held accountable. Those calls are eminently reasonable, as Smith tried to put Trump in prison for the rest of his life for exercising his First Amendment right to dispute a dubious election. Smith sought to cannibalize the Executive Branch by running roughshod over presidential immunity, a principle the Supreme Court thankfully affirmed in 2024. Requesting that the Justice Department investigate a purported crime is not retaliatory; it is consistent with the rule of law.

JACK SMITH HIT WITH CRIMINAL REFERRAL AS GOP MOVES TESTIMONY FIGHT TOWARD PROSECUTION

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Some also argue that prosecuting Smith would threaten the institutional independence of the Justice Department. But the Justice Department is not independent; it is part of the Executive Branch and therefore under the control of the president. Second, Smith, while a private citizen, allegedly committed a crime. It is inconceivable how holding him legally accountable for that conduct would threaten the Justice Department. Third, with respect to alleged crimes that Smith allegedly committed while serving as a special counsel, such as conspiracy against constitutional rights under 18 U.S.C. § 241, it is proper to hold prosecutors criminally liable for unlawful conduct in the same way it is proper to hold law enforcement officers accountable. If a police officer unlawfully beats a suspect without cause and violates his civil rights, that officer should face legal accountability. Holding him accountable is not a threat to law enforcement; it is consistent with the rule of law. The same applies to rogue prosecutors like Smith.

Jack Smith is an affront to the federal government and the legal profession. He tried and failed to alter the outcome of the 2024 presidential election by prosecuting President Trump across two jurisdictions on two absurd indictments. He then withheld material information—meaning, he lied—during a congressional deposition. This information came to light only thanks to Chairman Chuck Grassley. Smith’s best hope now is to try a Clintonian "depends on the meaning of ‘is’" defense, and let a dozen jurors decide whether they will swallow it.

World.title: Perception is reality, and the SEC needs to start winning again before it continues to puff out its chest
World.content:
With SEC Media Days now squarely in the rearview, each of the 16 teams from the Southeastern Conference will prepare for a pivotal year for the league.

It might sound crazy to most fans who don't have a team in the SEC, but it's been three years since the conference has won a national championship, and the natives are getting restless.

So restless, in fact, that they've resorted to all sorts of mental gymnastics about why the SEC is still the dominant conference in college football.

MISSOURI'S ELI DRINKWITZ BECOMES LATEST SEC COACH TO MAKE RIDICULOUS COMPLAINTS ABOUT BIG TEN SCHEDULES

Before I go any further, I have to point out that I am biased towards the SEC as a Florida Gator fan and I have defended the conference on numerous occasions.

But hearing some of the things being said as to why the league is still on top despite the Big Ten winning three straight natties is a bit hard to swallow, and it all culminated in the former Don of the SEC, Nick Saban, dropping this gem at Media Days on Thursday.

I want to make one thing perfectly clear: Saban is right, in a sense.

Top to bottom, the SEC is deeper than the Big Ten.

The SEC also has more talent than the Big Ten, based on both recruiting rankings and NFL Draft numbers.

The gap has closed, especially at the top, but the numbers still favor the SEC as a whole.

LANE KIFFIN MAKES RIDICULOUS EXCUSES FOR SEC'S POOR RECENT PERFORMANCE IN COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

All of that may be true, but in college football, perception is reality, and the SEC is doing itself no favors by doing all of this talking without backing it up in the College Football Playoff.

I mentioned an SEC team hasn't won a national championship in three years, but it's even worse than that.

Last year, no team from the SEC had a win over another Power 4 program from outside of the conference in the CFP.

Alabama and Ole Miss beat Oklahoma and Georgia, respectively, but those were obviously intraconference matchups.

Sure, the SEC may still have the deepest conference top to bottom, but all the blustering from within the league just sounds like coping to any of the outsiders.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

No one will take these claims seriously until the SEC gets back to the mountain top.

I reject theories like "the SEC is dead" or "The SEC and Big Ten aren't even close anymore," but fans need to acknowledge the fact that the league has some work to do to get back to its pre-2023 run of dominance.

That may never happen again, especially given the proliferation of talent in the NIL and transfer portal era, but in the meantime, the league needs to stop burying its head in the sand.

Talk is cheap. Go out there and start winning Playoff games and knocking the Big Ten from its perch.

World.title: From locker rooms to Congress: Jay Feely latest athlete seeking to take lessons in leadership to Capitol Hill
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former NFL placekicker Jay Feely is the latest professional athlete poised to transition to a congressional career, where leadership, performing under pressure and handling public scrutiny are essential in both arenas.

Fox News Digital reached out to Feely, who spent time with the New York Giants and Arizona Cardinals before becoming an "NFL on CBS" commentator, for his take on why professional sports prepared him for public life as he seeks the seat of retiring Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz.

"Especially as a kicker — to be a successful kicker in the NFL, you have to be able to handle pressure, and you have be able handle failure. And I think those two attributes are very tangible attributes that will help you as you try to navigate the political field and try to be effective," Feely said Friday in an interview with Fox News Digital.

He said the NFL also exposed him to teammates from different backgrounds and viewpoints, helping prepare him to represent a diverse constituency.

STATE OF PLAY: DEMS BATTLE FOR SHOT AT CRUCIAL ARIZONA HOUSE SEAT AMID GOP'S RAZOR-THIN MAJORITY

"[T]he greatest advantage of being an NFL player was to be in those locker rooms where racial walls were broken down and conversations happened and you got to know people which otherwise you might not ever get to know."

He recalled rooming with LeVar Arrington and Brandon Short while with the Giants in East Rutherford, sharing stories about their different life experiences and personal views as they played chess and other games.

NFL GREAT PATRICK PETERSON SAYS LOCKER ROOM POLITICAL DISCOURSE WAS 'UNNECESSARY,' MOST PLAYERS ARE UNINFORMED

"Your job is to represent everybody and i think those experiences certainly are an asset," Feely said.

He also mentioned a trip to the infamously unfriendly confines of Lincoln Financial Field to play the Philadelphia Eagles right after the "worst game of [his] career" against the Seahawks.

The prior night he had been "spoofed" on "Saturday Night Live," and while preparing for what was a game-winning kick after an apparent icing timeout, Philadelphia played a montage of his Seattle misses on the Jumbotron to mock him.

HALL OF FAMER TONY DUNGY ENDORSES MICHELE TAFOYA IN CROWDED MINNESOTA REPUBLICAN PRIMARY FOR U.S. SENATE

"They tried to deter me, but I made the kick and my career goes on for another nine years – you learn a lot through those processes," Feely said.

Feely added that he got to know another athlete-turned-public official through their time with the NFL Players Association (NFLPA).

"There's so many different correlations with the people in sports, and a lot of the best people I know that I met in sports have thought about getting into politics," he said, reflecting on his time working with HUD Secretary Scott Turner, a former Washington Redskin.

He said he also hopes to see other athletes regardless of viewpoint who have acted on issues close to them, like former New Orleans Saints Drew Brees and Benjamin Watson.

Feely will face former state Rep. Amish Shah, D-Phoenix, who also worked for about two years as the New York Jets' team doctor.

Just over two decades ago, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner was on the NFL gridiron, playing cornerback for the Washington Redskins and then-San Diego Chargers.

The skills and lessons learned on the field helped Turner grow into his new role at HUD, which was also preceded by a stint in the Texas House of Representatives.

"The Lord used football to change the course of my life, and through the game," Turner told Fox News Digital.

"He taught me lessons that continue to guide me every day in public service: discipline, teamwork, perseverance, humility, and working toward a mission bigger than yourself."

"Those values inform how I served in the Texas state legislature and how I lead HUD today. My experience on football teams shaped how I lead, how I serve, and the example I hope to set for the next generation."

Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., had a successful mixed martial arts career before shifting from dodging fists to political blows on Capitol Hill.

Davids, who tried out for "The Ultimate Fighter," compiled a 5-1 amateur record before a brief professional MMA career in 2013, when she went 1-1.

"Turns out getting punched in the face is pretty good preparation for Congress," Davids told Fox News Digital on Friday.

She first left the octagon to support Native American communities, focusing on community development and expanding economic opportunities for Native people.

Davids later won her 2018 congressional bid in an upset against Rep. Kevin Yoder, R-Kan., in the largely red state.

"But really, fighting professionally taught me that you don't solve every challenge by throwing punches. You have to stay disciplined, work hard, respect your opponent, and keep moving forward — and that's how I approach this job, too," she told Fox News Digital.

Former Auburn Tigers Coach Tommy Tuberville transitioned to the U.S. Senate in 2021 after compiling a slew of outstanding stats as a head coach.

The Republican — now running for governor of Alabama — declined comment for this story but spoke in 2020 about the parallels between success in athletics and government.

Asked about his then-11-month campaign against incumbent Democrat Sen. Doug Jones, Tuberville told the Alabama Daily News he had to approach it at "full speed" just like a football coach.

"We put together a good, good team. And a lot of people told me when I first got started they said, coach, this is just like being a head coach. You’re only as good as the team around you," he said.

One of the most recognizable Republican figures of the last century was former HUD Secretary and former Congressman Jack Kemp.

Kemp’s political peak came in 1996 when he was the vice presidential running mate of Sen. Bob Dole, R-Kan., against President Bill Clinton.

Prior to that, Kemp led the same agency Turner did under the first Bush administration, and previously represented western New York in Congress for almost 20 years.

Kemp's first public role, however, was as a journeyman NFL quarterback in the 1950s and 1960s. He played for the Pittsburgh Steelers, Los Angeles Chargers and Buffalo Bills, among others, and also spent time in the Canadian Football League with the Calgary Stampeders.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell — whose father Charles Goodell represented Kemp’s area as a Republican in Congress in the 1960s — was quoted as calling Kemp an "extraordinary American leader who became a trusted colleague and exceptional friend to countless NFL owners, team personnel and commissioners after his MVP playing career with the Buffalo Bills."

Kemp, who died in 2009, said that professional football gave him a "good perspective" for politics.

"When I entered the political arena, I had already been booed, cheered, cut, sold, traded, and hung in effigy," he said, according to the Bills.

The only active member of Congress with an NFL history is Rep. Burgess Owens, a retiring Republican from Utah.

Owens, a former New York Jets safety, has alluded to his NFL career at times, largely focusing on criticizing the politicization of sports.

He previously told Fox Business during a time when players were kneeling for the national anthem that he would be boycotting games until Goodell was fired.

"I’m done," he told host David Asman in 2020. "It’s time for these young men who make millions of dollars to say thank you [and respect the country]."

Owens did not respond to a request for comment.

Former longtime Philadelphia Eagles offensive tackle Jon Runyan Sr. also parlayed his playing career into one on Capitol Hill.

The Republican represented part of South Jersey for two terms in a district now represented by Rep. Herb Conaway, D-N.J., that covers part of the Pine Barrens and Philadelphia suburbs.

Runyan is now a vice president of policy and rules with the NFL and his son Jon Jr. is a guard with the Giants. He did not respond to a request for comment.

Another NFC East player who went on to serve in Congress was former Rep. Heath Shuler, D-N.C.

Shuler, who played quarterback for the franchise now known as the Washington Commanders, parlayed his playing career into a congressional career in 2006 before being succeeded by Republican Mark Meadows, a later close ally of President Donald Trump.

Colin Allred, a former Tennessee Titan, also moved on to Congress, where he served until 2025.

This cycle, he unsuccessfully challenged state Rep. James Talarico and U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, for Sen. John Cornyn’s seat.

Cornyn lost his primary earlier this year to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton who now faces Talarico.

There have been several other top-name lawmakers who themselves were former professional athletes.

Rep. Anthony Gonzalez, an Indiana Republican who chose not to seek re-election in 2022 over political fallout from voting to impeach Trump, was a former Indianapolis Colts wide receiver.

Former Seattle Seahawks wide receiver Steve Largent — an NFL Hall of Famer — went on to represent Oklahoma in Congress.

Former Philadelphia Phillies pitcher Jim Bunning went on to have a lengthy political career.

He was elected to the Kentucky State Senate in 1979, Congress in 1986 and later the U.S. Senate in 1999.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., now holds his seat.

New York Knicks star Bill Bradley, whose number 24 has been retired in MSG, went on to serve New Jersey in the U.S. Senate as a Democrat in the 1980s and 90s.

He also mounted an unsuccessful presidential primary bid against former Sen. Al Gore, D-Tenn.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Ex-Nebraska Cornhuskers head coach Tom Osborne – who briefly played for the Redskins – also served his college’s home state in Congress in the early 2000s.

Former Rep. Adam Wyant, R-Pa., had a 10-year career in the early days of professional football. He played for the Greensburg Athletic Association in the 1890s.

Laverne Dilweg, an early Green Bay Packer, also represented Wisconsin in Congress as a Democrat in the 1920s and 30s.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Former Arizona Democratic Congressman Mo Udall — whose family is considered political royalty throughout much of the Mountain West — spent three decades in Congress after a brief stint with the Denver Nuggets.

Olympic gold medal-winning decathlete Bob Mathias returned to the United States after the Helsinki Games and represented California as a Republican for about a decade beginning in 1967.

World.title: Cajun Navy leader warns Nolan Wells' search area has deadly 'washing machine' currents: 'Lots of drownings'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

MISSISSIPPI – A United Cajun Navy leader who helped search for Nolan Wells says the water around where the teen was found is notorious for deadly "washing machine" currents, and water conditions the day he vanished were far from ideal.

Wells, 18, disappeared July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. A National Park Service ranger found his remains on the island's northwestern tip two days later, on July 6, after crews searched the area.

Wells' friends returned to the mainland that afternoon without him. Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter has said investigators believe Wells chose to stay on the island. It wasn't until later that night that his mother learned from one of Wells' friends that he was missing, and she reported it to authorities.

SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST

The stretch of water between Horn Island, where Wells was found dead, and neighboring Ship Island is known to locals as a "washing machine" because of its deadly rip currents, United Cajun Navy Vice President Brian Trascher told Fox News Digital. Authorities previously told the Associated Press that foul play isn't suspected.

"Yeah, there is some kind of nickname for it, and it's because they've had a lot of drownings in that area and on that island. And to the west, there's Ship Island, just another few miles to the West. And in between those two islands, there's a strong divergent occurrence," Trascher said. "And that area is called the washing machine by locals."

Based on conversations with people who were on Horn Island on July 4, Trascher said the rip current that day was "extremely strong," adding that the water off the island's northwest tip can go from shallow to deep in just a few steps.

NOLAN WELLS' HOMETOWN OFFICIALS RALLY BEHIND SHERIFF AFTER 'DERELICT IN THEIR DUTIES' ATTACK

While Wells knew how to swim and swam regularly, Trascher said a strong rip current can overpower even an experienced swimmer, especially if panic, sun exposure or alcohol are factors.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Trascher said one of the biggest unresolved questions in Wells' death is what happened between when he was last seen, around 4 or 4:30 p.m. on July 4, and when his body was found, calling it a "gaping hole" that still needs to be answered.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I've heard virtually no explanation, no eyewitness accounts. Nobody seemed to see him after that... there don't seem to be any photographs or videos of him after that time. So what happened? It wasn't dark yet. There was still a lot of people on the island... why did he just vanish and show up dead two days later?" Trascher said. "That is a question that needs to be asked. And I'm not suggesting that means that there was foul play involved. I'm just saying that there is a gaping hole in the story that needs to filled."

NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS

During a Wednesday news conference, attorney Ben Crump revealed that an area of "red discoloration" was found on Wells' head, but said Dr. Roger Mitchell, who performed an independent autopsy, couldn't come to a conclusion on a cause or manner of death "pending further investigation." An official autopsy into Wells' death hasn't been completed.

SEND US A TIP

When asked by Fox News Digital about the case, forensic pathologist Dr. Michael Baden said the head injury doesn't point to foul play.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"So that could be from bumping into something in the water. There's a lot of debris in the water, for example. It depends how deep it is, but it's describing a really superficial impact that could have happened before death or after death," Baden said. "What he's describing is a minor injury that could be... totally innocent."

Without having additional information, Mitchell wrote in his report that he couldn't rule out the possibility that "non-accidental factors contributed to or caused the death."

World.title: Here's what you missed from Trump's first WHCA Dinner as president: 5 takeaways from his night with the press
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump attended the annual White House Correspondents Association (WHCA) Dinner Friday night for the first time in either of his two presidential terms.

The event was rescheduled from its original April 25 date after a crazed gunman allegedly tried to assassinate the 47th president, bull rushing security with several weapons and firing a shot before he was taken into custody.

Here are five top highlights from the dinner:

TRUMP HEADS BACK TO CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER MONTHS AFTER GUNFIRE FORCED EVACUATION

1. Journalists, Trump share heartfelt moments

Trump and the press typically find themselves at odds, and while Friday night had its share of uncomfortable moments, both sides were able to find some common ground — especially after sharing a scary moment at the originally scheduled dinner in April.

Before presenting one of the many awards of the night, ABC's Jon Karl thanked the president for his attendance.

"Mr. President, I want to say it matters that you came here tonight," said Karl. "For more than 100 years, presidents have chosen to sit in a room of reporters who asked tough and often uncomfortable questions, and who report without fear or favor. It's important. Thank you for being here."

TRUMP PRAISES PRESS AFTER WHCD SHOOTING, SAYS UNITY AT DINNER WAS 'BEAUTIFUL'

WHCA outgoing President and the dinner's emcee Weijia Jiang also had kind words for the president, just before she introduced him to speak and after discussing the importance of the First Amendment.

"President Trump, I've covered you for a long time, and so have many reporters in this room. When we ask questions, you push back, you give us answers and we push back," she said. "You have always been a deal guy. Well, that's the deal. And the First Amendment is a done deal. And that's what we toast tonight. The freedoms that brought us back together even after they were threatened."

"So let's raise a glass to what makes ours a beautiful country."

Later in the night, Trump concluded his speech with a warm message for the press delivered in his own style.

JOURNALISTS DEMAND WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' ASSOCIATION 'SPEAK TRUTH TO POWER' IN NEW DINNER WITH TRUMP

"I just want to say, this room — I have tremendous respect for the people in this room," Trump said.

"Sometimes I don’t feel you treat me fair, maybe you do, I don’t know," he continued. "I don’t feel that. But sometimes you treat me fairly, and I have a lot of respect for your profession. It’s amazing. And I just want to thank you for having me, and it’s been fun."

2. Trump razzes the press and members of his cabinet

Trump made a series of jokes throughout his speech, some targeting the press, and others targeting people he appointed to positions of power.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was on the receiving end of a quip from the 47th president after Trump told attendees he hoped they enjoyed their beef tenderloin dinner.

"I want you all to know that Bobby Kennedy, who's right here, personally ran over the cow with his car," he jabbed. "And he cut it up and he brought it here for you to eat tonight."

Kennedy is well known for his eccentric history with animals, including once saying he captured a raccoon and cut its genitals off, viral videos of him catching dangerous snakes and once using a chainsaw to remove the head of a dead whale that washed up on Cape Cod.

"Bobby also suggested an appetizer featuring his favorite cut of male raccoon roadkill. But we drew the line at that," the president went on. "We said, 'No, we're not doing that.'"

Kennedy is also known for pushing a more red-meat centric diet and has embraced the push for restaurants to use beef tallow to fry their food instead of seed oils.

Trump also joked about the shooting at the first WHCA dinner earlier this year, which pro-MAGA rapper Nikki Minaj attended.

"But after hearing the gunshots, many people yelled, ‘get down, get down!’ Which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking, do you believe? Get down! She's the only one that really understood what that meant," Trump joked, earning laughter from the tough crowd.

Throughout his speech, he repeatedly used one of his famous phrases — referring to the press as "fake news," but took some direct shots at certain outlets and figures.

He unexpectedly flipped the script in a misdirection from what seemed like an update on the Iran war.

"A once feared and powerful regime that relentlessly attacked America has finally been toppled," he said. "Their former leaders have been removed and they’re now being run by a gay dictator facing internal divisions. But I, for one, wish Bari Weiss all the best at CBS News."

Trump's nemesis, Kaitlan Collins of CNN, was also on the receiving end of a brutal blow.

"I thought Kaitlan Collins had really made it big with a major new sponsorship, but then I informed her that it wasn't her on the Bud Light can, it was Dylan Mulvaney," he said, referencing the beer brand's failed marketing campaign featuring a transgender influencer.

3. Unsuspecting Todd Blanche yanked into mentalist Oz Pearlman's routine

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, who is currently in the confirmation process to take on the job full-time, became part of mentalist Oz Pearlman's routine to close out the night.

In a convoluted bit, Oz asked Blanche to make up an amount of money he had in his wallet. Blanche said $130, but Oz guessed the correct amount — $85. Then, Oz asked a man sitting next to Blanche to choose a single bill from Blanche's wallet, and then had Blanche sign it. Blanche signed it, and was instructed to sit on it.

For the remainder of the act, Oz asked members of the crowd to stand — including Fox News' Kevin Corke — and dream up a person dead or alive who they wished they could interview. He guessed several of interview subjects' names correctly, and even enlisted the help of a member of the crowd, who also made correct guesses.

After that, he enlisted audience members, once of which was former National Security Administrator and current U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Watlz, to chose important dates and random numbers. When multiplied, those numbers equaled 53,670,682.

Oz then turned back to Blanche and asked him to stand up and look at the serial number of the bill he was sitting on. Audience members were stunned to find out it was No. 53670682.

4. Trump reveals how he communicates with the press

Trump explained that he was tired of asking his communications team, Karoline Leavitt and Steven Cheung, if he had received any calls from the press. So instead he started to give journalists his direct line, which has turned out to be a disaster.

"That was the stupidest thing I ever did," the president said. "I'm getting a call every 3.7 minutes."

"Every once in a while, it'll be one of the people in this room that I like and I'll pick it up," he said, referencing taking phone calls from Fox News' Jacqui Heinrich and joking that she only wants to discuss "horrible" subjects.

But he said that other callers are from outlets that he has never heard of or are just starting out.

"You know, I pick up every once in a while, 'hello, I'm from Reno, Nevada. We're a startup paper. We're calling us the Reno Express,'" Trump continued. "I'll say, 'Do you believe it, I'm the president of the United States.'"

"'Mr. President, could I have your views on Iran?' And I just hang up," Trump continued. "No, I get the craziest calls. I mean, some of them. My wife said, I can't believe you do this. This is a hell of a way to live."

5. Trump announces he WILL attend the 2027 WHCA Dinner, unless...

Trump had never attended the WHCA Dinner in either of his two presidencies, a total of five years, breaking with long-held tradition for a night of comradery with the press and government officials. His attendance Friday night was a major storyline — especially after the event in April was foiled by a lone gunman.

The president laid his plans for next year towards the conclusion of his hour-and-four-minute remarks.

"It's an honor to do it," Trump said of his attendance. "I've been to it numerous times, but as president, I haven't been here, and I'm glad."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump expects to attend again in 2027, but joked that his decision could depend on how the press behaves.

"They said, 'Would you do it next year?' I said, 'I will be back next year,'" Trump said. "Now if you get really, really nasty, maybe not. I don't know. But we're going to be back next year."

Trump attended the WHCA Dinner in 2011 and 2015, when he was a successful businessman, real estate tycoon and reality television personality.

Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., is questioning whether President Donald Trump's preferred candidate to succeed the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — his sister, Darline Graham — is even eligible to appear on South Carolina's Republican primary ballot.

"She has no record and I'm not even sure that she's qualified to be on the ballot," Mace told Fox News Digital.

Her comments come as Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., announced on Fox News that she will enter next month’s special primary election to run for a full term in the Senate.

DARLINE GRAHAM REVEALS WHAT TRUMP TOLD HER INSIDE OVAL OFFICE AFTER BROTHER LINDSEY'S DEATH

"Obviously I feel for her and losing Lindsey Graham — the entire state is mourning right now," Mace said of Graham.

"It's admirable and honorable what she's done to take the wings for the next six months, but she has no records and I am not even sure she's qualified to be on the ballot," she repeated.

Mace isn’t alone in her concerns over Graham’s qualifications to serve a full-term. Local South Carolina GOP Chairman CJ Westfall said in a statement that he is pursuing a formal determination of whether Graham meets the party’s qualifications to run.

He said the request followed conversations with local voters about Graham’s qualifications, including concerns over her lack of political experience and her voting record — concerns Mace shares.

"It's not clear that she's voted in enough Republican primary elections to be on the ballot," Mace said when asked why Graham may not be qualified.

MACE SNUBS TRUMP'S PREFERRED SENATE CANDIDATE, BACKS RALPH NORMAN INSTEAD

"By new state election laws of July of this year, you had to have voted in the last two of the last three Republican primaries and it's not clear she has."

Mace has instead chosen to endorse Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., for the Senate seat.

"He's a tried-and-true conservative," Mace said. "He doesn't bend, he does not back down, and he has a 100% conservative voting record.

"We have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to get a conservative into the U.S. Senate in this seat. We're not going to have this opportunity again in a while."

REP RALPH NORMAN ENTERS SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE DESPITE TRUMP'S ENDORSEMENT OF DARLINE GRAHAM

Mace herself was widely considered a likely candidate to enter the race for the South Carolina Senate seat, but she announced Monday that she would not run.

Trump, regardless of any doubts of qualifications, threw in his endorsement for Graham to seek a full-term seat, posting to Truth Social after a White House meeting with her, "run, Darline, run."

While Trump’s endorsements have oftentimes been the winners of their respective primaries, Mace isn’t sold on the idea that Trump’s pick will influence South Carolina voters heavily.

"I think that you'll see that South Carolina voters seem to be a little more… they're conservative, but they're also independent," Mace said. "Independent conservatives."

"They vote the way that they wanna vote, not because someone told them to. And I think you'll see that in this race."

World.title: Meghan Markle's 'MasterChef Australia' controversy may be exactly the point: experts
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Meghan Markle's upcoming appearance on "MasterChef Australia" has already sparked debate, with royal experts telling Fox News Digital the backlash may be just as important as the episode itself.

The hit reality cooking series announced in an Instagram post that the 44-year-old Duchess of Sussex would be joining the show as a guest judge for Sunday's episode, writing that Markle will be "bringing her love of food, entertaining and seasonal produce to one of the competition's most memorable challenges."

In a press release, Markle, who filmed the episode during her visit to Australia with her husband Prince Harry in April, explained why she wanted to take part in the episode.

'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS

"What attracted me to the MasterChef Australia kitchen? Two things: my love of food and my love of Australia. It was an easy yes," Markle said.

"It’s such a great show," she continued. "I’m just really honored that I was asked to be able to be here with you and to be able to judge some of these meals."

The press release noted that the cooks will take on the challenge of creating "a dish fit for a Duchess" using some of Markle's "favorite seasonal ingredients."

MEGHAN MARKLE'S SHOW EMMY NOMINATION 'SOMEWHAT BAFFLING' DUE TO LACKLUSTER RATINGS: EXPERT

In a preview of the episode that appeared on Sydney's 10 News, Markle appeared alongside season 18 "MasterChef Australia" judges Poh Ling Yeow, Sofia Levin and Jean-Christophe Novelli.

Markle introduced her chosen ingredients, noting that the chefs had "quite the bounty her" and proudly sharing that her children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, "eat Brussels sprouts."

"That’s impressive," Levin said.

PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S HOLLYWOOD DREAMS HIT WALL AS EXPERT WARNS OF ‘TOXIC BRAND’ STIGMA

"Food and cooking to me is really a love language," Markle explained later in the preview. "I think it’s such a great way to connect. It’s something that can feel sentimental and meaningful and It’s how I, it’s how I show my nurturing and love for my friends, family, and my kids."

Following the announcement, Markle's participation in "MasterChef Australia" was quickly met with a divided reaction on social media, earning both praise from supporters and calls for a boycott from critics.

"Why? She’s not a chef??? Not interested!" one Instagram user wrote.

"Can't stand her. She's not a chef," another agreed, adding, "Why is she even on this show."

"Thanks for the heads-up and making it easier to avoid," one critic commented as another chimed in, "Definitely won't watch it!"

"First time since the beginning of this show, that I WON’T be watching, first time!!" another detractor wrote.

However, others expressed their excitement over seeing Markle's appearance.

"Can’t wait to watch it!!!" one social media user commented.

"I'll be WATCHING!!" another added.

"I know she will do a great job," a fan enthused.

"I CAN'T WAIT!! WE LOVE YOU PRINCESS MEGHAN," another supporter wrote.

"I love this for her… she is working and finding opportunities for herself," one fan added.

"All the people saying they won’t watch are the first ones who will be watching and later criticizing," another commenter wrote. "I can’t wait to watch! Love Meghan!"

Markle's appearance also made headlines and fueled debate online after a report claimed her team requested that she not be referred to as "royalty" during filming.

The polarized reaction to Markle's latest gig underscores a familiar pattern for the Duchess of Sussex, whose post-royal ventures have often generated as much controversy as publicity.

Royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital the attention surrounding Markle's appearance, whether positive or negative, could ultimately benefit both the duchess and the cooking competition.

"Every time Meghan’s name gets in the papers, even if it is negative, it builds up the power of her brand," he said. "It also helps to hype the show before it starts."

"She was chosen as a guest judge to boost the ratings of the show," Fitzwilliams added.

While Markle's role has prompted questions about her qualifications, British broadcaster Helena Chard argued that professional cooking experience isn't necessarily a requirement for a celebrity guest judge.

"I don’t believe she’s a qualified chef. But then, they’ve had Steve Irwin as a guest judge before and he wasn’t a chef either," she pointed out. "So it’s not really about culinary credentials."

CLICK HERE TO 

The "Suits" alum's guest judging stint marks her latest foray into the food and lifestyle world. In March 2025, Markle's "With Love, Meghan" lifestyle and reality show premiered on Netflix. In the show, Meghan shared cooking, gardening and entertaining tips alongside celebrity guests. "With Love, Meghan" also served as a launchpad for her As Ever lifestyle brand.

In January 2026, Netflix reportedly canceled the show after two seasons and later announced that it was ending its partnership with the As Ever brand though Markle and Prince Harry retained a first-look production deal with the streamer. However, "With Love, Meghan" recently received a surprise Daytime Emmy Award nomination for outstanding lifestyle series. "Meghan does have an interest in food and entertaining," Chard noted. "So from a PR perspective, appearing on ‘MasterChef Australia’ alongside well-known hosts, strengthens her brand."

While Chard saw the guest judging role as a natural fit, other royal experts told Fox News Digital that the response illustrates the challenges Markle continues to face with public perception after stepping away from royal life.

"People are talking more about why she's judging than what she's judging," royal reporter Kinsey Schofield said. "An image reset only works if the audience buys into the new image, and right now many viewers still see a disconnect between Meghan's branding and her actual experience or authority in this space."

"Social media always amplifies the loudest voices," the "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered" host continued. "That said, there does seem to be a broader sense of Meghan fatigue. Every project arrives carrying years of baggage, and that's a challenge most celebrities simply don't have. She isn't launching from a blank slate. She's launching from a very divided public reputation."

Fitzwilliams agreed, saying there have been "sufferers from Meghan fatigue for some time" and that "a great many viewers feel this way."

"Lifestyle is aspirational, it's lucrative, and it gives celebrities tremendous control over their image," Schofield said. "The problem is that audiences don't just buy recipes or table settings anymore. They're buying authenticity."

Fitzwilliams shared his view that Markle's cameo is also tied to her broader business ambitions. "She is returning to food in the hope this boosts sales of the As Ever products," he said.

Schofield said that the guest judge appearance may not deliver the hoped-for results, arguing that every project that Markle takes on is now judged through the lens of the duchess herself.

"Meghan has had several opportunities to reinvent herself since leaving royal life, and the pattern has remained the same… enormous publicity followed by polarized reactions," she told Fox News Digital. "One television appearance probably won't rewrite that narrative overnight."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"People often react to the brand before they react to the product," she added. "That's the downside of building such a personality-driven business model. Every project becomes less about the content itself and more about whether people have bought into Meghan as the person selling it."

Beyond the public reaction, some royal experts questioned whether audiences would view her as a credible choice to critique contestants on "MasterChef Australia."

"Celebrity guest judges aren't expected to have Michelin stars, but they do need to bring something credible to the table," Schofield said. "Meghan's challenge is that she's still trying to establish herself as an authority in this space while much of the audience sees her as someone playing a part."

Royal expert Hilary Fordwich shared her opinion that Markle's divisive public image makes her guest appearance different from most casting decisions.

"Meghan is so polarizing that while such an appearance would be low-risk for any regular celebrity, it is likely to backfire," she said, adding that the duchess "has no credentials" and "doesn't come across as authentic."

"Given the failure of her previous cooking attempts, with lackluster ratings, this is all she can do now which is to be involved in a show which is already a success," Fordwich said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

However, royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner shared a more optimistic outlook on Markle's latest endeavor.

"Meghan is a master at reinventions, keeping herself in the public eye, and ‘MasterChef Australia’ is the latest platform to succumb to the real values of the lady and obviously cooking is one of many talents," he said.

Turner pointed to Markle's previous charitable work with the Hubb Community Kitchen, which was established in the wake of London's devastating Grenfell Tower fire. In June 2017, a fire ignited in the 24-story Grenfell Tower apartment block which killed 72 people and displaced hundreds of residents. After becoming involved with the community kitchen in 2018, Markle cooked alongside local women and helped publish a charity cookbook that raised money to support the initiative.

The royal expert told Fox News Digital that he also believed Markle would resonate with Australian audiences.

"Australia is a country which values people who have initiative and drive, and Meghan has that people's touch to support and offer cookery as one of her skill bases," he said.

For all the debate surrounding Markle's guest judging role, experts said the real question is whether the attention translates into viewers.

Schofield believes Markle's appearance could prove beneficial for "MasterChef Australia" if the buzz prompts audiences to tune in.

"Meghan guarantees headlines, and headlines translate into curiosity," she said. "Whether that curiosity becomes ratings or resentment is the million-dollar question. Producers know controversy can be good for television, but only if viewers stay for the episode instead of switching it off."

World.title: Trump orders signage warning visitors of ‘inaccurate information’ at Smithsonian
World.content:
While he continues to seek control of the exhibits inside the Smithsonian Institution’s museums, President Donald Trump is trying a new tactic in the front yard.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The president on Friday ordered that “warning” signs be placed in front of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History to inform visitors of the “inaccurate information presented in the Museum.”

The executive order comes after a White House report released July 4 claimed the museum “cannot be trusted to tell America’s story honestly and in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic.”

Trump said in March 2025 that he intended to force changes at the Smithsonian Institution, signing an executive order that sought to target federal funding for programs that present “divisive narratives” and “improper ideology.”

In his order on Friday, Trump wrote that the “Smithsonian leadership does not present American history as a shared national inheritance to be taught and celebrated, but instead views American history as a ‘prime tool’ to advance ideas of social justice and the radical transformation of our society.”

He wrote that the leadership of both the institution and of the museum “cannot be trusted to tell America’s story with honesty and gratitude.”

Trump directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to work alongside the National Park Service to install “temporary signage along the NPS-maintained sidewalks and walkways used by the public to access the Museum.”

The signage will “inform visitors” of the July 4 report and Trump’s demand that the report findings be enforced in accordance with his March 2025 executive order, Trump wrote.

Trump said that the signage will correct “inaccurate information presented in the Museum” and direct visitors to “locations and resources for accurate information regarding America’s history.”

The president directed that Burgum, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and the administrator of the General Services Administration alongside the assistant to the president for domestic policy shall “use all available authorities” to promote the order’s policies.

The Smithsonian declined to comment on Friday.

Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch defended the institution’s work in an email to NBC News earlier this month, writing that the White House’s report “is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History.”

“At the Smithsonian, our work is driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America’s story,” Bunch wrote.

He added that the institution remains “focused on what grounds us: a steadfast commitment to scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy, and integrity.”

World.title: Trump administration concedes that it canceled research grants in blue states
World.content:
The Trump administration admitted that it terminated nearly 300 federal research grants “solely because” the projects were connected to states that voted against President Donald Trump in 2024 and had two Democratic senators in office, according to court filings.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The administration made the admission in a court filing this month responding to a lawsuit brought by University of California researchers challenging the cancellation.

In the filing, the administration wrote as an undisputed statement of fact that on a list of more than 2,300 financial assistance awards across the Department of Energy, 624 grants on these lists were designated either “termination” or “cancel.”

Of those 624 grants, Jeff Novak, the principal deputy general counsel of the Department of Energy, wrote that in October 2025 the Office of Management and Budget identified 284 specific grants that were marked to be terminated.

Novak wrote that with one exception, “the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing Senators.”

Novak added that the remaining 340 grants proposed for termination were ultimately not canceled in October 2025 nor since then.

“All such grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election or has at least one Republican-caucusing Senator,” Novak wrote of the unterminated grants.

Novak wrote that the decision to cancel the grants listed in the October notice tranche — those 284 — was not “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor.”

“DOE accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, i.e., whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State,” Novak wrote.

He added that the Department of Energy “will not contend that it looked beyond the prime grantee(s) to consider the political identity or geographic distribution of downstream beneficiaries of the grant funds.”

The New York Times first reported this filing.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Department of Energy argued in a statement Friday that court filings did not show that termination decisions were made on a political basis.

“That is a misrepresentation of the court filing and of Mr. Novak’s words,” Ben Dietderich, press secretary for the Energy Department, said in a statement. “None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations. Secretary Wright has explained this numerous times in briefings on Capitol Hill.”

In an appearance before the House Science, Space and Technology Committee in June, Energy Secretary Chris Wright denied that decisions made around grant cancellations were partisan.

“No decisions were made on politics. I keep hearing that charge. It’s bulls---t. We’re going to say it a million times,” Wright said.

In a social media post in October, when the 284 grants were canceled, OMB Director Russ Vought wrote, “Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being cancelled.”

Vought listed 16 states where projects were canceled, including California, New York, Colorado, Vermont and New Jersey, among others.

The filing comes as the Office of Management and Budget proposed a new rule that would allow political appointees to gain unprecedented control over the $1 trillion per year that is provided by federal grants.

The office argues that the rule is meant to ensure that grants align with the sitting president’s priorities and to improve oversight. The rule proposes that political appointees screen grant applications to ensure they do not “promote anti-American values,” and they could terminate grants they saw as “no longer in the Federal Government’s interest.”

The 284 federal grants canceled by the Department of Energy are just one sect of funding that has been targeted by the Trump administration.

Since Trump began his second term, the administration has canceled grants for including mentions of DEI and has frozen research funding at universities like Harvard based on allegations of antisemitism.

Trump has also threatened to pull funding from states that do not conform to his policies. In January, he said he would deny federal funding to states that resisted his anti-immigration agenda and had so-called sanctuary cities.

World.title: Democrats poised to nominate Troy Jackson in must-win Maine Senate race
World.content:
BANGOR, Maine — Former state Senate President Troy Jackson is on the cusp of becoming Democrats’ Senate nominee in Maine, starting a 101-day sprint to Election Day in a nationally watched, must-win race for his party.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Hundreds of Democrats are gathering in Bangor on Saturday morning for a state convention to pick their Senate nominee after the primary winner, Graham Platner, ended his campaign earlier this month after a sexual assault allegation, which he denied.

Jackson is facing pharmaceutical executive Saundra Pelletier in his bid for the nomination at the convention. But Jackson, a veteran legislator, is expected to win the nod after delegate candidates supporting him dominated at county meetings last weekend and all of his major opponents dropped out.

The rapid series of events has shaken the Maine contest, where longtime Sen. Susan Collins, the only Republican representing a state President Donald Trump lost in 2024, is seeking a sixth term. Democrats are looking to net four seats and take control of the Senate this fall, and Maine represents one of their best opportunities to notch a win, at least on paper. If Democrats do not defeat Collins, they’ll have to pick up another seat in a state Trump carried by double digits.

Jackson previewed his case against the senator at rallies last weekend.

“In nearly 30 years, Susan Collins has told Mainers that she is concerned. She’s told us that she is troubled,” Jackson told his supporters at a Sanford rally, prompting one of his backers to remark, “She should be now.”

“Too often she’s stood with Donald Trump and the corporations that already have too much power,” Jackson later added, saying the senator voted for “tax giveaways to billionaires and corporations” and supported the nomination of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who then voted to overturn Roe v. Wade, the landmark case that had guaranteed a federal right to abortion.

“She stood by while the administration attacks federal workers, unions, immigrants, healthcare and the basic rights of Maine people,” Jackson said. “Maine does not need another six years of concern. We need courage. We need a fighter, and we need someone who remembers exactly who sent them to Washington.”

Asked to respond to Jackson’s attacks, the Collins campaign compared him to Platner.

“Troy Jackson is showing us the low-energy version of the Graham Platner campaign,” Collins spokeswoman Blake Kernen told NBC News. “He lies about the facts and makes empty promises without plans. That is why he came in third in the Democratic primary for governor a month ago.”

As his focus turns to Collins, Jackson must confront several daunting tasks, and with no time to spare.

He has to not only build a statewide campaign. He has to raise millions of dollars to compete on the airwaves.

Most of all, he has to convince huge numbers of Mainers who have repeatedly backed Collins for decades that it’s time for her to go.

Jackson’s path to victory

Many Democrats backed Jackson’s bid because they saw him as the candidate with the best chance of defeating Collins in November.

Supporters of Jackson, a former logger and longtime legislator from Allagash, a tiny town at the northern tip of the state, believe he will have unique appeal to working-class voters and cut into Collins’ margins in rural Maine. It’s the first time Collins, from Aroostook County, will be facing an opponent who also hails from the same sprawling area.

“The working class has been left behind and forgotten about,” said Shelly Mountain, a former Aroostook County Democratic Committee chairwoman and a pro-Jackson delegate at the convention.

“He is definitely working class and always — has always,” she emphasized again, “been a champion for the working class.”

A Democratic strategist with experience in Maine races, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the race and Jackson’s potential challenges, noted that a Democratic statewide win against Collins involves narrowing a likely loss in the rural 2nd Congressional District to high single digits.

“Being from Aroostook County and having shown a pretty significant overperformance in his state Senate races, [Jackson] is well-suited to do that,” the strategist said, later adding: “Of course, Sen. Collins is not a pushover. She’s done very well over the state but also particularly the 2nd District.”

Other Democrats noted that Jackson mainly has to run up the score in traditionally Democratic strongholds of Portland and other cities.

“There’s a path without expanding the map,” said David Farmer, a Maine Democratic strategist. He noted that Collins’ 2020 opponent, former state House Speaker Sara Gideon, underperformed the Democratic presidential ticket in Portland and other blue areas, due in part to a third-party candidate.

Farmer was optimistic that this year, Democrats would stay united.

“The reactions to Trump, to the ICE killing in Biddeford, to high prices, to the war [with Iran] — that solidifies Democrats so they’re less likely to drift than in 2020,” Farmer said.

But the Democratic strategist noted that when Jackson ran in the party’s primary for governor earlier this year, he struggled in more affluent parts of the state where Collins has performed well, even as they have shifted away from the GOP in the Trump era.

“He’ll need to do better in the greater Portland suburbs,” the strategist said.

The 2020 election provides some clues about Jackson’s challenges ahead. That year, Collins won re-election nearly 9 points even as Joe Biden carried the state by the same margin.

Exit polls show that Collins overperformed with independents, moderates and women. Independents who voted for Biden by 24 points also voted for Collins by 3 points. Self-identified moderates swung 24 points for Biden, but they voted for Collins by 7 points.

Women, who have long been key to Collins’ victories, broke for Biden by 23 points, but they voted for Collins by 3 points. Collins overperformed among women who didn’t go to college and limited the margin of defeat among white women with college degrees, one of Democrats’ strongest constituencies.

More challenges ahead

Jackson’s most immediate challenge is fundraising. His campaign announced Wednesday that it had raised over $600,000 in roughly 72 hours, surpassing $1 million since launching his Senate run on July 8. Collins’ campaign had $11 million to spend as of June 30, and Republican groups are gearing up to spend millions more.

Jackson is likely to get outside help, too, as Democratic groups that had abandoned Platner amid his scandals re-engage in the race.

Ahead of the convention, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, signaled that Jackson could expect full support from the deep-pocketed party apparatus once he clinched the nomination.

“We’re excited for Maine,” Gillibrand said, adding that after state Democrats “finish their primary,” the DSCC will “support whoever wins.”

Republicans, meanwhile, are gearing up to unload attacks on Jackson, particularly over his long tenure in the state Legislature and his ties to Platner.

Jackson and Platner were close allies and campaigned together, although Jackson quickly called on Platner to step aside following the sexual assault allegation.

Lance Dutson, a GOP strategist in Maine who worked on Collins’ past campaigns but is not involved in the race, suggested the contest resets without Platner, whose viral videos and impassioned critiques of the political and economic systems catapulted him to national fame.

With a “generic Democrat” as her opponent, Dutson predicted the contest would focus instead on their legislative records.

“People are going to be able to put his record up against Collins’ record. And there’s really no comparison between the two,” Dutson said, noting that Collins can point to “literally billions and billions of dollars” she has brought to Maine as a longtime member, and now chairwoman, of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee.

Collins herself has already started to try and define Jackson as out of step with Mainers.

She told NBC News earlier this week that Jackson “seems to be firmly aligned with the democratic socialists,” and she recently told CNN that Jackson is a “Bernie bro,” referring to his support for Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., during the 2016 presidential primary.

Sanders, who endorsed both Jackson and Platner in their primaries, stayed out of the brief race to pick a new Senate nominee. But he praised Jackson this week as someone who “understands the problems of the working class in Maine and throughout this country.”

Dutson, the GOP consultant, acknowledged that Jackson could have some appeal in rural parts of the state given his roots in northern Maine, but said his policies were still too far left.

“If you’re from Aroostook County, Maine, but you’re standing onstage with Bernie Sanders, that’s just a massive disconnect,” Dutson said.

Jackson has also drawn some headlines for his temper and heated confrontations with legislative colleagues. But his supporters aren’t worried that those episodes will hamper Jackson as he takes on Collins.

“I’m all for him getting passionate,” said Jim Gerritsen, an organic farmer representing Aroostook County at the convention, who has worked with Jackson on some pieces of legislation. “I’m all for him getting strong to fight for us because we know for sure that Susan Collins has never lifted a finger in her life to fight for the working class.”

“And, finally, we have a candidate here who is going to the mat for us,” Gerritsen said. “And that’s why we support him.”

One reason Democrats are relieved is Jackson wins them back voters like Carol Eisenberg, a lawyer based in Maine, who supported Janet Mills in the primary and was leery of Platner after he won the nomination.

Jackson “has my full support,” she said. “I would never cast a ballot for Susan Collins. I just wasn’t sure if I would be able to cast one for Platner.”

World.title: ‘Cockroaches won’: India’s education minister resigns amid massive youth protests
World.content:
India’s education minister resigned Saturday after escalating nationwide “Cockroach” demonstrations and an activist’s 26-day hunger strike demanding his resignation.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Dharmendra Pradhan announced his resignation on X hours before a third round of talks was set to begin between the government and an activist movement, the Cockroach Janta Party, which has demanded major reforms after the handling of an alleged exam paper leak triggered one of India’s biggest displays of public dissent in recent years.

“I hold deep respect for the aspirations, sentiments, and rightful expectations of the youth of this country,” Pradhan wrote on X. “Realising the dreams of India’s young generation has been the moral resolve of our political and social life.”

“Cockroaches won. Democracy won!” the CJP, a viral movement that began as an online parody of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), said in a post on X.

In New Delhi, crowds of students and activists were celebrating in the streets following the announcement, many of them waving India flags.

The scandal has been growing since May, when online leaks disrupted the NEET undergraduate exam, the fiercely competitive gateway to India’s medical schools.

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters celebrate the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on July 25. Sajjad Hussain / AFP via Getty Images

Anger among India’s young people has exploded onto the streets in recent weeks, with protests spreading from New Delhi to other cities around the country, including Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Ahmedabad. Authorities have struggled to contain the growing protests, with police deploying tear gas and batons against the vast crowds close to the country’s Parliament building in New Delhi earlier this week.

The CJP, named after a remark from India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant comparing unemployed young people to “cockroaches,” has been at the centre of what has become the biggest challenge to Modi in his 12 years in power.

As well as the minister’s resignation, protesters’ demands included compensation for the families of students who died by suicide after the exam paper leaks, and accountability over police suppression of their protests.

“The families of the children who committed suicide should receive compensation” of one crore rupees ($100,000), CJP posted Saturday. “And second, these police goons who acted on the 20th. Action must be taken against the police officers for that.”

“Remember, do not mess with cockroaches,” it added.

00:00 00:00 What's behind India’s Gen Z ‘cockroach’ movement 01:37

On Thursday night, Modi offered his first public comments in a video posted to Instagram. “I know the paper leak is not a trivial matter,” he said, announcing fast-track courts to prosecute cases involving examination paper leaks, while defending his government’s handling of the scandal.

But protesters said his response fell short of their demands for accountability and hundreds of people returned to the streets of New Delhi on Friday even as authorities shut 18 stations across the city’s metro network, disrupting a vital mode of transportation for its 23 million residents.

A 26-day hunger strike by activist Sonam Wangchuk had further galvanized the protests this week, after police forcefully admitted him to a hospital last weekend. He said in a post on X Friday that he ended his fast after appeals from dozens of members of Parliament and following “a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country.”

Wangchuk on Saturday called Pradhan’s resignation “a victory of peace, patience & perseverance.”

“Congratulations CJP, Gen Z of the nation and thank you all citizens for shedding fear and the fear of fear and rising up from every corner of the nation,” he posted on X.
