World.title: Evacuations ordered in Bordeaux suburbs as wildfires continue to ravage southern Europe
World.content:
French authorities have announced evacuation orders for three suburbs of the city of Bordeaux in southwestern France, as wildfires continue to devastate southern Europe.

 

Residents of Le Haillan, Eysines, and Mérignac have been told to leave the area immediately via planned evacuation routes.

An "unprecedented" wildfire has burned through around 19,000 hectares in the Gironde department this week, prompting the evacuations of around 110,000 people.

The blaze began in the town of Saumos on Tuesday before moving towards the areas of Le Porge and Lège Cap-Ferret. It has since spread east towards the Bordeaux metropolitan area, where smoke is visible from the fires raging in the Arcachon Basin.

Bordeaux has opened the Parc des Expositions exhibition centre to accommodate evacuees.

Two firefighters died while tackling flames in Mérignac on Tuesday. French President Emmanuel Macron has paid tribute to the pair in a post on social media.

"I extend the nation’s condolences, gratitude and support to their families, their loved ones and the firefighters of France," he wrote.

France has requested assistance to tackle the fires through the European Union's civil protection mechanism. The bloc said on Friday that planes and helicopters from Portugal, Croatia, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia would be sent to provide help.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has announced that Sweden was also sending firefighting aircraft to assist as part of the programme.

People watch massive plumes of smoke caused by wildfires in Le Porge, western France, Thursday, July 23, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Spain

In Spain, fires are continuing to rage in the Madrid area and in the province of Ávila, with tens of thousands forced to flee their homes.

The Spanish government has declared a national emergency over fires threatening communities in the regions, where more than 60,000 people have reportedly been evacuated.

Isabel Díaz Ayuso, the president of the Community of Madrid, said on Friday that the blaze affecting the area was "the worst" in local history.

Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said the priority now was to "safeguard lives, protect communities and fight the fires."

All levels of government are working together to coordinate resources to provide an effective response and help evacuees, he said, adding that affected areas would also receive governmental support during the recovery process.

Spain's Civil Guard has mobilised 650 officers, 60 vehicles, and two helicopters as part of efforts to help with evacuations.

According to EU figures, 1,254 fires have burned through around 254,388 hectares in Europe since the beginning of the year.

World.title: 'I do not want to replace models with AI': Fashion designer Steven Passaro plans industry revamp
World.content:
One of the most anticipated names at this year's Paris Fashion Week may not be one you've heard before.

 

Steven Passaro has earned praise and recognition from LVMH, the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode, and the French Ministry of Culture, to name just a few.

The French-Portuguese fashion designer graduated from the prestigious Duperré School of Applied Arts in Paris and the University of the Arts London. Before launching his eponymous label, he honed his craft at renowned fashion houses including Hermès, Loewe and Christian Dior.

In an exclusive interview with Euronews Culture, the visionary designer reflected on his creative process, his work, and the evolving landscape of the fashion industry.

Euronews Culture: You initially studied architecture. How did that experience influence your transition into fashion design?

Architecture was kind of my first love. I really developed my mindset around visualizing 3D thanks to the constructions we do in architecture. To me, it was natural to keep the skills of what I've been learning in architecture and translate them into fashion.

Your collections feature strong, structured silhouettes and rigid forms. What draws you to this approach?

The way I see it is there are two ways to dress the body.

In the West, they cut fabric to shape a body, and in the East, they have more of this approach to wrap the body with fabric. I really wanted to have this conversation in duality in the silhouette design.

I really wanted to build a language that you can evolve and adapt season after season.

The architecture allowed me to have this kind of tension between the two, where you sometimes have very strong, almost sculptural aspect in the silhouette, but also some fluidity.

The Spring-Summer 2026 collection called Moonlit Lover explored "toxic love" - secret love affairs, late-night obsessions, and illusions that end up hurting more than they heal. The Fall-Winter 2026 collection called Ethereal Shift delved into personal transformation, letting go, and finding meaning in a chaotic world. Where do you seek get your inspiration from?

The collection is always a continuity of the story of the previous season. In French we say "le fil rouge" [guiding thread] - to me, there is no break [between the collections].

I really wanted to build a language that you can evolve and adapt season after season. It's one big main theme, and each one is a different angle to describe the subject. There is a phase of transformation from a point A to point B, but I think it's very intuitive work at the end of the day.

There's some inspiration on psychology, on spirituality. Also what's happening in the world right now.

The last collection we just presented - I call it the “glimpse” - because it's that moment where you're going to step into something, you really want it, but you're also very afraid of it. It's the feeling I have towards the world right now, with all the political aspects, where there's a very good thing happening in the world, but also a very bad thing. It's this in between tension of “I want to, but I'm afraid to”.

So, hopefully, the next season will be a bit lighter.

Your design process differs from that of many traditional fashion designers. You rely heavily on digital 3D modelling before creating physical prototypes. What led you to adopt this approach, and what advantages does it offer?

At the London College of Fashion, we had a Department for Technology in Fashion, where you can learn about all this technology around the industry, and what people will use in the future.

I came across the software and it was like "Oh, that feels like what I was doing in architecture, but for fashion." I’ve always been a huge nerd, so to me, it was kind of natural to experiment with it.

The calculation became clear when I started to understand that I can make a pattern in two hours compared to by hand, when it takes me two-three days, or even more.

I like the craftsmanship a lot, so to me it was like "Okay, I'm going to save time on the pattern, to be only digital, and then have the time and the resources for the craft."

When you do couture and bespoke tailoring, you need time, and be hands on the [sewing] machine and fabric, so the advantage of using the 3D modeling technology was obvious for me.

Innovation and sustainability are both central to your work. How do your collections reflect your vision of environmental responsibility, and what practical measures do you take to make your design process more sustainable?

It is a very important topic for me. The entire phase of product development is thought with this idea in mind of how we can do less harm to the environment.

There is a lot of education that has to be done today for the consumer. Passaro on the presence of ultra-fast fashion

By using the "Style3D" software, we are able to do virtual sampling and virtual pattern cutting on a digital avatar. This, therefore, reduces the waste.

We use fabrics sourced in Europe that are from LVMH.

Such an approach allows us to focus on the craftsmanship. There's a lot to learn and we always try to improve the process in this sense.

In 2025, Shein opened a retail space inside BHV in Paris, a move that sparked significant public criticism. BHV described the partnership as a “strategic mistake” and ended the collaboration. What are your thoughts on the growing presence of ultra-fast fashion brands in traditional retail spaces and online?

There is a lot of education that has to be done today for the consumer.

People don't know how to consume actually good, because if you buy a t-shirt for €3, which I don't even know how it's possible to make as even the fabric does not cost this price per metre, after three washes is going to be dead. If you buy a t-shirt for maybe €15-20, you're going to have, perhaps, 10-20 washes, so it's going to be cheaper at the end for you.

Now in Europe, even in France, we have a new rule for ultra-fast fashion, which I think is important. There need to be regulations to protect the people and the environment. It's a very difficult topic to discuss because different people have different budgets to afford garments.

Many major luxury fashion houses are increasingly using AI to create campaign imagery and photoshoots. What is your stance on this?

When it's big brands or big corporations using it, I find it quite questionable, because they are the ones with the big budget for models, for photographers, stylists and everything else.

If they start replacing a human behind the images with only AI, then a lot of people going to lose jobs. I do not want to replace models with AI. I think it's nice to gather people, exchange ideas - you get more creative.

Listen to the feedback, but not too much. On launching own luxury fashion brand

If the big brands stop paying models, who is going to pay? Smaller brands. We cannot afford the fees anymore as the modelling agencies double or triple the fees, compared to a year before, for example.

The responsibility is at the different levels of the process. It's image reputation, industry and impact on other people as well.

You used to give lectures at the French Institute of Fashion, one of the world's leading fashion schools. What is the most valuable piece of advice you would give to young designers hoping to launch their own clothing brand today?

Do not run. It's pointless to run. Even if you have the checklist of “I want that magazine, I want that press, I want to be with the fashion week” or whatever - it's very tough.

You need to be smart on the product design. Make sure you find your audience. You need the right people that surround you: friends, acquaintances you make on your journey and business partners.

Listen to the feedback, but not too much. You need to have kind of a filter.

Take your time. Do not rush. The point is a marathon - not the sprint.

That would be my best advice.

Steven Passaro at the photoshoot for the Spring-Summer 2027 "A Glimpse" collection Sebastien Giraud / Steven Passaro

Watch the video in the player above for more from Steven Passaro.

This interview was edited for brevity and clarity.

World.title: Zelenskyy warns of 'massive' Russian attack within 48 hours
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned of a "massive" new Russian attack on Ukraine.

 

In a post on X, the Ukrainian leader said intelligence suggested Moscow had "readied missiles" for an attack "within the next 48 hours."

"Please take care of yourselves and pay attention to air raid alerts," he wrote.

It comes after Ukrainian authorities said Russian missile strikes on the Kyiv region on Friday killed at least 10 people and injured around 100 more. The strikes reportedly hit an arms exhibition where representatives of the Ukrainian defence industry were present.

A further five people were killed following guided aerial bomb strikes in Slovyansk, per Zelenskyy.

Latvia's foreign minister confirmed that the Latvian consulate in Slovyansk was damaged in the attacks.

Responding to the news in a statement posted to social media, Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said the strike on the consulate "underscores Moscow’s utter disregard for international law."

"Latvia has our full support," she added.

Zelenskyy to meet with Trump

Zelenskyy is due to meet with US President Donald Trump in Washington next week as the US and Ukraine continue to discuss peace proposals to end the war, which began following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he had spoken with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, about efforts to end the conflict.

"A good and important conversation about how to energize diplomacy and bring peace closer," he said.

Earlier this week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov sat down with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) foreign ministers' summit in the Philippines.

Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, second from right, attends a meeting with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. AP photo

According to the Kremlin, Lavrov used the meeting to warn Washington against continuing arms sales to Kyiv.

"Lavrov briefed his American counterpart on the actual situation along the front line and emphasised that it would be unacceptable to further arm the Kyiv regime," a statement from the Russian foreign ministry read.

Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Rubio said the pair had a "good," "frank" conversation but declined to go into more detail.

Asked specifically about the Kremlin's statement, Rubio said: "We sell arms via PURL, which is an initiative we have through NATO and that's what we're involved in. There's been no change to our policy in that regard".

"We want a peace deal. We want the war to end," he added.

World.title: Wildfire smoke is crossing borders as climate change intensifies Europe's blazes
World.content:
A national emergency declared in Spain, thousands forced to flee in France, and thousands of hectares scorched in Italy: wildfires are burning more often, and more intensely, as the climate changes.

 

And their danger does not end when the flames are put out. Smoke carries black carbon – tiny particles of partly burnt material – that can travel hundreds, even thousands, of kilometres from the fire itself.

"The pollution can blow quite long distances," Jane Burston, CEO of the Clean Air Fund, tells Euronews Earth. Some particles are small enough to pass through the lungs into the bloodstream, she says, triggering asthma in the short term and, over years, lung cancer, heart attacks, strokes and even dementia.

Burston pointed to Canada's record 2023 wildfire season as a stark example: an estimated 82,000 people died from the resulting toxins and pollution across Canada, the US and Europe, long after the fires themselves had stopped burning.

Jane Burston, CEO, Clean Air Fund Euronews

Wildfire smoke is an underestimated danger

Recent research backs her concerns. A study in The Lancet Planetary Health, covering 32 European countries, found that mortality linked to wildfire smoke may be underestimated by 93 per cent, because fire-related fine particles appear more harmful than pollution from other sources.

Separately, US researchers reported that global wildfire emissions of health-harming gases may run around 21 per cent higher than earlier estimates suggested.

Burston says drought combined with heatwaves, both intensified by climate change, is creating the conditions for fires to spread rapidly. "We're going to expect a longer and more intense wildfire season every year," she tells Euronews Earth.

Breaking the 'vicious circle' of climate change, wildfires and air pollution

Burston describes air pollution, climate change and wildfires as a self-reinforcing loop: pollutants released alongside greenhouse gases when humans burn fossil fuels raise temperatures, fuelling more wildfires, which in turn produce more pollution.

"We really need to tackle other causes of air pollution as well as the wildfires," she says, adding that cutting pollution also saves money for health systems and boosts productivity.

She calls for stronger early warning systems, noting that some regions in Latin America already use air quality monitors to detect fires before they are spotted visually.

Governments, she says, need to pair forecasting with clear guidance on when people should stay indoors, use air purifiers, or evacuate.

World.title: Wealth per adult rankings: How does Europe compare with the world’s richest countries?
World.content:
Wealth per person across the globe varies significantly as shown by the UBS Global Wealth Report 2026.

 

The US is home to 38.1% of personal wealth out of the 56 countries in the report which represent over 92% of the world's wealth.

Western Europe follows at 21.9%, while Eastern Europe accounts for only 3.3%.

Average and median wealth per adult also differ widely across countries with 18 of the global top 30 economies in average wealth per adult being in Europe. This rises to 19 markets for median wealth.

So which countries are the richest in terms of wealth per adult? And how much wealth per adult do Europeans have?

As of the end of 2025, Switzerland leads the global top 30 list with an average of €777,506 per adult. The US ranks second with €594,651 (or $696,277). Luxembourg (€559,170) is the EU country with the highest average wealth per adult.

Hong Kong, Australia and Singapore follow, with over €450,000.

Denmark (€446,959), Norway (€363,303) and the Netherlands (€354,673) are the other European countries in the top 10.

Average wealth per adult is also above the €300,000 level in Belgium (€348,382) and Sweden (€347,089)

No big gap among Europe's major economies

Europe's five largest economies also appear on the list.

Germany ranks highest at 14th, while Italy sits lowest at 23rd, but the average wealth levels are not too different.

Germany's average is €296,023 compared with €238,653 in Italy. France follows at €291,536, then Spain at €261,689 and the UK at €250,071.

Ireland (€268,312), Austria (€239,123), Finland (€178,610), Portugal (€167,188), Malta (€139,769) and Greece (€122,421) are the other European countries in the top 30 list.

Median wealth tells a different story

When wealth per adult is examined by median rather than average, both the amounts and the rankings change significantly. A median is the middle number in a list sorted from lowest to highest, or highest to lowest.

"The conclusion we can draw is that each market has a different distribution of wealth, therefore appearing wealthier or poorer depending on which segment of the adult population we look at," the report said.

Luxembourg leads the global median wealth list at €336,498. This is less than half of the top average wealth figure. Belgium ranks second but median wealth falls to €236,712.

Australia (€180,018), New Zealand (€176,460) and Hong Kong (€160,533) are also in the top 10, as they are in the average wealth rankings.

Denmark (€174,029), Switzerland (€124,310) and Norway (€119,569) are the other European countries in the top 10.

Big shift among Europe's five largest economies

The rankings change entirely among Europe's five largest economies. Italy has the highest median wealth per adult at €111,881, ranking 11th globally. Germany, in contrast, has the lowest figure at €45,679, ranking last globally.

The UK (€107,042), France (€104,106) and Spain (€95,290) are closer to Italy, making Germany's figure stand out as significantly lower.

When both lists are compared, Slovenia replaces the UAE in the median wealth ranking.

Heavy concentration of extreme wealth

The US ranks third from the bottom at €58,927, compared with second in the average wealth ranking. This is by far the largest single drop in the list.

Germany also dropped 16 places, from 14th to 30th. The drop is also above 10 places in Sweden and Singapore.

These countries rank significantly higher in average wealth than in median wealth, indicating a heavy concentration of extreme wealth at the top.

Japan climbs 14 places, from 24th to 10th. Malta, Italy, Belgium and the UK are other countries with significantly higher positions in the median rankings compared with the average. This points to a broader and more evenly distributed middle class.

The report emphasised that median wealth is known to paint a more accurate picture of the wealth levels prevalent in the middle of the scale.

However, all of these data tell us nothing about purchasing power.

Looking at broader regional terms, the US clearly has the highest average wealth per adult compared with other regions, including Europe.

It stands at €594,651 in the US whereas average wealth in Western Europe is less than half that. It is €287,884 Western Europe while this falls to €53,055 in Eastern Europe.

World.title: Niger still seeking stability after 3 years of military rule
World.content:
The military government in Niger promised social, security, and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.

The military seized power in Niger on July 26, 2023. General Abdourahamane Tchiani , who became head of state, justified the coup by citing the poor security situation, which he said persisted despite international support.

In the weeks that followed, the military government announced a transitional period that was to last a maximum of three years.

However, the political promises made upon taking office have not been fulfilled. The transitional government continues to hold all the reins of power, and the security situation in the Sahel country remains fragile.

In the Tillabery region in southwestern Niger, attacks by jihadists are on the rise. Thousands of people have been forced to flee their villages, plunging the region into a severe humanitarian crisis.

Niger's military government has struggled to end an Islamist insurgency despite promises to do so Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

"Today, attacks on the armed forces and the civilian population are significantly more frequent and violent than they were three years ago," Maiga, who lives in the city of Tera, which has a population of 30,000, told DW. Maiga wished to remain anonymous for security reasons.

"Life used to be better despite the insecurity; the weekly markets operated normally and supplies arrived regularly," he said, adding that at the moment entire villages had fled and schools are closed.

The independent conflict monitor ACLED has also said the the security situation has deteriorated since the 2023 coup.

According to the organization, the Tillaberi region remains the main hot spot for clashes between two rival Islamist groups, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and the so-called Islamic State in the Sahel Province (formerly ISGS). This rivalry has resulted in numerous casualties among soldiers and civilians.

In 2025, nearly 1,200 deaths were recorded in the region. For Heni Nsaibia, a staff member at ACLED, these figures attest to the scale of the security crisis affecting Niger.

The most recent major attack, on July 17, claimed the lives of at least 16 soldiers and 15 terrorists, according to Niger's state media, ANP.

"The situation in Niger has worsened, particularly in the Tillaberi region, where the death toll is the highest in the central Sahel," Nsaibia told DW.

Insecurity taking a toll on civilians

"We live in makeshift shelters and are defenseless against the elements; we take on small odd jobs to survive," a woman told DW.

"I used to be able to live with dignity from my work, but right now it's very difficult; even drinking water is a problem for us," added a local herder.

Young Nigeriens are torn between disappointment and optimism: In the youth assemblies, known as "Fadas," the topic continues to spark discussion. Some — like Fadila — believe that the situation is gradually stabilizing after the turmoil of the first few years.

There was much optimism in Niger after the military took over power three years ago Image: AFP/Getty Images

"For a while, it wasn't easy at all: Salaries weren't paid on time, food supplies… that wasn't easy. But for some time now, things have been going pretty well overall," Fadila told DW.

General Tchiani has emphasized that young people can once again participate in politics. "Before the coup, young people were excluded from decision-making bodies." But in the meantime, he said, an advisory commission has been established that includes young people. "So that means the concerns of young people are now being taken into account in decision-making bodies."

Just two days after the ouster of President Mohamed Bazoumin 2023, junta leader Tchiani announced plans to combat corruption and boost the economy.

But three years later, the people of Niger are no better off, noted Tahirou Garka, a close ally of Bazoum, and spokesperson for the G25, a movement advocating for a return to constitutional order in Niger.

"They have failed economically and socially," he said, referring to the military government. "People are struggling to find drinking water; there is no water, no electricity, no fuel."

What is the Alliance of Democrats for the Sahel? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Hamani Oumarou of LASDEL, a social sciences research institute based in Niamey, takes a different view. According to him, the socioeconomic situation has improved for a large portion of Niger's population, especially for those who are not part of the middle class or the elite.

"Households with low incomes have more money left over to feed their families," Oumarou told DW. However, Niger is also forced to import food at certain times of the year, which leads to a sharp rise in prices.

Rebuilding ties with ECOWAS

Along with Mali and Burkina Faso, Niger is a founding member of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), formed in 2023 after all three countries withdrew from the West African regional organization ECOWAS.

The AES has distanced itself from Western partners and is seeking closer ties with Russia.

Pape Ibrahima Kane, an expert on international organizations, now hopes for a rapprochement between the AES member states and their longtime allies in West Africa.

The military leaders of the Sahel Alliance support one another militarily and economically, but still face political sanctions by the African Union Image: Mahamadou Hamidou/REUTERS

He sees a positive sign in the fact that former Guinean Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate was elected chief negotiator for ECOWAS a few days ago. According to Kane, Kouyate seems to have been accepted by the AES.

"We are at the beginning of a promising process, as both sides are truly on the same page when it comes to starting talks," he told DW.

For him, economic negotiations should also play a role. Niger depends on access to the port of Benin and on its electricity supply from Nigeria and Benin, both of which are ECOWAS member states.

Reliou Koubakin and Ali Abdou contributed to this article, which was originally written in German.

Correction, July 24, 2026: A previous version of this article stated that Lansana Kouyate is Guinea's current prime minister. This has been corrected.

World.title: Europe wildfires rage on, forcing 200,000 from homes
World.content:
Hot, arid weather and strong winds have continued to fuel wildfires in France, Spain and Italy, devastating huge swaths of land and forcing mass evacuations. As national emergencies are declared, the danger remains.

As wildfires continue to engulf massive stretches of western France and central Spain, some 200,000 people have been forced to flee, with flames devouring forests and homes near Bordeaux and Madrid.

Firefighters have said that the blazes, the largest recorded in both countries in recent years, are so massive that they cannot be tackled head on.

On France's Atlantic coast, 44,000 people were removed from the Cap Ferret peninsula, many by boat.

Towns near Bordeaux, the famed winemaking town popular with tourists, were evacuated "as a precaution" as strong winds fueled approaching flames.

On Saturday morning, regional authorities further ordered the evacuation of three of the city's western suburbs "to ensure residents' safety."

In all, French authorities say more than 140,000 people have been evacuated in France's western Gironde and Landes departments.

In Spain, the Interior Ministry said 60,000 have been forced to flee.

Wildfires in southern Europe cause mass evacuations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU sending firefighting aircraft to France and Spain

Authorities in France say the country's two main blazes were sparked accidentally, however, as summers become drier and hotter the magnitude of such fires has increased exponentially.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who said the government would do everything possible to protect citizens, warned that a wind shift had transformed the Cap Ferret blaze into "a large, self-sustaining fire that is extremely difficult to bring under control."

"It is now moving east, toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area," added Nunez, who pledged, "We are going to reorganize our response so we can fight it from the ground and prevent it from advancing toward Bordeaux."

French President Emmanuel Macron called for European Union assistance on Friday as well as the mobilization of the French army to halt fires that have so far destroyed 22,000 hectares (54,000 acres) of land.

The European Commission announced that it is sending three firefighting aircraft to France and four to Spain in an effort to gain the upper hand.

This week's fires have injured dozens of firefighters and killed three of them — two in western France and one in Sicily, Italy, which is now also battling blazes.

Heat waves fuel wildfires across southern Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Spain declares national emergency

In Spain, the government has declared a national emergency as two of the country's three current fires, all burning near the capital Madrid, merge into one.

Madrid's regional emergency management services said the massive blaze has now reached "its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain."

The largest active fire in the region, in Guadalajara province, has already laid waste to some 32,000 hectares.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is scheduled to visit affected areas west of the capital on Saturday, as temperatures in the region are expected to top 39 degrees Celsius (102 Fahrenheit).

High winds are also in the forecast, which will make things even more difficult for firefighters.

NASA abandons comms facility amid Spain's summer of fire

The US space agency NASA on Saturday reported that it had been forced to evacuate its Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex (MDSCC), which is located in the region. The facility is one of three worldwide that allow the agency to communicate with spacecraft in distant parts of the galaxy — the others are located in Australia and the US.

"The safety and well being of our personnel is our highest priority and our thoughts are with the families and neighbors who are also experiencing the impact of the wildfires in the surrounding communities," said a statement released by the agency.

Wildfires raging near the Spanish capital Madrid forced the evacuation of a NASA deep space communications center Image: Gabri Solera/Europa Press/IMAGO

Spain, which regularly sees wildfires, has experienced an especially devastating summer. Earlier this month, fires in the south of the country killed 13 people.

Environmental officials say that 1,140 square kilometers (440 square miles) have already been lost to flames this year, more than five times the area burnt throughout the first half of 2025.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

World.title: Eco wins: Cities, creatures, and tech are saving the day
World.content:
From an AI-powered cute little pangolin, heat mapping to cool down cities and animals reducing wildfire risks by doing their thing, these real-world climate hacks are helping communities stay ahead of a changing planet.

Nature's own firefighters

Sometimes the best climate solutions have four legs. From goats and sheep in the United States to donkeys in Spain, grazing animals are helping reduce wildfire risk by clearing dry vegetation that can fuel fires.

Carefully managed grazing not only slows the spread of potential wildfires but can also create access paths for emergency crews. It's a simple yet effective example of how working with nature can help communities become more resilient to a changing climate.

Keeping cities cool: Reclaiming the right to a livable future

Young voices and urban innovators are driving change in the fight against extreme heat. Climate activist Che Chen is taking Taiwan's government to court because he believes access to a livable, cooler environment is a basic human right for his generation and those to come.

At the same time, urban heat expert Tzu-ping Lin is developing practical solutions such as wind corridors, greener buildings and heat mapping to make cities more resilient.

In scorching Taipei, locals seek ways to survive urban heat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One of the world's most threatened animals speaks up

Conservationists and storytellers are finding new ways to connect people with endangered wildlife in South Africa by helping audiences imagine the world through the eyes of a pangolin.

The cute, AI-powered creature speaks South Africa's 11 official languages, answers questions, reacts realistically and ultimately highlights the threats facing the world's most trafficked mammal, which is poached primarily for its meat and scales.

The initiative is driven by a desire to inspire empathy and action, showing that protecting biodiversity starts with understanding the species we share our planet with.

What if you could talk to an endangered pangolin? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: India: Education minister resigns amid student-led protests
World.content:
Skip next section 'Remember, do not mess with cockroach': Dipke

07/25/2026 July 25, 2026 'Remember, do not mess with cockroach': Dipke

When Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan broke the news of his resignation in a two-page explanation letter, the Cockroach Janta Party's immediate reaction — at least on social media — was not celebration.

The political pressure group simply posted an "update" on its core demands from the government.

"1.Dharmendra Pradhan must resign - *CHECK*

2. 1 crore to the families of all students who died by suicide - PENDING

3. No action against any of the student protesters - PENDING," the post said.

In a speech addressing protesters at Jantar Mantar, CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke said action must be taken against the police officers who injured women and students by the use of inappropriate and brutal force.

He named certain police officers accused of brutality and said, "if we can make a minister resign, what are you?" he said.

"Remember, do not mess with cockroach," Dipke said, adding: "and to the people of India, this is how a democracy should be."

Also in a moment of humility, Dipke asked supporters not to make him a "hero" because of Pradhan's resignation. "Don't make this mistake...The country has been ruined because of making one person a hero," he said, alluding to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

World.title: Iran war: Houthis vow response to 'dangerous escalation' by Saudi Arabia
World.content:
07/25/2026 July 25, 2026 Yemen's Houthis vow retaliation for Saudi strikes

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have accused Saudi Arabia of targeting civilian infrastructure, amid an escalating flare-up with Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia on Friday hit the Houthi-held port city of Hodeida with strikes, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said, in response to the rebel group attacking Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea as part of a maritime blockade.

"The Saudi enemy's targeting of civilian facilities in Hodeida and Kamaran island constitutes a dangerous escalation," the Houthis' Ansarollah media posted on Telegram.

"We affirm that these recent crimes will not go unanswered."

Houthi-run Al Masirah television said on Saturday that Saudi strikes had targeted facilities belonging to the state telecommunications corporation and Kamaran island, off Yemen's western coast.

The broadcaster reported that one worker was wounded in Hodeida while a woman was also injured on Kamaran Island.

The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, claimed that it hit "Houthi military sites" and destroyed targets that were posing a threat to commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

Riyadh said it would do everything necessary to protect its ships, warning the Houthis that if they continued "hostile acts then there will be no hesitation in responding."

For Saudi Arabia, a top oil producer, the Red Sea had emerged a critical shipping alternative to the ​war-blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Trump addresses rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner
World.content:
The event was originally scheduled for April but was disrupted by the alleged attempted assassination of Donald Trump. His hourlong speech combined jokes with attacks on members of the press.

US President Donald Trump addressed hundreds of journalists at a scaled-down and rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner on Friday night.

The gala was held amid heightened security measures, three months after the original event was cut short by an alleged attempt to assassinate Trump.

Trump delivered the speech at Washington's Waldorf Astoria, a smaller venue that held only about 700 people, instead of its usual venue, the Washington Hilton.

Trump jokes about possible third term

"Just like my presidency, the second time is always better. It's always better," Trump said. "And the third time will be better yet."

"I'm only kidding," he added.

Trump has repeatedly suggested that he would entertain the idea of a third term, despite the 22nd Amendment of the US Constitution barring a president from being elected more than twice.

US press freedom no longer a matter of course under Trump To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump makes light of shooting incident, praises Secret Service officer

Trump also joked about the incident during April's gala, when a gunman tried to storm a security checkpoint before he was stopped by security personnel before making it into the ballroom where the dinner was being held.

"After hearing the gunshots, many people yelled, 'Get down! Get down!', which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking. Do you believe it? Get down!" Trump said.

The president also praised Victor Gonzalez, the Secret Service officer who was shot during the April confrontation with the suspect. "What he did was amazing," Trump said. "We salute you and we thank you with all of our hearts."

What else did Trump say during the White House Correspondents' Dinner?

This year's events were the first Trump has attended as president. He did not appear at any correspondents' dinners during his first term.

Trump said he had not attended previous dinners because the press has treated him "unfairly," although he promised to come back next year.

The US president has long had a hostile relationship with many journalists and media outlets .

During his speech, he attacked some journalists, including CNN's Kaitlan Collins — whom Trump repeatedly complained about not smiling enough — and Josh Dawsey of The Wall Street Journal. Both were honored with journalism awards at the gala.

Despite those barbs, Trump ended his speech, which lasted over an hour, by saying that he has "tremendous respect" for the reporters attending the dinner.

"I have tremendous respect for the people in this room. Sometimes I don't feel you treat me fair. Maybe you do. I don't know," Trump said.

Trumps say comedian Jimmy Kimmel should be fired To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump vs the media

The Trump administration has filed lawsuits against multiple media outlets, barred the Associated Press from the White House ​press pool and limited journalists' access ‌to the Pentagon, among other measures.

Trump has maintained that the measures aim to improve accountability and address media bias.

Speaking in the Oval Office on Friday, he defended federal subpoenas — which were later withdrawn — issued to New York Times journalists over their reporting on the security of the new Qatari-donated Air Force One.

"We're not after journalists. We're after leakers. We're after people that are cowards, people that are unpatriotic, people that ⁠are treasonous in many cases. And the way ​you find them is through the journalists," Trump said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Starship completes 1st test flight since SpaceX IPO
World.content:
Starship splashed down in the Indian Ocean to complete its 13th test flight and its first since Elon Musk's SpaceX went public in June.

SpaceX's Starship megarocket completed a test flight on Friday, the first since Elon Musk's company went public on Wall Street in June.

The ship splashed down into the Indian Ocean, which was celebrated by SpaceX employees watching along from the firm's headquarters in Starbase, Texas.

"Starship is intact, floating in the ocean and transmitting telemetry!" Musk said on X.

This was the world's most powerful rocket's 13th flight.

Previous tests had ended with Starship in flames or exploding at splashdown, or breaking up in midair.

What do we know about the latest SpaceX Starship test?

Starship, which is around 122 meters (400 feet) tall, deployed 20 Starlink satellites into suborbital space.

After ​briefly contacting SpaceX's network of around 10,000 orbiting satellites, they reentered Earth's ​atmosphere and burned up as planned.

It was the 13th test flight and the second this year of the third-generation Starship, dubbed V3 Image: Eric Gay/AP Photo/picture alliance

The hourlong test "will provide critical data as we prepare to expand our Starlink constellation" of the company's satellite internet service, SpaceX said.

By the end of 2026, SpaceX aims to use the Starship rocket to expand its Starlink network with the latest V3 satellites, providing coverage in remote areas where traditional cellular networks are unavailable.

World.title: ‘Nekonomics’ o la gran economía gatuna japonesa
World.content:
El gasto en estos animales es de casi 16.000 millones de euros y tiene una cara oculta: el creciente número de estas mascotas sin hogar

El cariño que sienten los japoneses por los gatos se traduce en un gasto que este año ascenderá a 2,9 billones de yenes (unos 15.980 millones de euros), una cifra casi igual al impacto económico de la Exposición Universal de Osaka 2025. Pero esta cantidad no incluye la cara oculta de la economía gatuna: el cuidado de los felinos que se quedan sin hogar.

Las estadísticas de las mascotas japonesas han ocupado un lugar prioritario desde principios de este siglo cuando el número de gatos y perros empezó a superar a la población infantil. En 2025, Japón tenía 8,8 millones de gatos y 6,8 millones de perros, un total de 15,6 millones de mascotas, que superó en dos millones a los 13,6 millones de niños menores de 15 años, según cifras de la Asociación Japonesa de Alimentos para Mascotas y la Oficina de Estadística de Japón.

La magnitud de la economía gatuna es calculada desde 2015 por Katsuhiro Miyamoto, profesor emérito de la Universidad de Kansai y autor de un término ya habitual en los informativos nipones: Nekonomics, acrónimo de neko, gato, en japonés, y economics. El novedoso cómputo incluye el gasto directo en alimentos, servicios veterinarios o vacunas. También suma las cafeterías para sentarse acompañado de gatos, los videojuegos y otros productos audiovisuales, además de excursiones a 14 islas donde abundan los gatos.

La previsión para este año se acerca a los tres billones de yenes aportados a la economía en 2025 por la Exposición Universal de Osaka, el evento de seis meses en el que participaron 158 países y regiones de todo el mundo. “De esas cifras no nos llega nada a nosotras”, declara a EL PAÍS Naomi Furukawa, directora de Chiyoda Nyan to Naru Kai, una ONG situada en el distrito de Chiyoda, en Tokio, que en 100 metros cuadrados acoge 49 gatos rescatados en la calle o abandonados.

“Mientras las ganancias de Nekonomics benefician a quienes comercian con la imagen de los gatos, organizaciones de rescate como la nuestra dependen de donaciones y subvenciones públicas que casi nunca son suficientes”, explica la responsable del refugio. El céntrico distrito de Chiyoda alberga el Palacio Imperial de Japón y, a pesar de ser la sede de grandes corporaciones y bullir de gente durante el día, es el menos poblado de Tokio, con menos de 70.000 residentes. En 2011 fue el primer distrito en Japón en haber reducido a cero el sacrificio de los gatos callejeros o abandonados, el procedimiento más común para controlar la superpoblación de esos animales hasta finales del siglo pasado. Para la gestión actual de gatos callejeros la administración de Chiyoda recurre al método TNR (siglas inglesas para Trap, Neuter, Return), equivalente al CER (captura, esterilización, retorno) usado en España.

Gran longevidad

El distrito de Chiyoda paga también unos 150.000 yenes (unos 810 euros) para el examen veterinario obligatorio de los felinos cuyo amo ha fallecido y deben ser llevados a convivir con otros animales en un refugio. Al igual que la población humana nipona, considerada una de las más longevas del mundo, los gatos japoneses domésticos viven más años y entre los que se quedan sin amo muchos padecen enfermedades crónicas que encarecen su cuidado.

“El gasto en atención veterinaria por gato asciende a unos 200.000 yenes (1.010 euros) y a menudo tenemos que financiarlo nosotras”, añade Furukawa. Explica que los gatos callejeros han dejado de ser el problema más acuciante. “Ahora el problema es el aumento de gatos que son dejados por personas mayores que ingresan a un hogar de la tercera edad o fallecen”, añade. Su ONG también organiza jornadas de adopción que tienen éxito relativo debido a la preferencia por los gatitos. Cuenta que los vecinos más influyentes del barrio, la familia del emperador Naruhito y la emperatriz Masako, han aceptado en palacio gatos callejeros rescatados por su ONG en dos ocasiones.

“Que figuras públicas adopten gatos mestizos de refugio en lugar de comprarlos en tiendas, contribuye a normalizar la adopción de los animales rescatados”, concluye Furukawa.

World.title: Blood on Her Tongue: A modern vampire tale not for the squeamish
World.content:
Johanna van Veen’s gothic horror Blood on Her Tongue offers up a classic vampire tale with some modern contemplations.

The book follows Lucy Goedhart as she is called to the ominously named Zwartwater (black water) estate, where her sister has taken ill. In 1887, there isn’t much in the way of medical treatment, but Lucy’s sister Sarah isn’t fighting off a regular illness.

Sarah has become obsessed with a body found in the bog of the vast estate and since interacting with the 300-year-old corpse she has become increasingly incoherent, struggles with taking care of herself and has developed an insatiable hunger.

As Lucy tries desperately to save her sister, she finds that her sister’s husband, her sister’s doctor and childhood friend, and several other characters who are present at the remote manor house all have their own interests and motivations – some as dangerous as whatever condition is plaguing Sarah.

The book is not for those easily bothered by gore. The title – Blood on Her Tongue – is a pretty good indication of what is to come. Van Veen does not shy away from the horror elements, including two separate scenes of eyeball gouging.

Like any good horror novel, the macabre monster is not the scariest part. The threats Lucy faces are from the men surrounding her sister. Her brother-in-law attempts to seduce Lucy while badgering her to send Sarah away to an asylum.

Sarah’s doctor expresses his own interest in Lucy, pushing his vision of the future while supposedly devoting himself to his patient. The mores of 19th-century upper-class society may be the biggest piece of villainy of all.

In the tradition of Dracula, Blood on Her Tongue tells its story through letters, journal entries and newspaper clippings. The personal correspondence adds to the claustrophobia of the work, with everyone limited to an isolated house, but the media reports remind the reader that the world outside does exist.

The work is the second book from Dutch author Johanna van Veen. It was published in 2025 in English and became a USA Today bestseller. Her first book, My Darling Dreadful Thing, was nominated for the Bram Stoker Award for best horror novel. Van Veen grew up in the Netherlands as a triplet, something that influenced her writing about the sisters Lucy and Sarah.

If horror is your thing, Blood on Her Tongue will creep you out and keep you turning the pages.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Thousands cross finishing line as Nijmegen Vierdaagse ends
World.content:
The 108th edition of the Nijmegense Vierdaagse (four-day march) ended on Friday, with tens of thousands of walkers being welcomed with flowers by well-wishers.

British walker Simon Brownlee crossed the finishing line ahead of the rest of the walkers for the 27th time, local media reported. Brownlee, who completed the distance before 10am, told local broadcaster Omroep Gelderland that the walk “felt like home”. “I’m happy it is over and I can now relax,” he said.

Wheelchair participant Ronald van Dort was the very first person to finish, picking up his seventh medal for completing the event.

Over 45,000 walkers from 70 countries took part in this year’s series, which is proving increasingly popular among the young. Ten years ago, 7.5% of the walkers were aged 21 to 30, but this year their number rose to over 20%.

This year the event was marred by a fatal shooting just outside the area where the Vierdaagsefeesten, the street festivities accompanying the annual four-day marches, were taking place. One man has been arrested.

The shooting, and other crowd problems, led the organisers to cancel performances by urban scene artists such as Ronnie Flex and Lil’ Kleine because their presence was “attracting the wrong sort of people”, the AD reported.

World.title: Dozens of women forced into prostitution by Romanian gang
World.content:
Dozens of women may have been forced into working as prostitutes in Amsterdam’s red light district by a Romanian gang, Dutch police confirmed on Friday.

The statement follows a joint Dutch and Romanian campaign against human trafficking in the area earlier this month. Seven men were arrested during a string of raids on July 14 – four in the Netherlands and three in Romania. All were Romanian nationals.

Shortly after the arrests, police issued a video interview with one of the victims speaking Romanian, which has led more women to come forward and has resulted in other information reaching the police, the statement said.

Police now say they have spoken to several victims and say they believe more women have been trafficked. They too are said to be Romanian.

The women were lured to Amsterdam with the promise of high earnings but found themselves forced into working in brothels and handing over their earnings to the gang. They were also forced to pay “rent” for their rooms.

None of the men had jobs but were big spenders, buying expensive clothes and cars and gambling heavily, the statement said. The gang also treated part of the red light district as their “personal kingdom”.

Four men remain in custody in the Netherlands, one of whom was extradited from Romania. Another man may also be extradited soon, RTL said. They are all suspected of human trafficking and forming a criminal organisation.

According to the Parool, two of the suspects are half brothers aged 44 and 45 who have earlier convictions for trafficking in women in Romania.

More arrests have not been ruled out.

A year ago, Dutch and Romanian police arrested 13 people in a joint investigation into human trafficking and the forced prostitution of Romanian women, mainly in and around Amsterdam.

World.title: Singer Sophie Straat cleared of discrimination over mosh pit
World.content:
Discrimination hotlines in both the Netherlands and Belgium have concluded that Dutch singer Sophie Straat did not discriminate when she asked “all white men to step back” during two of her recent performances.

Last month at the Best Kept Secret festival in Beekse Bergen, Straat — real name Sophie Schwartz — asked for space for women, queer people and people of colour in the “mosh pit”, an area in front of the stage where fans dance chaotically.

She made the same request on Monday during a performance in Ghent, Belgium.

The Dutch discrimination hotline Discriminatie.nl said it received hundreds of complaints but maintains that Straat’s comments do not amount to discrimination against white men based on their colour or gender.

“The call only concerned one short, one-off mosh pit for these groups,” said the hotline. “Therefore, visitors were not refused entry to the concert.”

Belgian authorities reached the same conclusion after receiving some 200 complaints following her performance in Ghent.

“Although the statement may be perceived as polarizing or offensive, in this context it must be seen as a symbolic and artistic expression,” a spokesperson for the Belgian discrimination hotline Unia told the Flemish broadcaster VRT.

“According to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, artistic and political expressions enjoy broad protection under freedom of expression, even when they provoke, shock or offend.”

Hate messages and death threats

Straat wrote on Instagram earlier this month that she has received “a wave of sexist, antisemitic hate messages and (death) threats, some more explicit and creative than others”.

She has also questioned where the left-wing media has been in all this, saying the public narrative is being controlled by the right.

The singer, who was raised in a Jewish home in Amsterdam’s de Pijp neighbourhood and is known for her protest songs, has said she never wanted to exclude anyone but rather wanted to make room for people who feel unsafe in a mosh pit.

World.title: Youngster arrested for participating in sadistic online network
World.content:
Police have arrested a young man from Noord Holland who they suspect of being part of the sadistic online Com network “764”.

The public prosecution department reported the arrest on Thursday, saying the suspect encouraged underage girls to cut themselves and write his online name on a wall with their own blood—so-called “bloodsigns”.

He also is said to have prompted them to write his name on their bodies with a marker, known as“fansigns”. Both are practices within the Com movement—short for The Community—for members to gain prestige.

The suspect himself, who was also charged with aggravated assault, exploitation of underage girls and possession of images of sexual child abuse, was a minor at the time of the alleged crimes. Because of that, no further details are being released.

The Com network consists of various chat groups where members recruit vulnerable young people and force them to commit acts including assault, sexual abuse and murder.

The members, from all corners of the globe, then share images of these acts online in private chat groups, using such platforms as Telegram and Discord.

According to NOS, at least 70 Dutch people are involved in this movement known as “nihilistic extremism” because the incitement to commit such extreme violence doesn’t have a clear ideological motive.

The phenomenon is especially attractive to young men.

World.title: Dangerous drivers face extra surveillance under points system
World.content:
The police and justice ministry officials are working on a system which would see traffic offenders being given points for dangerous driving – which will lead to persistent offenders coming under extra surveillance.

Motorists who have collected six points for using a mobile phone while driving or not wearing a seatbelt would come under the tougher regime, RTL Nieuws reported on Friday. No start date has yet been set.

The points will be awarded in addition to regular fines. The number of points will depend on the seriousness of the offences and speeding tickets recorded by camera will not be included.

The new system is being devised in an effort to tackle persistent offenders who do not change their behaviour despite being fined multiple times, RTL said. Last year, almost 30,000 people would have had at least six points if the new system had been in existence.

“Research shows that people who don’t stick to the rules are often responsible for accidents,” Achilles Damen from the public prosecution department told the broadcaster.

The privacy implications of monitoring specific individuals are still being assessed, RTL said.

World.title: Ajax beat Vojvodina in Conference League qualifier, Twente lose
World.content:
Ajax kicked off their European football campaign with a 4-1 win over Serbian club Vojvodina in the second qualification round of the Conference League competition in Novi Sad on Thursday evening.

The simple win sets the Amsterdammers up in a strong position ahead of the return match next week. If Ajax win again, they will meet either Irish side Shelbourne FC or Estonian club Nõmme Kalju in the third qualification round for the third-tier European competition.

The Amsterdam goal total included one for 16-year-old debutant Mohamed Abdalla, who became the youngest player to score for a Dutch club in Europe.

There was disappointment for FC Twente, who are hoping to qualify for the group stage of the Europa League. They lost 1-2 at home to Hungarian side Ferencváros and will have to pull out all the stops during the away leg next week to remain in the competition.

If they do lose, Twente will move down to the qualification rounds of the Conference League.

PSV Eindhoven and Feyenoord have qualified directly for the Champions League while NEC is taking part in the qualification competition. AZ, as winners of the KNVB Cup last season, will take part in the Europa League competition.

World.title: Unilever backs London for food division secondary listing
World.content:
Unilever’s food division, which is being sold to US sauce and spice producer McCormick, will have a secondary listing on the London stock exchange, despite an intensive lobbying campaign to list in Amsterdam.

Unilever itself has been based in London, and listed there, since 2020.

Unilever said in a statement that the secondary listing is separate to McCormick’s plans to establish an international headquarters in the Netherlands and maintain Unilever Food’s R&D facilities and operations in Wageningen.

This “reflects its commitment to the European market and the critical role the Netherlands will continue to play in the combined company”, the statement said.

Economic affairs minister Heleen Herbert said in a reaction to the sale when it was announced in March that the cabinet had already discussed developments with Unilever and would talk to the new owner “such as about a listing on the Amsterdam stock exchange”.

Unilever’s ice cream arm, spun off in 2024, is listed on the Amsterdam stock exchange as the Magnum Ice Cream Company and is headquartered in the Dutch capital.

The sale of the food arm means there is nothing left of the original Dutch part of Unilever, which was set up in 1930 through the merger of the Dutch Margarine Unie and British soap maker Lever Brothers. Unilever now focuses on personal care and household cleaning products.

World.title: Three quarters of Poles support cooperation with Ukraine against Russia despite historical dispute
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A new study shows that, while most Poles were angered by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, they still overwhelmingly support cooperation with Ukraine and believe that Russia benefits from the dispute. The study, carried out by Polish state research agency CBOS, also finds that a large majority of Poles believe good relations with Ukraine will only be possible once historical issues are resolved. The polling was carried out this month in response to the ongoing diplomatic crisis that began in May, when Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. The UPA is widely revered in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-backed Soviet rule. However, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians – mostly women and children – were slaughtered during World War Two, often with great brutality. Zelensky’s decision sparked anger in Poland, where the massacres are regarded as a genocide (though Ukraine strongly rejects that label). In June, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest honour, which he had received in 2023. In its new survey, CBOS found that 59% of Poles support Nawrocki’s decision, while only 28% oppose it. However, they were divided over the consequences, with 41% saying it would bring Poland more losses than benefits and the exact same proportion saying the benefits would outweigh the costs. More broadly, 84% said the Polish state should react when another country glorifies historical figures responsible for crimes against Poles. However, when asked if Ukrainians have the right to honour their own historical heroes, even if those figures left a negative mark on Polish history, 44% agreed and 42% disagreed. At the same time, over three quarters of respondents (77%) said that good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past, but a similar proportion (73%) also believe that politicians on both sides “fuel conflicts between Poles and Ukrainians for their own political gain”. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Yet the survey also showed that, for Poles, historical disputes have not displaced security concerns, and in particular the view that, for Poland and Ukraine, Russia is a shared enemy. Some 75% of respondents agreed with the statement that “Poland and Ukraine should, above all, cooperate in the face of the threat from Russia, rather than focus on the issues that divide them”. The most frequently cited priorities in relations with Kyiv were security cooperation (61%), building good neighbourly relations (46%), commemorating victims of the Volhynia massacres (43%), strengthening Poland’s regional leadership (41%), and ensuring Polish companies participate in Ukraine’s reconstruction (40%). Just over half of Poles (52%) agree that “Poland and Ukraine have more common aims and interests than conflicting ones”, while 32% disagreed. A huge majority (80%) agreed that “Russia benefits from the Polish-Ukrainian dispute”. W ocenie społecznej zdecydowanym priorytetem w relacjach z Ukrainą powinna być współpraca na rzecz bezpieczeństwa – wskazało ją 61% badanych.📊 ➡️Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Wokół polsko-ukraińskiego sporu o imponderabilia i nie tylko":https://t.co/pIvYbu8gyz#Ukraina #relacje pic.twitter.com/LOpmAKNnXn — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) July 23, 2026 Based on the answers in the survey, CBOS identified three broad groups of respondents classified by their views of the dispute. The largest, described as “moralists”, accounted for 46% and placed greater emphasis on historical grievances. Among this group, 99% supported Nawrocki’s decision and said good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past. “Pragmatists”, who made up 34% of respondents, placed greater emphasis on future cooperation. Some 96% said Poland and Ukraine should cooperate against the Russian threat rather than focus on historical disputes. The smallest group, labelled by CBOS as “withdrawn”, represented 20% of respondents who were more likely to lack a clear view on Polish-Ukrainian relations. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Recent weeks have seen moves from Ukraine towards finding a diplomatic solution to the crisis. In early July, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha visited Warsaw to propose an “anti-crisis package” of measures. Last week, Zelensky himself outlined a five-point plan to alleviate the dispute, including opening up Ukrainian historical archives and permitting more exhumations of victims of the massacres, most of whom remain buried in mass graves in Ukraine. The Polish authorities have cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement, though also emphasise that they are waiting to see concrete action. Meanwhile, there is no indication that Zelensky will change his decision to name a unit after the heroes of the UPA. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. Police officers and rangers have stepped up joint patrols in Poland’s mountainous Tatra National Park during the peak summer season, following a spate of rule-breaking including swimming in the park’s lakes and ponds, driving cars and going off marked trails. Meanwhile, national park authorities have repeated warnings that bathing, littering and breaking other rules can damage the park’s fragile ecosystem. Local police officers have joined Tatra National Park rangers on patrols on popular tourist routes. On one such patrol last week, officers focused on education and prevention, reminding visitors not to leave marked trails or litter and explaining how to behave safely and responsibly in the mountains. They also checked that organised groups were accompanied by qualified mountain guides, as required by law. Fines for such offences range from 50 zloty (€11.55) to as much as 1,000 zloty (€231) in the event of environmental damage or multiple offences. Police said that all visitors encountered during the patrol were complying with the park’s regulations. However, they added that similar patrols would continue on a regular basis. The Tatra National Park, home to Poland’s highest peaks, and the nearby mountain resort of Zakopane are among the country’s most popular holiday destinations, with crowds taking to park trails in the summer season. The park, the most visited of Poland’s 23 national parks, welcomed a record 5.3 million visitors in 2025 and offers 275 km of marked hiking trails, including high-altitude routes that connect at several points with the adjacent national park in Slovakia. 🚨 Ukraiński Influencer wjechał nielegalnie samochodem na Morskie oko 🗣️: Jesteśmy pierwszymi ludźmi w historii, którzy wjechali samochodem nad Morskie Oko. In May, a Ukrainian social media influencer sparked outrage after driving a sports car along a road closed to traffic to Morskie Oko, a picturesque lake nestled between the mountains. As a result, he was banned from entering Poland and other Schengen Area countries for five years. Tourists have also been filmed entering Morskie Oko and other protected lakes and ponds, which is not permitted in the national park. This month, a group of young Dutch tourists were filmed bathing in Przedni Staw Polski in the Valley of the Five Lakes, one of the Tatras’ best-known hiking destinations. Witnesses repeatedly warned the group that entering the lake was prohibited, but they ignored the warnings, reports Gazeta Wyborcza. Park authorities have responded to such incidents by reminding visitors of the reasons for the strict rules. “Tatra ponds are incredibly delicate ecosystems. Cosmetics, UV filters, insect repellents, and bacteria entering the water can have a long-lasting impact on its chemical composition and the organisms living in the lakes,” they warned. World.title: Polish opposition PiS party set to split, with over 30 MPs being expelled
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. More than 30 MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, have effectively resigned after refusing to sign a loyalty pledge, party leader Jarosław Kaczyński has announced. The dispute centres around a more moderate faction in the party aligned with former prime minister and deputy PiS leader Mateusz Morawiecki, who is one of those now set to be expelled from the party. They have for months been unhappy with PiS’s move in a hard-right direction. 💬 Prezes PiS Jarosław Kaczyński @OficjalnyJK. 👉 Udostępnij pic.twitter.com/bycjE0Yq0f — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 24, 2026 “Around 30-something…of our group’s MPs have resigned,” revealed Kaczyński at a press conference on Friday. He added that their departures would be formalised at a meeting of the party’s political committee scheduled for Tuesday next week. Kaczyński’s announcement came after a deadline expired at midnight on Thursday for its MPs to sign a pledge of loyalty to the party that included a commitment not to be members of any external political associations. That measure was aimed in particular at an association called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) founded by Morawiecki in April. The former prime minister had always insisted that his organisation was intended as complementary to PiS, rather than a rival to it. However, many figures in the party saw it as an attempt by Morawiecki to create a separate centre of power, and potentially to use the association as a launchpad for creating his own party ahead of the autumn 2027 parliamentary elections. The right-wing opposition PiS party has threatened disciplinary action, including exclusion from electoral lists, against dozens of its MPs who have joined a new internal group led by former PM @MorawieckiM and intended to appeal to more moderate voters https://t.co/y62Cm361U2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 17, 2026 After PiS issued a resolution on Wednesday last week requiring that its parliamentarians pledge to withdraw from any such associations, most of its 186 MPs quickly complied. However, a group of between 30 and 40 who are part of Development Plus refused to do so. “Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” said Kaczyński on Friday. “And so they made the decision they did.” “In this situation, we cannot view the [Development Plus] association as anything other than a component of a plan…to split our party,” he added. However, although its supporters will now leave PiS, “we want to part ways without any animosity”, said Kaczyński. After Kaczyński’s announcement, senior figures from Development Plus made clear that no one from their association had resigned from PiS. They had simply not signed the declaration of loyalty demanded by the party. Later, Morawiecki himself held a press conference in parliament surrounded by his supporters. He claimed that an unnamed “small group of schemers” within PiS had been seeking to turn Kaczyński against him and push him out of the party. “We fought for the unity of Law and Justice until the very end,” declared Morawiecki, who said that his group included 40 MPs, one senator and three MEPs. However, three of the MPs are not members of PiS, and therefore were not expected to sign the loyalty declaration. Szanowni Państwo! 🟦Do ostatniej chwili walczyłem o jedność Prawa i Sprawiedliwości. Nie o stanowiska. Nie o osobiste ambicje. Nie o wpływy. 🟦Walczyłem o jedność obozu, który przez osiem lat zmieniał Polskę – budował jej bezpieczeństwo, rozwijał gospodarkę i przywracał godność… pic.twitter.com/PP7sOkzMHp — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 24, 2026 If the expulsion of Morawiecki’s supporters is confirmed, it will mark a major shake-up of Poland’s political landscape. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, PiS has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemyszław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Morawiecki, who was an international banker before joining PiS to become finance minister and then prime minister, wants the party to focus on more technocratic issues, such as economic development, rather than Euroscepticism and culture wars. That has led to frequent public sparring between his supporters and others in the party. In April, PiS threatened disciplinary action against members of Development Plus. Kaczyński and Morawiecki then reached an agreement that allowed the association to continue. But that uneasy truce has now fallen apart.
